¶ Que sit armatura militie spiritualis. tum sicut iacobus dicit in epistola. fed o- portet fidei coniungere christiane opera pietatis. Vos creditis in vnum deuꝫ om̄ nipotentem. creatorem celi et terre: patreꝫ et filium et spiritusm sanctum. Bene facit᷑ Et demōes credūt et cōtreminiscūt. Quid enim? Ubi sunt opera: ꝑ que fides vestra declaretur in christo formata? Ociosa et mortua est fides: qͥue sāctis et necessarijs non cōmendatur operibus. In christum credimus: bene est si christi sequamur ex- empla. Nam si christum pietatis operibꝰ non sequimur: frustra nobis de sola fide blandimur. Uos inquam creditis: et de- mones credunt. Auꝫ dilectione fides est christiani: sine dilectiōe fides diaboli. Re- cte creditis: si deum ex toto corde pro viri bus amatis. Si autem vere deum nō di- ligitis: fidem ociosam et mortuam habe- tis. Probatio autem dilectionis sācto gre- gorio testante exhibitio est operis. Sic enim loquitur in euangelio dn̄s. Si qͥs diligit me: sermonem mēu seruabit. Hec ergo est fides vera: bonis et sanctis operi- bus secundum christi doctrinam ordina- ta. Si fide simul et opere in dominum ie- sum creditis: certe scutum salutis in ma- nidus tenetis: in quo cunctos aduersari- os ipso largiente domino facile supabitis De hac armatura scriptum est. Sancti per fidem vicerunt regna: operati sunt iu- stitiam: adepti sunt repromißionem. Io- annes quoqꝫ ait. Omne qđ natum est ex deo vincit munduꝫ: et hec est victoria que vincit mūdum: fides nostra. Et princeps apostolorum petrus ita nos cōmonest di- cens. fratres sobꝛij estote et vigilate. quo- niā aduersarius vester diabolus tanquā leo rudiens circuit querens quem deuo- ret: cui resistite fortes in fide. Uera fides et confidentia in dominum nostrum iesum christum est armatura inuincibilis atque fortissima: cui nemo vnquam aduersario rum potuit resistere: sicut in libro parali- pomenon scribitur. Dixit rex iosaphat ex ercitui suo. Credite in domino deo vestro et securi eritis. In ecclesiastico etiam sic le- gimus. Qui timetis dominum credite il- li: et non euacuatitur merces vestra. Et iterum. In opere tuo crede ex fide anime tue: hec est enim conuersatio mandato- rum. Qui credit deo. attendit mandatis: et qui confidit in illo. non minoratus erit Curate nunc igitur fratres charissimi et summo studio semper elaborate vt scu- tum hoc fidei sanctis operibus formate contra omnes hostium vestrorum incur- sus manibus portetis: quia nunquā ab- aduersario vincitur: qui hoc scutu inex- pugnabili munitur. Hoc diuus confir- mans Augustinus d̄ verbis domini ait. Nulle maiores diuitie, nulli thesauri. nul- li honores: nulla huius mundi maior est substantia. quam est fides catholica: que peccatores homines saluat: cecos illumi- nat. infirmos curat. cathecuminos bapti- zat. fideles iustificat: penitentes reparat. iustos augmentat: martyres coronat: vir- gines et viduas et coniugales casto pudo- re ꝯseruat: clericos ordinat. sacerdotes cō- secrat: credentes in hereditate eterna cuiri sanctis angelis locat. Sicut in radice ar- boris nulla proꝛsus apparet pulchritu- dinis species. et tamem quicquid est in ar- boꝛe pulchritudinis vel decoris ex illa p̄- cedit: sic ex fide peccatum est: quoꝫiam sine fide impossibile est pla- cere deo. Credere enim oporitet acceden- tem ad deum. quia est. et inquirentibus se remunerator. Quamto autem quisqꝫ plus diligit: tanto in fide ampliꝰ profectit. Nāqꝫ fides sine charitate: est sicut proiectum in- utile. ac sine retinaculo scutum. O thesau- rus omnibus opulētior fides: que forma- ta in mente hominis mortalem immorta- libus comparas: demōes vincis et regna cunctaqꝫ dura superas fortiter et aduersa Fides est fundamentum omnium virtu- rum: sine qua nullum spirituale subsistit edificium. Fides illuminatrix est mentiū et principale spiritualis milite instrumen- tum. Nam sine fidei scuto diabolus non vincit̄: nec lasciue carnis īpetꝰ supraf. Cogitemus ergo fratres quā necessaria sit nobis fides ꝑ charitatē formata adsa- lutē siue q̃ in hac milicia nobis certantibꝰ neqꝫ victoria cōcedit̄: neqꝫ cōfidētia reser- uat̉. Fides em̄ est scutuꝫ in quo facilime hoste salutis nostre vincimꝰ: si ansā diui- ni amoris adiūgamꝰ. Dicit namqꝫ beatꝰ papa gre. Tūc ei veraciter fideles summꝰ: si quod v̓bis ꝓmittimꝰ. opibꝰ adīplemꝰ. In hac armatura fides cū sit fu̇damētuꝫ oīm bonoꝝ operū: cūctas oꝑatiōes nr̄as

What the armor of spiritual warfare is.

As James says in his epistle. But works of piety must be joined to the Christian faith. You believe in one almighty God, creator of heaven and earth: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. You do well. The demons also believe and tremble. What then? Where are the works by which your faith may be shown to have been formed in Christ? Idle and dead is the faith that is not commended by holy and necessary works. We believe in Christ: it is well, if we follow Christ's examples. For if we do not follow Christ in works of piety, in vain do we flatter ourselves about faith alone. You, I say, believe, and the demons believe. With love faith belongs to a Christian; without love faith belongs to the devil. You believe rightly if you love God with all your heart according to your powers. But if you do not truly love God, you have an idle and dead faith. The proof of love, as Saint Gregory testifies, is the performance of work. For thus the Lord speaks in the Gospel: If anyone loves me, he will keep my word. This, therefore, is true faith: ordered according to Christ's teaching by good and holy works. If with faith and work together you believe in the Lord Jesus, surely you hold the shield of salvation in your hands, in which, by the Lord himself granting it, you will easily overcome all adversaries.

Of this armor it is written: By faith the saints conquered kingdoms, worked righteousness, obtained the promise. John also says: Everything that is born of God conquers the world; and this is the victory that conquers the world, our faith. And the prince of the apostles, Peter, thus admonishes us, saying: Brothers, be sober and watchful, because your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking whom he may devour; resist him, strong in faith. True faith and trust in our Lord Jesus Christ is an unconquerable and most powerful armor, against which no adversary has ever been able to stand, as is written in the book of Chronicles. King Jehoshaphat said to his army: Believe in the Lord your God and you will be secure. In Ecclesiasticus also we read thus: You who fear the Lord, believe him, and your reward will not be made void. And again: In your work believe from the faith of your soul, for this is the practice of the commandments. He who believes God attends to the commandments; and he who trusts in him will not be diminished.

Take care now, therefore, dearest brothers, and always strive with the highest zeal to carry in your hands this shield of faith, formed by holy works, against all attacks of your enemies, because he who is fortified by this unconquerable shield is never conquered by the adversary. Confirming this, Saint Augustine says on the words of the Lord: No riches are greater, no treasures, no honors, no substance of this world is greater than the Catholic faith, which saves sinners, enlightens the blind, heals the sick, baptizes catechumens, justifies the faithful, restores the penitent, increases the righteous, crowns martyrs, preserves virgins and widows and married persons in chaste modesty, ordains clerics, consecrates priests, and places believers in the eternal inheritance with the holy angels. Just as in the root of a tree absolutely no appearance of beauty is visible, and yet whatever beauty or comeliness is in the tree proceeds from it, so from faith [unclear] is; since without faith it is impossible to please God. For one who comes to God must believe that he exists and that he is a rewarder of those who seek him.

But the more anyone loves, the more he advances in faith. For faith without charity is like a useless shield thrown away and without a strap. O faith, treasure richer than all things, when formed in the mind of a human being, you make the mortal equal to the immortals, conquer demons and kingdoms, and bravely overcome all hard and adverse things. Faith is the foundation of all virtues; without it no spiritual building stands. Faith is the enlightener of minds and the chief instrument of spiritual warfare. For without the shield of faith the devil is not conquered, nor is the attack of wanton flesh overcome. Let us consider, therefore, brothers, how necessary for salvation faith formed by charity is for us, without which, as we fight in this warfare, neither victory is granted to us nor confidence reserved. For faith is the shield in which we most easily conquer the enemy of our salvation, if we attach the handle of divine love. For blessed Pope Gregory says: Then are we truly faithful to him, if what we promise in words we fulfill in works. Since in this armor faith is the foundation of all good works, all our operations

Quoniam vero iaꝫ quod etiam iubet fideler creditis: sūda- mentũ spiritualis edificij super firmã pe- tram collocatis: nunc oportet vt etiaꝫ re- liqua ad perfectionem restantia sine mo- ra faciatis. Pacem igitur et veritatem di- ligite: quatenus infide christi vt veri mi- lites possitis omni tempore stabiles et fir- missimi permanere. Quid nani aliud est veritatem diligere: qua esse hominē id quod esse iubetur. et traviuere ad normam iustitie. verum et solidū. qua- lem nature per gratiam sancta perfectio requirit? Dinc firmianus lactantius inquit. Qui veritati studet. abijciat inimicas illi et anxias voluptates que animuꝫ sibi vinciunt: et liberum esse non permittunt. Semper autem preferat vera falsis eterną breuibus. vtilia iocundis. Nihil aspectui gratum sit: nisi quod iuste. quod pie. quod religioso fieri possit: nihil audi- tui suaue: nisi quod animaꝫ reddit melior. Milites itaqƺ lũbos in veritate habent precinctos: qñ carnis illecebris et mũ di vanitatibus pro dei amore contempti ita student pro viribus conuersari et viure re: quatenus summeveritati que deus est valeant in omnibꝰ complacere. Post hec miles christi loricaꝫ iustitie iubetur inducre: sine qua nemo recte ac fructuosę poterit domino militare. Iustitia vero est ser- nara et distribuere vnicuiqƺ quod sibi secūdum legem vel naturam debetur. Et hec est omnium virtutum preclarissima: sine qua nulla potest esse pietas, nulla religio nulla sanctitas. nullaqƺ bonorum maloꝝ ve discretio. ipsa enim est lux et splendor magnus. ex qua totius boni confurgit inter mortales vis atqƺ dominatio. Justitia mater innocentie: concordie nutrix: parēs amicicie: pietatis genitrix: et seruatrix religionis. Iustitia sicut testatur scriptura ꝑpetua est et immortalis: iniustitia autem mortis est acquisisitio. Quibꝰ vero modis hanc iustitie loricam christianus miles debeat induere: ipse saluator noster in sancto euangelio denunciat dicens. Omni quecumqƺ vultis vt faciant vobis ho- mines: et vos facite illis similiter. Homily III. VIII

rightly ought to precede, so that the mind may be able to arrive at love. For unless faith is first held, spiritual love is by no means reached. For charity does not precede faith, but faith precedes charity, because no one can love or hope for the good which he refuses to believe.

But since you now faithfully believe also what he commands, and have set the foundation of the spiritual building upon a firm rock, now you must also without delay do the remaining things that are left for perfection. Therefore love peace and truth, so that in the faith of Christ, as true soldiers, you may be able at all times to remain stable and most firm. For, as Scripture bears witness, truth is great and stronger than all things, and there is nothing unjust with it. He who loves truth is a true disciple of Christ, and loves Christ himself, who says in the Gospel: “I am the way, the truth, and the life.” All the ways of the Lord likewise are mercy and truth; from this [unclear] fell through pride, because he did not remain in eternal truth.

Therefore holy [Christophilus?] Paul commands the soldiers of the Lord to gird themselves in truth; in this he wished to show the state of perfection toward which cloistered persons especially ought to aspire. For what else is it to love truth than to be the person one is commanded to be, and to live according to the rule of justice, true and solid, such as holy perfection by grace requires of nature? Hence Firmianus Lactantius says: “He who is zealous for truth should cast away pleasures hostile to it and troubling, which bind the soul to themselves and do not allow it to be free. But let him always prefer true things to false, eternal things to brief ones, useful things to pleasant ones. Let nothing be pleasing to the sight except what can be done justly, piously, religiously; nothing sweet to the hearing except what makes the soul better.”

Thus soldiers have their loins girded in truth when, out of love for God, despising the enticements of the flesh and the vanities of the world, they strive according to their powers so to conduct themselves and live that they may be able in all things to please the highest Truth, which is God. After this the soldier of Christ is commanded to put on the breastplate of justice, without which no one will be able to serve the Lord rightly and fruitfully. Justice is to preserve and distribute to each one what is owed to him according to law or nature. And this is the most excellent of all virtues; without it there can be no piety, no religion, no holiness, and no discernment of goods and evils. For it is light and great splendor, from which the force and dominion of every good arises among mortals. Justice is the mother of innocence, the nurse of concord, the parent of friendship, the begetter of piety, and the guardian of religion. Justice, as Scripture bears witness, is perpetual and immortal; injustice, however, is the acquisition of death.

By what means the Christian soldier ought to put on this breastplate of justice, our Savior himself declares in the holy Gospel, saying: “All things whatsoever you wish that men should do to you, do you also do likewise to them.” Therefore, my brothers, keep this manner of living in our [unclear]: that each one do to his fellow-soldier in all things just as, according to the right judgment of reason, he desires at all times that it be done to him by others. For this is the first duty of justice, that one harm no one; then that in common uses [unclear] to his brother what conduces to salvation by just reason as his own. O what great peace mortals would enjoy if they followed the exhortations of the Apostle, by which each is commanded to bear the burdens of the other. Everyone, says Scripture, who does justice is now born of God.

This, brothers, is the breastplate of justice: to keep the commandments of God, to love one’s neighbor, and to love God most ardently above all things. This is the strongest garment of our warfare: to show worship and piety to God, holiness to ourselves, and brotherly charity to our neighbor. Whoever has not been under justice shows that he belongs not to Christ’s soldiery but rather to the company of demons. For justice is the greatest virtue, which distributes to each one what is his; unless you keep it most diligently, you lose the name both of monk and soldier. Therefore render worship and piety to God; obedience to your [unclear] or rector, together with reverence, of which one belongs to the heart, the other to action. Nor is it enough to obey superiors outwardly, unless from the inward affection of the heart we likewise think rightly about them. And the true justice of monks, brothers, is this: that each one conducts himself without offense according to the prescribed rule of the law, granting to each his own proper dignity: reverence to his superior, concord to his equal, discipline to the lesser, worship and obedience to God.

sibi sanctimoniam: inimico patientiam: pauperi misericordiam: omnibus frater nam in domino charitatem. Ergo sacer christophilus inquit. Debitores sumus fratres non carni, vt secundum carnem vivamus. Si enim secundum carnem vivemus: si autem spiritu faciem carnis mortificaueris, viueris. Recte igitur militat do: q̄ distribuit vnicuiq̄ quod suum est. Calciatos de hinc pedes habe re iubemur in preparationem evangelii pacis: quatinus bonum quod ipsi domino largiente cognouimus: etiam alius hilariter communicemus. Ex enim nostra fratres secundum quam domino militare iubemur evangelium est iesu christi: ad quod omnes claustralium regulae et constitutiones ordinantur. Non enim prope constitutiones monasticae evangelium: sed propter evangelium statuta sunt facta monachorum. Christianus nam igitur saluari potest non monachus: sed monachus saluari non poterit nisi fuerit christianus. Pudeat quosdam nimis supersticiosos et fatuos claustrales, qui regulae et statuta sua pluris faciunt quam evangelii christi: qui traditiones hominum custodiunt usus ad carceres et vincula: dei aut constitutiones et iure universalis ecclesie non ad uertit. Ips verbis saluatoris nostri recte coueniuit indeis cata matheum dicentis Quare et vos trasgressimini mandatui dei: propter traditionem vestram. Quagelica nacq doctrina, omnibus totius mundi constitutionibus loge est preferenda. Post evangelium vero primum auctoritatis locum statuta obtinent ecclesie universalis et nul le monachorum constitutiones aut regulae illis dignitate comparantur. Curem ad evangelicam vivere puritatem: et erimus in monastica patrum conversatione perfecti. Sint pedes nostri calciati semp in preparatione evangelii pacis: vt mortificemus in nobis desideria carnis: et per amorrem dei et proximi pace habeamus cum omnibus. Nam sine pace et concordia fraternitatis: nihil prodest maceratio carnis: sancto dicete hieronymo. Quisquis corpus affigit. sed concordiam deserit: deum quidem laudat in tympanos: sed non laudat in choro. Hinc salomon pacificus laudans virum dicit in proverbiis. De/lieor est bucella sicca cum gandio: quaz do mus plenavictimis cum iurgio. Et iteru Omelia. III. Fo. Et qui accipit teneat: qui perdi cir repetat: qui amicit exquirat: quoniam qui in eadem inuentus non fuerit: a pa tre abdicatura filio expéredatur: et nibi ominus a spiritu sancto alienus efficiur. Ad hereditatem domini nunc potest ac cedere: qui testamentum pacis noluit ob servare. Locus in dei in pace est: diaboli autem mansio in ira et perturbatione. Om nis itaç homo qui hanc triplex pacem in corde suo non habuerit: qui eam in ore non prestiterit: nec in operibus ostende rit: nec monachus est dicendus: nec chri stianus. Nunc dicit in evangelio domini Beati pacifici: quoniam filii dei vocábu tur. Si dei vocantur filii qui pacem faci unt: proculdubio satáhane sunt filii qui pa cem confundunt. Unde frátres mei char rissimi habéte inter vos pacem illam quá mundus dare non potest: quae est pac dei et díni nostri iésu christi: de qua dígit eis ías prophetae. Et erit opus iustitie paci: et cultus iustitie silentium: et secúritas vso in sempitérnum. Deus enim pacis et dile ctionis est dominus: unde quicunque pacem et fraternam dilectionem violat: quod verus dei amator non sit manifestus. Si pac chris tis vera in coaeribi: vestris: et nul la hui? mundi aduersa formidabítis. In ter vos etiam sit pac vera: nó fuçata: quo niam christus pacem non ex ore sed ex co de desiderat: et affectu potius quam labis is vult proximum salutari. Unde si con tristauerit quispiam ex vobis in aliquo fra erem fuunt: satis faciat illi quam primu ante solis occasu: et cauete omnes ne sol occidat super iracundiam vestram: quo niam ira inueterata generat odium: et spo liat animam omníomatu virtutum. Ergo monaché si peccaueris in frátre tu um: mor age penitentiam coraeco: ac pro cidens ad genua veniam precare. Et gla divum inquit spiritus: quod est verbú dei per omnem orationem et obsecrationem in manibus christi milites semper tenea mus. Verbum dei quod in sanctis conti netur scripturis victorius est contra omi nes demonum incursiones muniment: si cúr salvatoris nostri monemur exempló: qui temptatus a diabolo: tranquilla man

to oneself holiness; to an enemy patience; to a poor man mercy; to all men brotherly charity in the Lord. Therefore holy Christophilus says: “We are debtors, brothers, not to the flesh, that we should live according to the flesh. For if you live according to the flesh, you will die; but if by the spirit you put to death the deeds of the flesh, you will live.” Therefore he serves God rightly who gives to each what is his.

Then we are commanded to have our feet shod in preparation for the gospel of peace, so that the good which we ourselves have come to know by the Lord’s generosity we may also cheerfully share with others. For our law, brothers, according to which we are commanded to serve the Lord, is the gospel of Jesus Christ, to which all rules and constitutions of cloistered persons are ordered. For monastic constitutions were not made on account of the gospel, but the statutes of monks were made on account of the gospel. For a Christian who is not a monk can be saved, but a monk cannot be saved unless he has been a Christian. Let certain excessively superstitious and foolish cloistered persons be ashamed, who value their rule and statutes more than the gospel of Christ; who keep the traditions of men, customs leading to prisons and chains, but pay no heed to the constitutions of God and the law of the universal Church. The words of our Savior, speaking to the Jews according to Matthew, rightly apply to them: “Why do you also transgress the commandment of God for the sake of your tradition?” For evangelical doctrine must be preferred by far to all the constitutions of the whole world. But after the gospel the statutes of the universal Church hold the first place of authority, and no constitutions or rules of monks are comparable to them in dignity. Let us take care to live according to evangelical purity, and we shall be perfect in the monastic way of life of the fathers.

Let our feet always be shod in preparation for the gospel of peace, so that we may put to death in ourselves the desires of the flesh, and through love of God and neighbor have peace with all. For without peace and the concord of brotherhood, mortification of the flesh is of no benefit, as Saint Jerome says: “Whoever afflicts the body but abandons concord does indeed praise God with timbrels, but he does not praise him in the choir.” Hence peaceful Solomon, praising the man, says in Proverbs: “Better is a dry morsel with joy than a house full of victims with strife.” And again

Homily III Fol. IX

he restrains anger, treads down the proud, loves the humble, calms the discordant, reconciles enemies; with all he is gentle, burdensome to none, troublesome to none, oppressive to none; he does not know how to be exalted, he does not know how to [unclear]. And let him who receives it hold it fast; let him who loses it seek it again; let him who has cast it away inquire after it, because whoever is not found in that same peace will be disowned by the Father, disinherited by the Son, and nevertheless made a stranger to the Holy Spirit. He cannot now approach the inheritance of the Lord who has refused to observe the testament of peace. The place of God is in peace, but the dwelling of the devil is in anger and disturbance. Therefore every man who does not have this threefold peace in his heart, who does not offer it with his mouth, nor show it in his works, is to be called neither a monk nor a Christian.

Now the Lord says in the Gospel: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God.” If those who make peace are called sons of God, without doubt those who confound peace are sons of Satan. Therefore, my dearest brothers, have among yourselves that peace which the world cannot give, which is the peace of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, of which Isaiah the prophet says: “And the work of justice shall be peace, and the service of justice silence and security forever.” For God is the Lord of peace and love; therefore whoever violates peace and brotherly love is made manifest as not being a true lover of God. If the true peace of Christ is in your hearts, you will fear no adversities of this world. Among you also let there be true peace, not feigned, because Christ desires peace not from the mouth but from the heart, and wishes one’s neighbor to be greeted with affection rather than with lips. Therefore if any one of you has saddened his brother in anything, let him make satisfaction to him as soon as possible before sunset; and take care, all of you, that the sun not set upon your anger, because inveterate anger generates hatred and strips the soul of every adornment of virtues. Therefore, monk, if you have sinned against your brother, quickly do penance before him, and falling at his knees beg pardon.

“And,” he says, “the sword of the spirit, which is the word of God, through every prayer and supplication”: we soldiers of Christ should always hold it in our hands. The word of God, which is contained in the holy Scriptures, is a victorious defense against all assaults of demons, as we are admonished by the example of our Savior, who, when tempted by the devil, with calm hand

Explicit Omelia .ij. ¶ De lectione et studio diuinarū scripturarū: Omelja quarta. Cum omnis scriptura di uinitur? inspirata vt sacer christophilus inquit vti lis sit ad docendū: vel ad arguendū: ad corripien- dū ad erudiendū in iusti cia: vt perfectus sithō dei: ad omne opus bonū instructus: libenter debemus lecti- oni diuinarū scripturarũ insistere: et om̄ie studii litterature secularis in quo aliquā- do desudauimus: ad huius speculatiōis aciem ordinare. In scripturis nanqꝫ diui nis quicquid salutaris requirit scientia copiosissime reperitur expressiuꝫ: vt quod ibi non inueneris: minime ad salutē sit ne cessariū. Daiestas etenim diuinarū scri- pturarū omnem totius mundi scientiam atqꝫ doctrinam longe procul transcendet qua spiritus sanctus hominiꝝ dei vt scri beretur infudit: et vt intelligatur a studio sis lectoribus illustratiōis sue gratiā im- pendit. Dancfratres mei scriptura sedu lo cuꝫ puritate mentis et feruore gemine charitatis reuoluite: qm̄ quisquis decum veraciter diligit: omne tempus quod in- uenire potest ad ociū in sacris lectionibꝰ consumit. Sint vobis incitamēta precor ad salubre studiū scripturarū furiosa vt īta dixerim gesta amatorū carnaliū: qui li teras et eulogia suarū accipientes ama- tricū legere non cessant: sepiusqꝫ et relegūt et osculantur: et quod maioris est indicieuꝫ amoris vel ad collū suspendūt vel ad pe- ctus: quatens nunqꝫ a mente recedat ei us qua cupiunt dilecte memoria. Consi- derate fratres carnaliū in amore demen tiam: et vestra circa dei amorē erubescite repiditatem. Quis vestru circa scriptu- ras dei sanctas tāto cordis amore afficit̉ quanto cecus amator circa literas ama- torias spurcas et vanissimas vnius mere tricule infanissimas pre dilectione inflamat̉ Ille propter absentis qua cupit amoreꝫ literas et munuscula crebris osculis pro- sequitur: apices singulos pre nimio amo re considerando iteratis vidibus rimatur in omnibus que agit semper absente co/ gitat: ad eius venire conspectum anxius festinat. O si nos qui monachi dicimur christiani: qui regi supremo et immortali christo iesu militamus: qui deum nostrū super omnia iubemur diligere: et nihil in hoc mūdo preteripsum precipimur ama re: si inquam tanto creatorem nostrū pro sequeremur amore: quanto suas amicas corruptibiles et mortales: obseruant et di- ligunt homines carnaliter sapientes. De um nobis scriptura sancta qnotidie lecta insinuat: eius voluntatem nobis manife stat: quid facere debeamus nos instruit: et quid cauere pandit. Per ipsaꝫ omnipo tens nobifcum loquitur: et iniuisibili nos magisterio informans cōsolatur: sancto dicēte apostolo. Quecunqꝫ enim scripta sunt ad nostram doctrinam scripta sunt: vt per pacientiam et consolationē scriptu rarū spem habeamus. Unde verus chri- sti miles et precipue claustralis: q̄ deū in toto corde suo diligit eiqꝫ soli placere ꝯcu piscit: scripturas diuinas et maxime san- ctum euangelium affectuose amplectit̉: et in eius lectione meditando assidue oc- cupatur. Quicunqꝫ autem diuinarū scri pturaruꝫ lections negligitur: quod verus dei amator nō sit manifeste osciendit. Sꝫ quid ait ipsa scriptura? Qui auertit aurē suam ne audiat legeꝫ: oratio eius erit exe crabilis. Teati vero qui scrutantur testi monia domini: in toto corde exquirūt cū uos itaque fratres mei si dominum ie- sum in toto corde vestro veraciter diligiti- tis: si complacere illi super omnia vt veri milites desideratis: si deniqꝫ ad perfectio nem vite monastice cupitis proficere: in lectione diuinarū scriptuarum debetis vos semper cum affectione feruida occu pare. Quam sit vtilis lectio scripturarū: beatus Hieronymus insinuat dicens. Ama scientiam scripturarū et carnis vi- cia non amabis. Nihil enim post deū in hac vita suauius sumitur: nihil duieius sentitur: nihil mentem ab amore huius mundi validius separat: nihil contra om nes aduersariorū temptationes militem christi adeo confortat: nihil monachum ad omne opus bonum in tantum dispo- nit et confirmat: quemadmodum lectio frequens et studium ardens scripturarū. On the reading and study of the divine Scriptures

by us. For everyone who sins mortally opens the door of his heart to the devil; he closes it to God; nor can he trust in the help of the Most High so long as he has remained lying in crime without repentance.

Here ends Homily 2.

On the reading and study of the divine Scriptures: Homily Four.

Since every Scripture, divinely inspired, as the holy apostle of Christ says, is useful for teaching, or for arguing, for correcting, for training in justice, so that the man of God may be perfect, equipped for every good work, we ought gladly to devote ourselves to the reading of the divine Scriptures, and to direct all the zeal of secular literature in which we once labored toward the point of this contemplation. For in the divine Scriptures whatever saving knowledge requires is found most abundantly expressed, so that what you do not find there is in no way necessary for salvation. For the majesty of the divine Scriptures far surpasses all the knowledge and teaching of the whole world: the Holy Spirit poured it into the men of God so that it might be written, and, so that it may be understood by studious readers, bestows the grace of his illumination.

Turn this Scripture over diligently, my brothers, with purity of mind and the fervor of twofold charity, because whoever truly loves God spends in sacred readings all the time he can find for leisure. Let there be for you, I pray, incentives toward the wholesome study of the Scriptures in the frenzied deeds, so to speak, of carnal lovers: when they receive the letters and gifts of their mistresses, they do not cease to read them, and often read them again and kiss them; and, what is a greater sign of love, they hang them either from the neck or at the breast, so that the dear memory of her whom they desire may never depart from the mind. Consider, brothers, the madness of carnal people in love, and blush at your own lukewarmness toward the love of God. Which of you is affected toward the holy Scriptures of God with such love of heart as a blind lover is inflamed with desire toward the filthy, utterly vain, and most mad love-letters of one little prostitute? He, because of love for the absent woman whom he desires, follows her letters and little gifts with repeated kisses; examining each stroke because of excessive love, he searches it out with repeated looks; in everything he does he always thinks of the absent woman; anxiously he hastens to come into her sight.

O if we who are called Christian monks, who serve the supreme and immortal king Christ Jesus, who are commanded to love our God above all things, and are ordered to love nothing in this world except him: if, I say, we pursued our creator with as great a love as carnally minded men observe and love their corruptible and mortal girlfriends. Holy Scripture, read every day, brings God to our minds; it makes his will manifest to us; it instructs us what we ought to do, and lays open what we should beware. Through it the Almighty speaks with us, and, forming us by an invisible instruction, consoles us, as the holy apostle says: For whatever things have been written were written for our instruction, so that through patience and the consolation of the Scriptures we may have hope.

Therefore the true soldier of Christ, and especially the cloistered one, who loves God in his whole heart and desires to please him alone, embraces the divine Scriptures, and most of all the holy Gospel, with affection, and is constantly occupied in reading it with meditation. But whoever neglects the reading of the divine Scriptures plainly shows that he is not a true lover of God. But what does Scripture itself say? He who turns away his ear so as not to hear the law, his prayer will be detestable. Blessed indeed are those who search the testimonies of the Lord; with their whole heart they seek him. Therefore you, my brothers, if you truly love the Lord Jesus in your whole heart, if as true soldiers you desire to please him above all things, if finally you desire to advance toward the perfection of the monastic life, ought always to occupy yourselves in the reading of the divine Scriptures with fervent affection.

How useful the reading of the Scriptures is, blessed Jerome indicates, saying: Love the knowledge of the Scriptures, and you will not love the vices of the flesh. For after God nothing in this life is taken up more sweetly, nothing is felt more pleasantly, nothing more powerfully separates the mind from love of this world, nothing so strengthens the soldier of Christ against all the temptations of adversaries, nothing disposes and confirms the monk so greatly for every good work, as frequent reading and ardent study of the Scriptures. Indeed, if the benefits of the Almighty which

X. humano impendit generi per totam late scripturam legendo ad memoriam studi osa deuotione reducimus: materiam et occasionem prestabunt nobis maximam qua in dei amore per amplius ardentes proficiamus. Tota enim series diuinarū scripturarum quid continet aliud quam textum quendam bonoruꝫ ordinem: que deus hominibus vel iam prestitit: vel eti am se daturum repromisit? Aut quid est quod nos ad tolerantiam maloruꝫ adeo corroborare queat et voluntarie reddere patiētes: sicut si legamus in euāgelio pas sum innocenter pro nobis dei filiū: et post eum martyrum victorias sanctoruꝫ? Sa cra nanqꝫ scriptura cōtinet que nobis ad scientiam salutareꝫ sunt necessaria: et mo/ net nos quid in hac peregrinatione mili tantes vtiliter debeamus appetere: quid etiam declinare. Dinc diuis iterum di/ cit Hieronymus. Nostre diuitie sunt in lege dei meditari die ac nocte. Prepaꝛe/ mus igitur nobis fortitudinem: assuma/ mus nobis perfectum robur: vt inter er/ rorum tenebras et confusioneꝫ noctis: sci entie christi lumen appareat: diesqꝫ et no/ ctes lucem habeant protegentem: vt scri ptura duce ad terram sanctam pertuenire valeamus. Quid naꝫ hac eruditione me lius: quid suauius disciplina? Quid dul/ cius domino nostro ieisu christo: qui vera est salus et dulcedo fideliū animarum? Sit autem nobis conuiuium christus sit lectio sacra cibus noster et potꝰ. Quid enim potestesse vita monachi sacerdotis sine scientia scripturarum? Abhꝛistum nō visu non auditu nō tactu sed lectione scri pturarum cognoscimus: et quanto plus legendo ad veram scientiam proficimus tanto in scripturis sanctis amplius dele/ ctamur. Quid enim dulcius: quam dei scire voluntatem: et promißionum precia non ignorare? Nam sicut Hieronymus dicit: pinguissimus est ager diuini sermo nis: qui omnes in se habꝫ delitias: et quic quid volueris ex illo nascitur: sicut tra/ dunt indei quod manna in deserto quan/ do comedebatur secundum voluntatem et desiderium in ore sapiebat comedentis. Diuinas igitur scripturas fratres mei se pius legite: per quas potestis volunteateꝫ dei plane cognoscere: et cōtra insidias di/ aboli fortissime vos armare. Nam si iu/ xta apostolum Paulum: christus dei vir tus est: et dei sapientia: qui nescit scriptu/ ras: nescit dei virtutem et sapieniam: et chri/ stum quomodo sciet? Ignorantia em̄ scri pturarum: ignorantia est christi: et qui ne/ scit christum: ad eius non pertinebit con/ sortium: sancto dicente christophilo: quo niam si quis ignorat: certe et ignorabitur. Quanto autem quis in studio diuinarū scripturarū magis assidueus fuerit: tan to ex earum lectione maiorem intelligen/ tiam et dulcedinem capit. Uos autem ma xime decet fratres diuinas scripturas qͦ/ tidie legendo et discendo reuoluere: qui/ bus et tempus copiosum ab occupationi/ bus feriatum conceditur: et locus rarita/ te occurrentium satis conueniens offer/ tur. Idcirco vos hortoꝛ et moneo si ve/ stram salutem diligitis: vt diuinas lectio nes in manibus semper habeatis: quate/ nus omne tempus quod vobis post ora/ tionis cultum sine labore permittitur: ad sacre scripture studium expendatur. Nō p̄tereat dies vlla: fratres mei: in qua mo/ nachus christo militans non aliquid le/ gat ex sacris voluminibus quod cum in sancto proposito faciat meliorēm. Quin potius diui Hieronymi sequatur consili um dicētis. Sint scripture semper in ma nibus diuine: et iugiter mente voluantur: nec tibi sufficere putes mandata dei me/ morie recondere: nisi studeas illa etiam operibus adimplere. Duo em̄ deus a no bis fratres mei requirit. Primo em̄ vult nos scire sanctissimam voluntatem suam secundo vt agnitam faciamus. Scire au tem eius mandata non possumus: si di/ uinarū scripturarū scientiam ignore mus. Necqꝫ voluntatem dei facit qui eam ignorat: neqꝫ sciet qui nondidicit. Discito igitur que sit dei voluntas beneplacens vt facias: facito cognitam: vt amplius intelligas. Nemo enim dei voluntateꝫ me/ lius intelligit: quam ille qui cognitam ex amore facit. Itaqꝫ si doctissimus diuina/ ruꝫ scripturarū paraphrastes cupis euā dere: non a verbis sed in sanctis operibꝰ scientie studium discas inchoare. Tunc enim sacre lectionis vberem comprehen des scientiam: si munduꝫ custodieris coꝛ tuū ab om̄i peccato: et feruens in dei amo re sancta cōpunctꝰ iugiter reuolueris scri ptura s. Scientia em̄ diuinarū scripturaꝝ altus est mons in quo cum domino moꝑ ses loquitur: ad quem accedere vitioruni b ij

Homily IV. Fol. X.

...bestowed upon the human race, when by reading through the whole wide extent of Scripture we call it back to memory with zealous devotion, they will furnish us the greatest matter and occasion by which, burning more deeply in the love of God, we may advance. For what else does the whole sequence of the divine Scriptures contain than a certain ordered fabric of good things which God has either already bestowed on human beings, or has promised that he will also give? Or what is there that can so strengthen us for the endurance of evils and render us willingly patient as if we read in the Gospel that the Son of God suffered innocently for us, and after him the victories of the holy martyrs?

For sacred Scripture contains the things that are necessary for us unto saving knowledge, and it warns us what, as soldiers in this pilgrimage, we ought profitably to seek, and what also to avoid. Hence again Saint Jerome says: "Our riches are to meditate on the law of God day and night." Let us therefore prepare strength for ourselves; let us take up perfect might, so that amid the darkness of errors and the confusion of night the light of Christ's knowledge may appear, and days and nights may have a protecting light, so that with Scripture as guide we may be able to come to the holy land.

For what is better than this instruction? What sweeter than this discipline? What more delightful than our Lord Jesus Christ, who is the true salvation and sweetness of faithful souls? Let Christ be our banquet; let sacred reading be our food and drink. For what can the life of a monk or priest be without knowledge of the Scriptures? We know Christ not by sight, not by hearing, not by touch, but by the reading of the Scriptures; and the more we advance by reading toward true knowledge, the more we take delight in the holy Scriptures.

For what is sweeter than to know the will of God and not to be ignorant of the prizes of his promises? For as Jerome says, the field of the divine word is exceedingly rich, having in itself every delight, and whatever you wish is born from it, just as they report of the manna in the desert, that when it was eaten it tasted in the mouth of the eater according to his will and desire.

Therefore, my brothers, read the divine Scriptures more often, through which you can plainly know the will of God and arm yourselves most strongly against the snares of the devil. For if, according to the Apostle Paul, Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God, he who does not know the Scriptures does not know the power and wisdom of God; and how will he know Christ? For ignorance of the Scriptures is ignorance of Christ, and he who does not know Christ will not belong to his fellowship, as holy Christophilus says, because if anyone is ignorant, surely he will also be ignored.

Moreover, the more constant anyone has been in the study of the divine Scriptures, the greater understanding and sweetness he receives from their reading. But it especially befits you, brothers, to turn over the divine Scriptures daily by reading and learning, since to you both abundant time free from occupations is granted and a place sufficiently suitable because of the rarity of those who come by is offered. Therefore I exhort and admonish you, if you love your salvation, always to have divine readings in your hands, so that all the time which, after the worship of prayer, is allowed you without labor may be spent on the study of sacred Scripture.

Let no day pass, my brothers, on which the monk serving as Christ's soldier does not read something from the sacred volumes that may make him better in his holy purpose. Rather let him follow the counsel of Saint Jerome, who says: "Let the divine Scriptures always be in your hands and be continually turned over in the mind; nor should you think it enough to store the commandments of God in memory, unless you strive also to fulfill them in works."

For God requires two things of us, my brothers. First, he wishes us to know his most holy will; second, that we do what we have come to know. But we cannot know his commandments if we are ignorant of the knowledge of the divine Scriptures. Nor does he do the will of God who is ignorant of it; nor will he know it who has not learned it. Learn, therefore, what is the pleasing will of God, so that you may do it; do what is known, so that you may understand more fully. For no one understands the will of God better than he who, once he has known it, does it out of love.

And so, if you desire to become a most learned interpreter of the divine Scriptures, learn to begin the study of knowledge not from words but in holy works. For then you will grasp the rich knowledge of sacred reading, if you have kept your heart clean from every sin and, fervent in the love of God, have continually turned over the holy Scriptures with compunction. For the knowledge of the divine Scriptures is the high mountain on which Moses speaks with the Lord, to which the [unclear] of vices...

Delectiōe et studio diuinarū scripturarū fordibus pollutus homo prohibet̉. Sic nancꝫ in exodo legitur. Lauete ne ascen- datis in montem: nec tangatis fines illi- us. Omnis qui tetigerit montem morte morietur. Siue iumentum fuerit siue ho- mo: non viuet. Homo siquidem monteꝫ tangit et moritur: quotiens quis literatu- ra seculari turgidus in simplicitate diui- narum scripturarum scaudaliʒatur. Be- stia vero montem tangit et lapidibus ob- ruitur: quotiens homo carnaliuꝫ furore passionum immersus: ad sacre scripture studium non purgatus animo progredi- tur. Si ergo lectiones diuinaruꝫ scriptu- rarum salubriter vultis euoluerē: si ad ve- ram scientiam legendo cupitis peruenire: omnem curate in primis et elationem su- perbice: et temeritatem perfide deponere: acdeinde cubiculū cordis vestri ab om- ni immundicia carnaliū voluptatum ex- purgare Deus em̄ vt ait scriptura cano- nica: superbis resistit: humilibus aūt dat gratiam. Nemo superbus: clatus: arro- gans: et temerarius: nemo carnis ani- mo: luxuriosus vel inquietus: ad studiuꝫ sacre scripture habetur idoneus: sed hu- milis duntaxat: mitis: mansuetus: pudi- cus: castus: corpore et mente tranquillus Dine prosper in epigrāmate dicit. Man- data dei scrutari nisi quieta mens nō po- test. Utergo religiosum exercatur studi- um: obijcienda sunt iurga malignorum. Scrutari legem possunt vtcuncꝫ quiete: si mūdi a strepitu libera corda vacent. Ut mens ergo pijs studiiʒ intenta inuenitur: prelia diuinus carnea vincat amor. Naꝫ templum domini per sacra filēta crescit: et tacite strnuitur: nō ruitura domus. Dū datis igitur animis et corde in dei amore compuncto: atqꝫ in vera contritione hu- miliato: ad studium scripturarum proce- dite: quia non illuminabit vos dominus nisi ab omniprius fecerit iniquitate pur- gatos. Nanqꝫ vt scriptura ipsa dicit: per- uerse cogitationes separant a deo: proba- ta autem virtus corrīpit insipientes: quo- riam in maliuolam animā non introibit sapientia: nec habitabit in corpore subdi- to peccatis: qui spiritus sanctus discipli- ne effugiet fictum: et auferet sea cogitati- onibus que sunt sine intellectu. Ideocꝫ orandum nobis est cū sancto David cre- brius ad dominū. Aor mundum crea in me deus: et spiritū rectuꝫ innova in visce- ribꝰ meis. Nemo em̄ sacras dei scriptu- ras vtiliter intelligit: qui se in toto corde suo ad dominū per potentiā non conuer- tit. Ideocꝫ si vultis diuina eloquia et re- cte et salubriter intelligere: summo in pri- mis curate studio: mundos vos ab omni pollutione peccati pro viribus custodire. Non vos precor seducat quorundaʒ mo- nachorum vesana stultitia: qui suā igno- rantiam trito conantur excusare prouer- bio dicentes. Ad quid nobis scientia scrip- turarum: qui predicationis nullum ha- bemus officium? Uiri sapientis amplecti- mur consilium: qui dicit in libro prouerbiorū. Qui ambulat simpliciter: ambula- lat confidenter. Sufficit nobis simplici- ter viuere: quoniā scrutus sciens volunta- tem domini sui et nō faciēs vapulabit pla- gis multis: qui aūt non cognouiit et cōmi- fit digna plagis vapulabit paucis. O stu- liti et perditissimi petrones qui scientiaꝫ salu- tarēm contemnitis: et ignorantia diui- natū scripturarū potius q̄ intelligenciaʒ amatis. Nunqͥd affectata ignoraria pau- cioꝛibꝰ vos plagis reddet obnoxios? Aut propterea delinquentes eritis coram deo innoxij: quia mandatorū dei voluntarie estis ignari? Duplici pena cruciandi cri- tis: altera quod scire viā mandatoꝛuʒ dei contemptitis: altera quod sermones eius nō custoditis. Non est quā allegatis sim- plicitas: sed duplex potius impietas. Nā si iuxta prophetā beati sunt qui scrutant̉ testimonia domini: quis dubitet illos ef- se maledictos qui nec deū exquirunt nec scripturas eius aduertunt: sed indurato magis anīo contentunt? Audite quid vo- bis salomon dicat in prouerbijs. Ubi nō est scientia anime non est bonū et stultitia hominis supplantat gressus eius. De vo- bis etiā o sultissimi tenebriones illud in- telligitur sancti Hieronymi: quoniaꝫ ibi non est ignorantia iā excusabilis: xvi sci- tur quid fit illud quod ignorat̉. Magis aūt cauendū vobis ne cū illis tandē com- putenmini qui dixerūt deo recede a nobis: viā scientiarū tuarū nolumus. Uerbū salomonis male intelligitis: qui de ignoraʒ tia dictū simpliciter putatis. Qui ambula- lat simpliciter sine aliqua deceptrione proxi- mi: ambulat confidenter in custodiendo mādata dei: qui aūt deprauat vias suas nō pōt latere sed manifestus erit. Dine rusius ait: Labia itusti crudiunt pluri-

On the reading and study of the divine Scriptures

A man polluted with filth is forbidden. For thus it is read in Exodus: “Take care that you do not go up onto the mountain, nor touch its borders. Everyone who touches the mountain shall surely die. Whether it be beast or man, it shall not live.” A man indeed touches the mountain and dies whenever someone, puffed up with secular literature, takes offense at the simplicity of the divine Scriptures. But a beast touches the mountain and is overwhelmed with stones whenever a man, sunk in the fury of carnal passions, advances to the study of sacred Scripture without a purified mind.

If, therefore, you wish profitably to turn over the readings of the divine Scriptures, if by reading you desire to arrive at true knowledge, take care first of all to put away every swelling of pride and every rashness of unbelief, and then to cleanse the chamber of your heart from all uncleanness of carnal pleasures. For God, as canonical Scripture says, resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble. No proud, inflated, arrogant, and rash man, no man of carnal mind, luxurious or restless, is held fit for the study of sacred Scripture, but only the humble, gentle, mild, modest, chaste man, tranquil in body and mind.

[Dine prosper?] says in an epigram: “A mind that is not quiet cannot search the commandments of God. Therefore, that religious study may be exercised, the quarrels of the wicked must be cast aside. Hearts free from the tumult of the world may search the law in whatever quiet they can. Therefore, that the mind may be found intent upon pious studies, let divine love conquer fleshly battles. For the temple of the Lord grows through sacred threads, and silently the house that will not fall is built.”

Therefore proceed to the study of the Scriptures with devoted minds and with a heart pierced in the love of God and humbled in true contrition, because the Lord will not enlighten you unless he has first made you cleansed from every iniquity. For, as Scripture itself says, perverse thoughts separate from God; but proven virtue corrects the foolish, since wisdom will not enter a malicious soul, nor dwell in a body subject to sins; for the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit and will withdraw himself from thoughts that are without understanding. Therefore we must pray more often to the Lord with holy David: “Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within my inward parts.” For no one understands the holy Scriptures of God usefully who does not turn himself to the Lord with his whole heart through [unclear].

Therefore, if you wish to understand the divine utterances both rightly and profitably, take care first of all with the utmost zeal to keep yourselves, as far as you can, clean from every pollution of sin. I beg you, do not let the mad folly of certain monks seduce you, who try to excuse their ignorance with a worn-out proverb, saying: “What need have we of knowledge of the Scriptures, we who have no office of preaching? We embrace the counsel of the wise man, who says in the book of Proverbs: ‘He who walks simply walks confidently.’ It is enough for us to live simply, since the servant who knew his lord’s will and did not do it will be beaten with many blows; but he who did not know it, and committed things worthy of blows, will be beaten with few.”

O foolish and utterly ruined [unclear], who despise saving knowledge and love ignorance of the divine Scriptures rather than understanding. Will deliberately sought ignorance make you liable to fewer blows? Or will you therefore be guiltless before God when you sin, because you are voluntarily ignorant of God’s commandments? You will be tormented with a twofold punishment: one because you have despised knowing the way of God’s commandments, the other because you do not keep his words. What you allege is not simplicity, but rather a double impiety. For if, according to the prophet, blessed are they who search the testimonies of the Lord, who could doubt that those are accursed who neither seek God nor attend to his Scriptures, but rather despise them with hardened mind?

Hear what Solomon says to you in Proverbs: “Where there is no knowledge of the soul, there is no good, and the folly of a man supplants his steps.” Of you also, O most foolish men of darkness, that saying of Saint Jerome is understood: that there ignorance is no longer excusable, where it is known what it is that is being ignored. But you must beware still more lest at last you be counted with those who said to God: “Depart from us; we do not want the way of your sciences.”

You understand Solomon’s word wrongly, who think it was said simply about ignorance. “He who walks simply,” without any deception of his neighbor, “walks confidently” in keeping God’s commandments; but he who corrupts his ways cannot lie hidden, but will be made manifest. [Dine?] again says: “The lips of the righteous instruct many—

An vt legerent ab eis intelligeren- turqꝫ vel vt nō lecte contemerent? Cer- te vt legerent eas mortalibus sunt date scripture mandatorū dei: postea vero vt opere complerent. Uos aūt qui deiscri- ptores animo deliberato vultis ignora- re: quomodo voluptas dei sunt volu- minas omnibus suis tradidit scripturam? An utile est esse poteritis: qui audi- tores ante non fuitis? Fieri nanqꝫ po- test vt sciens voluntatem dei aut obseruet eam: aut negligat: sed fieri non pōt vt eaꝝ ignorans impleat. Animero facilius ali- quis non faciet bonū quod nouit: quā im- pleat opere quod ignorat. Nemo aūt fa- cit bonū quod necit. Dicit de ignorantia: bus in quo dā loco sanctus Augustinus. Non omnis ignorans immunis est aculpa. Ille em̄ ignorans pōt excusari a pena qui quod disceret non inuenit. Illis aūt ignoscio nō poterit: qui a quo discerent ha- bentes: discipline operaz non dederunt. Hinc et sanctus leo papadicit. Si in laicis videtur intollerabilis inscicia: quā to- magis in his qui presunt: nec excusat ioēe est digna nec venia. Undefratres non fa- cit vos ignorantia diuinarum scripturarū excusatios coram deo sed dupliciter reos qui ne dei voluntate oporteat vos facere eaꝫ penitus cupitis ignora. Homo em̄ diuine voluntatis nō debet esse ignorarū excepti sui: vnicuiqꝫ mortalium necessaria est ad salute: quā usque inueniet sine noticia scripturam. Animero sicut ex cognito ne sui venit in hominez timor dei: et ex ei? notitia nasceat amorita prouenit ex igno- rantiā putabitis excusablem perquam facti estis primum voluntatis dei sunt date scripture mandatorum dei: postea vero vt opere complerent. Vos aut qui discipulos turpias ignorans mente disco- los et vagos: quibus eo magis imputa- mus ignorantiam: quo minus inclinantur ad disciplinam. Turpe quidem est nescire quod scire iuberis: turpior non disceret: turbissimum vero contemnere. Nam studijs meis nōnulli vestruꝫ vsqꝫ ad inuidiam grauiter aduersati sunt: pientes me illorum hortatu in abnegatione traducere scripturarū: vt ruricolami facerent et porcorum curatorez potius quam animarū. Sed frustra conantur diuinū impedire oraculum: quo impellente omnes mundi honores atqꝫ diuitias qua diu vi- xero studio postponere decreui scriptura- rum. Abbas sum vester quam diu voluerit ille qui me vocauit: si alterū e duobꝰ opor- teat: abbatiam malo dimittere: quam san- cto scripturarū estudio renunciare. Scio em̄ vere nihil in hac vita homini clausira li salubrius posse contingere: quam si diuisas ceperit scripturas veraciter amare. Qui quis vestrum habe in institutionem meam sequi voluerit: me ducem itineris pariter et comitem habebitur. Qui aut sequi discentem contempserit: docentem nihilominus audi re compellet vel inuitus. Hec dixerīt in eos qui terrencia sapientes et caduca: timorem a se domini adijciunt: qui omnia pe- ne ignorantes discerent contemnunt. Ego noui pecoris mei vultū: et singulorum inclina- tiones cordium vestrorum me credo nō penitus ignora. Idcirco non cessabo vos cohortari ad sancta studia scripturam: sciens quod amator sacre lectionis: nō pōt carnaliū operator esse vitiorum. Quāto em̄ b ij

All Things, IV. Folio XI.

[unclear]: but those who are unlearned will die in poverty of heart. What is more pitiable than an unlearned priest, who, even if he does not have the office of preaching, is nevertheless, by reason of the order he has received, bound to knowledge of the Scriptures?

For God wills that everyone fulfill his holy will, which no one who is ignorant of it is able to do. Therefore the Lord first commands that you learn what is pleasing to him; secondly, that you do it. How then will you think ignorance of the law excusable, through which you have first become transgressors of the will of God?

Why do you think almighty God handed over to human beings the volumes of his Scriptures? Was it so that they should read them, and that they should be understood by them, or so that, unread, they should be despised? Certainly the Scriptures of God’s commandments were given to mortals so that they should read them, and thereafter so that they should fulfill them in deed. But you, who with deliberate mind wish to be ignorant of God’s writings: how [unclear] God’s pleasure handed over the volumes of Scripture to all his own? Or will you be able to be useful, who were not hearers before?

For it can happen that one who knows the will of God either observes it or neglects it; but it cannot happen that one who is ignorant of it fulfills it. Indeed, someone will more easily fail to do the good that he knows than fulfill in deed what he does not know. No one does the good that he does not know. Saint Augustine says in a certain place concerning the ignorant: Not everyone who is ignorant is free from fault. For that ignorant person can be excused from punishment who did not find what he might learn. But it will not be possible to pardon those who, having persons from whom they might learn, did not give their effort to instruction.

Hence also Saint Leo the pope says: If ignorance seems intolerable in laypeople, how much more in those who are in authority; nor is it worthy of excuse or pardon. Therefore, brothers, ignorance of the divine Scriptures does not make you excused before God, but doubly guilty, you who desire to be utterly ignorant of what it is fitting for you to do concerning the will of God. For a man ought not to be ignorant of the divine will [unclear]; it is necessary for the salvation of every mortal, which [unclear] he will find without knowledge of Scripture.

Indeed, just as from knowledge [unclear] the fear of God comes into human beings, and from its knowledge love is born, so from ignorance there comes [unclear] you will think excusable, through which you have first become transgressors of the will of God. The Scriptures of God’s commandments were given; thereafter, that they should be fulfilled in deed.

But you, who [unclear] disciples, shamefully ignorant in mind, unruly and wandering, to whom we impute ignorance all the more because they are less inclined to discipline. It is shameful indeed not to know what you are ordered to know; more shameful not to learn it; but most shameful of all to despise it. And there are some among you who do not know saving knowledge [unclear], if I should add that there are also others who utterly despise the knowledge of the divine Scriptures. Certainly I do not lie: you know that what I say is true.

For some of you have opposed my studies gravely, even to the point of envy, seeking, at their urging, to bring me into denial of the Scriptures, so that they might make me a tiller of fields and a keeper of pigs rather than of souls. But they strive in vain to hinder the divine oracle; under its impulse I have resolved, as long as I live, to set all the honors and riches of the world beneath the study of the Scriptures.

I am your abbot as long as he who called me shall will it. If one of the two is necessary, I prefer to give up the abbacy rather than renounce the holy study of the Scriptures. For I know truly that nothing more salutary can befall a cloistered man in this life than if he has begun truly to love the divine Scriptures.

Whoever among you wishes to follow my instruction will have me as leader of the journey and likewise as companion. But whoever has scorned to follow me as I learn will nevertheless be compelled to hear me as I teach, even unwillingly. These things have been said against those who, savoring earthly and passing things, cast away from themselves the fear of the Lord; who, ignorant of almost everything, despise learning.

I know the face of my flock, and I believe that I am not wholly ignorant of the inclinations of each of your hearts. Therefore I shall not cease to exhort you to the holy studies of the Scriptures, knowing that a lover of sacred reading cannot be a doer of fleshly vices. For the more

De quotidiana renouascti propositi. monachus in perdiscendis scripturis fu¬ erit studiosior: tanto minus carnaliuꝫ vo¬ luptatum ardoribus inflammatur. Quā¬ uis enim: uxta sententiaꝫ diui Hierony¬ mi: monachū non docentis: sed plangē¬ ris potius videatur habere officiū: quia tamen christi profitetur militiam: congru̇ it immo necessariuꝫ est vt dei omnipoten¬ tis in cuius verba iurauit et arma: bene¬ placitam nouerit voluntatem. Uerum si¬ cut miles voluntatem domini sui procul abscentis scire non potest nisi per nuncios et cpistolas: ita monachꝰ eterni regis pre¬ cepta non intelliget nisi per saceros lectio¬ nes atqƺ sermones: euangelicas scriptu¬ ras. Iannuam salutis nescientibus lectio scripturarum aperit: studiosum lectorem recto tramite ad dei notitiam introducit amatorem sui facit omnia mundana con¬ tennere et nihil aliud qͣꝫ veram sapienti¬ am amare. Nihil autem turpius quam in spirituali conuersatione monachū nol¬ le proficere et voluntateꝫ dei scienter vel¬ le ignorare. Nemo sibi de sua infirmitate vel ignorantia blandiatur: quoniam qui ignorat ignorabitur et qui scientiam odit saluarem merito condemnatur. Missu¬ rus in omnem terrā predicatorē domi¬ nus premonnit dicens. Prudentes esto¬ re sicut serpentes: et simplices sicut colū¬ be: ne vel supplāteris ab aliquo per igno¬ rantiaꝫ: vel iniuriā struas alicui per frau¬ dem. Paruꝫ nanqƺ distati in vitio: vel de¬ cipere posse vel decipi. Rogo vos igitur fratres charissimi vt in regulam dūi pa¬ tris nostri Benedicti velitis intendere: que vos monet in plerisqƺ locis frequen¬ tius lectionibus diuinarum scripturarū insudare. In scripturis em̄ docemur ad omnim pietatem informati quemadmo¬ dum in hac breuissima peregrinatiōe hu¬ ius incolatus debeamus viuere: vt do¬ mino deo nostro possimus super omnia placere. Monachorum nanqƺ est mundū et omnes voluptates presentis vite pro dei amore contemnere: motus carnis illici¬ tos viriliter compꝛimere: orationi quoqƺ lectioni et meditationi scripturarum inisi¬ stere: et mentem a terrenis ad celestia iu¬ giter eleuare. Beatus ille monachꝰ qui non abijt in consilio impioꝛū: et in via pec¬ catorum non stetit: et in cathedra homi¬ num pestilentiuꝫ non sedit: sed in lege do¬ mini meditatū die ac nocte: discens hic in scripturis dei sapientiaꝫ: cuius fructuꝫ recepturus est post huius peregrinatio¬ nis terminum vitam eternam. De quotidiana reno¬ uatione sancti propositi: Omnia quinta: A Udiuin? fratres charissi¬ mi lectionē nob̓ recitataꝫ de libro sancti iob: in qͣ hu¬ mani generis deplangit miseriam: et huius calamī¬ tatem vite: simul ac insta¬ bilem breuitarem. Homo inquit natus de muliere: breui viuens tempore: reple¬ tur multis miserijs: qui quasi flos egre¬ ditur: et conteritur: et fugit velut vmbra: et nunquam in eodem statu permanet. Ec¬ ce inquit breues anni transeunt: et semi¬ ram per quam non reuertar ambulo. De¬ ficiet omnis caro simul: et homo in cine¬ rem reuertetur. Quid inter hec fratres animaduertitis: quid ue cogitatis? Est ne in nobis homo qui se nesciat esse mor¬ talem: qui cum veritate possit dicere: non mouebor in eternum? Heu fratres mei quam sumus ceci oculos tenentes aper¬ tos: quam obliuiesi viatores summis et de¬ sides: qui nos certo certius nouimus esy¬ ste morturos: erita in vanitate presentis vite confidimus: ac si non essemus moꝛ¬ tales. Sed quis est homo: qui viuet nō videbit mortem: eruet animam suam de¬ manu inferi? Ecce ait scriptura: omnes moritur: et quasi aqua dilabimur super terram. Idcirco memoria estote fratres meū: quoniam mors non tardat: et breue computabitur omne quod preterijt: quia vt sanctus ait christophilus paulus: sta¬ turum est hominibus seinel mori: quam¬ le gem necessitatis communem nemo po¬ terit subterfugere. O si nūc venture moꝛ¬ tis horam quam vnusquisqƺ nostrum ne¬ cessario subibit in breui: quotidie ante me̓¬ tis intuitum poneremus: taliterque vi¬ tam disponeremus et moꝛes quo semper mueniremur parati: qͣꝫ felix et tuta fieri posset emigratio nostra. Nonne et rex vi¬ uorum et mortuorum ipse christus domī¬ nus noster ad mortem nos semper volēs esse paratos in sancto euangelio premo¬ nuit dicens? Ideo et vos estote parati: quia qua hora non putabitis: filius ho¬ minis veniet. Quantum vero prosit ad

On the daily renewal of resolve.

... the more zealous a monk has been in learning the Scriptures, the less is he inflamed by the fires of carnal pleasures. For although, according to the opinion of Saint Jerome, the monk seems to have the office not of one who teaches, but rather of one who laments, nevertheless, because he professes the warfare of Christ, it is fitting, indeed necessary, that he know the well-pleasing will of almighty God, to whose words and arms he has sworn. But just as a soldier cannot know the will of his lord when he is far absent except through messengers and letters, so the monk will not understand the commands of the eternal King except through sacred readings and sermons, the evangelical Scriptures.

The reading of the Scriptures opens the gate of salvation to those who do not know; it leads the studious reader by a straight path to the knowledge of God; it makes the lover of it despise all worldly things and love nothing other than true wisdom. But nothing is more shameful than for a monk in the spiritual life to be unwilling to make progress, and knowingly to wish to be ignorant of the will of God. Let no one flatter himself on account of his weakness or ignorance, since he who is ignorant will be ignored, and he who hates saving knowledge is deservedly condemned. When the Lord was about to send the preacher into all the earth, he forewarned him, saying: Be prudent as serpents and simple as doves, lest either you be tripped up by someone through ignorance, or you contrive injury against someone through deceit. For there is little difference in fault between being able to deceive and being deceived. I ask you therefore, dearest brothers, that you be willing to attend to the Rule of our lord father Benedict, which admonishes you in many places to toil very frequently in readings of the divine Scriptures. For in the Scriptures we are taught, instructed unto all piety, how we ought to live in this very brief pilgrimage of our sojourn, so that we may be able to please the Lord our God above all things. For it belongs to monks to despise the world and all the pleasures of the present life for the love of God; manfully to restrain the unlawful motions of the flesh; to devote themselves also to prayer, reading, and meditation on the Scriptures; and continually to raise the mind from earthly things to heavenly. Blessed is that monk who has not gone away in the counsel of the impious, and has not stood in the way of sinners, and has not sat in the chair of pestilential men, but meditates on the law of the Lord day and night, learning here in the Scriptures the wisdom of God, whose fruit, after the end of this pilgrimage, he is to receive: eternal life.

On the daily renewal of holy resolve: [unclear] the fifth:

You have heard, dearest brothers, the reading recited to us from the book of holy Job, in which he laments the misery of the human race, and the calamity of this life, together with its unstable brevity. “Man,” he says, “born of woman, living for a brief time, is filled with many miseries; he comes forth like a flower and is crushed, and flees like a shadow, and never remains in the same state.” “Behold,” he says, “the brief years pass by, and I walk a path by which I shall not return.” “All flesh will fail together, and man will return to ashes.” What, brothers, do you observe among these things, or what do you think? Is there any man among us who does not know himself to be mortal, who could truthfully say, “I shall not be moved forever”? Alas, my brothers, how blind we are, though we hold our eyes open; how forgetful and sluggish we are as travelers, we who know most certainly that we are going to die, and yet trust in the vanity of the present life as if we were not mortal. But who is the man who will live and not see death, who will rescue his soul from the hand of hell? Behold, Scripture says, all die, and like water we flow away upon the earth. Therefore remember, my brothers, that death does not delay, and all that has passed will be counted brief; because, as the holy lover of Christ Paul says, it is appointed for men to die once, and no one will be able to escape this common law of necessity. O if now we were daily to set before the gaze of the mind the hour of coming death, which each one of us must necessarily undergo shortly, and if we were so to order our life and conduct that we might always be found prepared, how happy and secure our departure could become. Did not the King of the living and the dead, Christ himself our Lord, wishing us always to be prepared for death, forewarn us in the holy Gospel, saying: Therefore you also must be ready, because at the hour when you do not think it, the Son of Man will come. But how much it profits to...

For purity of mind, frequent meditation on death: the Wise Man in Ecclesiasticus warned us, saying: “In all your works remember your last things, and you will not sin forever.” Thought of future death brings in fear; fear, however, necessarily shakes the mind, and, like a nail driven by a hammer, fastens all the movements of the flesh and of pride to the wood of the cross. In consideration of this opinion, many of the gentile philosophers used to say that the whole life of a wise man is a certain continual meditation on death.

Hence Saint Jerome also says: Nothing will profit you so much toward temperance in all things as frequent meditation on this brief and uncertain life, which passes away like a leaf carried off by the wind, and, when it is not feared, falls into death. Therefore remember your death, which you can escape by no counsel, and you will easily be able to overcome all movements of the flesh. For he who daily thinks that he is going to die despises present things, and, unless he is utterly foolish, will prepare himself for the things to come.

For I know, and I confess that I have in part experienced it, that the will of the human mind cannot long remain uniform in the holy fervor of the spiritual life; and therefore it has seemed good to call the memory of death often back before your eyes, so that, while the mind is shaken by fear of future things, the fervor of the holy purpose may be renewed daily. For the human spirit, bound to the body for the exercise of itself, is exceedingly fluid and unstable: now it is snatched toward this, now it is moved toward that. Therefore the Wisdom of God says in Proverbs through Solomon: “My son, give me your heart, and let your eyes keep my ways.” As though he were saying: Unless you have enslaved the whole love of your heart to divine wisdom, you will never be stable and confirmed in keeping the commandments of the Lord.

For just as the heart is the first principle of motion in a human being, so there is the greater need to guard it for the preservation of life, since, if it is struck by an uncertain disease, the whole life of the body is already in danger. Hence it is written: “With all watchfulness keep your heart, because life proceeds from it.” By the name of the heart, however, we understand the affection by which someone is drawn aside toward love of some thing, clinging to it so much that it involves the whole will. Hence the psalmist says: “If riches abound, do not set your heart on them,” that is, do not love them from the desire of the will.

Nothing is more changeable than the human heart, which is altered by almost every thought and can with difficulty remain in the same purpose unless it restrains itself by a certain violent intention. Saint David, not ignorant of this, said to the Lord: “But I said in my abundance: I shall not be moved forever. Lord, in your will you gave strength to my beauty. You turned your face away from me, and I was troubled.”

Therefore, my most beloved brothers, if any one of you desires to serve our Lord and Savior in true purity of heart, if anyone wishes to be a monk both in deed and in name, let him learn first not to trust in himself but in God, and let him take care to renew the good purpose of holy conduct always by fresh instruction, not only daily but, as far as he is able, even at each hour and moment. For the fervor of spiritual conduct, to whose practical operation the whole institution of cloistered life is recognized to be ordered, cannot long remain at the same point, since, if it does not always advance toward what lies ahead, it necessarily runs back toward lower things and, what is worse, weaker things.

In the arena of spiritual exercises there is no lingering permanence of station, because it is the property of the human heart by its natural motion always either to advance toward better things or to fall back into that which is evil. Hence, if you do not make progress in spiritual conduct, you necessarily fail; if you do not go forward toward holier things, you certainly retreat. Since experience has made this clear to us, I do not cease to admonish your charity that you always stretch your desire in good conduct toward what lies further ahead, lest you fall into the destructive danger of failing in the very place where you have not renewed the appetite for making progress.

The fervor of a spiritual purpose directs one toward the love of God, and it is preserved in no other way than in him. Now the love of God is not absurdly to be compared to fire, because, just as fire, when the fuel of wood has been withdrawn, is necessarily extinguished, so the love of God, if the continual exercises of good works are lacking, is in danger of dying and vanishing away. Hence there is that saying of the Savior in the Gospel: “I have come to send fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it burn?” O monks, happy is that conscience in whose breast nothing burns except the love of Christ, which loves God above all things, which despises all pursuits of vanity. Now, brothers, consider your consciences most diligently and examine them exactly, whether you love God above all things

Si ardet in vobis iam ignis dmini amoris: quatenus fomentum adhibeatis nev tessariu: ne quando per vestra tepiditate sancti fervoris igniculu sentiatis penieet extincetu. Areditte mihi fratres q̄ mi experientia me docuit igne in vobis divini fervoris ardentē faciliore exercitio conserva binis: quam extincuti denuo succendatis. Quicunque igitur ia in se dei experit amorem: quicunque celestē in corde suo recepit charitatem: summa cum sollicitudine carēt in prioris vite regligentias recedere: fomenta adhibeat necessaria spiritualius exercitioru quatenus proficiente in se dei fervorem queat conservare. Cauet non solu peccata grandia: sed etiam negligentias paruas 7 quanti poterit minimas: q̄ qui minimā sperit paulatim decidit 7 qui non semper metuit periculū spirituālis fervoris ac s propositi cito sentier de erimentu. Dicit em scriptura: Si non in stanter tenueris te in timore domini: cito subvertetur domus tua. Beatus igitur homo qui semper est pauidus: qui de acceptris virtutibus non presumit qui certo stimat se deficere: quotiens se nó inveinerit singulis momentis ad altiora profecisse. Sed vere? fratres 7 vehemiciet stimo: nisi me operu quozundam fallat stimatio: sonullis in vobis igne suivius sancti neçdum adcesse fervoris: quippe cum vera monachoru studia paru videantur diligere: quod et illori sonversatione cusit manefistũ: nullus vestru3 poterit ignoreare. Quos monere quidem non duripenitus superfluũ: quis parum hacetenus vi clear profeciffe: cuni nó sit abbreviata ma nus domini: quo min? queat salutare pe nitentes. Cofido em in misericordia dei viventis: qui propter nicã in cos charita sem1 7 exercitia pietatis illoru qui ad pu ritatem segule in vobis ambulant: dabit eiis aliquando seipsicere: studia sancti fervoris ardentius amare. Quid est fra tres quod nó monastice in monasterio vi vitis: 7 profetis sonversatione spiritus: se cũduz carne ambulatis: si nescitis quã sit periculorum in cenobio monachu seculariter viuere: 7 votis sancte puritatis q̄ semifimus omnes: tepida sonversatione violare. Ognoscite precor: q̄i nouiffima omniu clausariu extremitis sunt pro pima: ve boni 7 zelosi amatores propriie salutis monachi: non vulgariu sed masi Omelia. V. Fo. XIII.

On the daily renewal of holy purpose.

If the fire of divine love now burns in you, apply the necessary fuel, lest through your lukewarmness you should at some time feel the little flame of holy fervor utterly extinguished. Believe me, brothers, for my own experience has taught me: you will preserve the fire of divine fervor burning in you with easier exercise than you will kindle it again once it has been extinguished.

Whoever, therefore, has already experienced in himself the love of God, whoever has received heavenly charity in his heart, let him take the greatest care not to fall back into the negligences of his former life. Let him apply the necessary fuel of spiritual exercises, so that he may be able to preserve in himself the fervor of God as it advances. Let him beware not only of great sins, but also of small negligences, and, as far as he can, of the very least; for he who despises the least things gradually falls, and he who does not always fear danger to spiritual fervor and holy purpose will quickly feel the loss.

For Scripture says: “If you do not steadfastly keep yourself in the fear of the Lord, your house will quickly be overthrown.” Blessed, therefore, is the man who is always fearful, who does not presume upon the virtues he has received, who judges with certainty that he is failing whenever he has not found himself advancing at every moment toward higher things.

But truly, brothers, I judge very strongly, unless the assessment of certain works deceives me, that in some of you the fire of holy fervor is not yet present, since they seem to love the true pursuits of monks but little. That this is manifest from their conduct none of you will be able to ignore. I have indeed not considered it wholly superfluous to admonish those who so far seem to have made little progress, since the hand of the Lord has not been shortened so that it cannot save the penitent.

For I trust in the mercy of the living God, who, because of his very great charity toward them and because of the exercises of piety of those who walk among you according to the purity of the rule, will grant them at some time [to conquer themselves?], to love the pursuits of holy fervor more ardently.

What is this, brothers, that you do not live monastically in the monastery, and, having professed the life of the spirit, walk according to the flesh? Do you not know how perilous it is for a monk to live in worldly fashion in a cenobium, and by lukewarm conduct to violate the vows of holy purity which all of us once made?

Know, I pray, that the last things of all cloistered persons are very near the end, so that, as good and zealous monks who love your own salvation, not of common things but rather
