Melia .XI. carnalibus: ex abundantia cordis nihil aliud quam vana et carnalia loquun- tur. Corrumpunt enim mores iuuenum bonos: senū colloquia praua. Vana sunt cuncta illorum studia: et mutiles immo pestiferi sermones: qui carnali ter sapientes diuini amoris exercitia nō nouerūt. Eīn uero sicut vna ouis morbida paulatim rniuersum corrumpit ouile: ita vnus in cōgregatione monachus accidiosus et ꝑuersus: multarū sepe fit causa transgressionum. Quemadmodū sancto christophilo testante modicum fermentum totā farine massam cui miscetur suo corrumpit odoꝛe: ita monachi iuuenes atqꝫ non cij qui cuꝫ tepidis et accidiosis conuersantur senioribus illorū prauis moribus imbuuntur: et nun deinceps ad sancti feruoris integritate̓ reformantur. Quo circa vobis senioribus dico: Estote bonis operibus castisqꝫ et semp̄ pudicis sermo- nibus iuuenum forma viuendi: vt quotiens pro suis emendantur delictis: senio- rũ se non tueantur exemplis. Turpissimum est enim seniores in illis esse culpa- biles: pro quibus merito corripiuntur iniores. Ita precor senes viuite: vt coram vobis nihil quod videatur esse reprehensibile: iuniores aut loqui presumāt aut facere. Iudices vos timeant maloruꝫ: non patronatus vicem agentes: quoniā quotquot exemplo vestri peccauerint: vestro perisse magisterio reputantur. Nō fit inter vos tepidus quisquā aut desidiosus: quoniā et desideria occidunt pigruꝫ: et perimit vanitas omnium monachū ociosuꝫ Non sit in vobis homo verbosus: girouagus: circumcellio: murmursans et inquire- tus: quoniā quisquis talibus delectatur studijs: et se malo perdit opere: et fratrem suu̓ occidit exēplis. Non sit inter vos irrisor simplicium: nō humiliꝫ contemptor: aut temerarius quis taxator: quoniam qui ad irridentū est promptulus: in stuilititia sua consūmabitur: et non erit gloriosus. Os suū aperit contra humileꝫ: semper queritur iurgia: et gaudet se factis aliorum esse loquacem. Non prosperabitur in consilio suo: et si fuerit aliquo sublimatus honore: cito corruet in ꝓfundū. Odi bilis est deo superbia eius: quoniam cuꝫ fit stultus et fatuus: crudituꝫ se gloriatur et sapientē. Lito denudabitur insipientia eius: et grauis cum occupabit interitus. F o . XXVI. Cor eius meditaritur stultitay: et non est pax in circuitu eius. Odio erit proximis atqꝫ vicinis: et nullus illuꝫ fidelis profe- quetur amicus. Uitam ducit in hypocrifi assumpta simulationis: et multos suastultitia trahet in auersionem. Dace̓ odit discordiam diligit: in ignauia mentis sue capietur: et non erit qui condoleat. Affli- ctione duplici cōteretur: pro eo qđ habentibus paceꝫ non permisit. Diabolus in lingua eius nidum composuit: et sathanas in mente illius fixit domiciliuꝫ. Propter ea non est amor fratrum in corde ipsius. quoniam disseminat inter pastoꝛem et oues discordiam. Amicum se dei gloria- tur et similem in obseruantia regulari ne minem accipit: sed maximum ornamen- tum monachi humilitateꝫ non intelligit. Os suum ad verba spiritualis edificatio nis non aperit: et ex corde illius nihil aliud quam vanitas procedit. Diem totam mēte dissolutus et corpore vagus: discurrit in cenobio: sermoni vacat inutili et penitus ocioso: nihil de salute anime cogitar: ventrem pro deo curat. Custodi mentem tuam ab eius eloquio: et in viam fermonum eius pedem tuum ne posueris. Quisquis te monachum et dei ministrū exhibere desideras: quisquis domiuꝫ iesuꝫ in toto corde veraciter amas esto cautus et vigilans in omnibus operibus tuis: et consortia semper eorum fugito: in quorū vita nihil doctrine celestis contempsitur: Humilium et perfectionem fecantium monachorum comes esto et sommo qui omni vento cedit agitatus: sed confirma in bono proposito animam tum amare: aut prauorū decipiari costilio. Optimum est enim gratia stabiliꝛe cor: et exemplo instruit ad bonum: ama et venerare vt patrem. Cum fratre inquieto non habeas aliquod familiaritatis com̄ertium: ne quando eius confortatus prauo exemplo in rebellionem incidas superborum. Monachus iracundus et murmuratorne plenus non fit in latere tuo: et cum qui

Homily XI.

...with the carnal: out of the abundance of the heart they speak nothing but vain and carnal things. For the wicked conversations of old men corrupt the good morals of the young. All their pursuits are vain, and their speeches useless, indeed pestilential, since, being carnally minded, they have not known the exercises of divine love. Indeed, just as one sick sheep gradually corrupts the whole sheepfold, so one slothful and perverse monk in a congregation often becomes the cause of many transgressions. As Saint [Christophilus?] bears witness, a little leaven corrupts with its odor the whole mass of flour with which it is mixed; so young monks, and [unclear], who associate with lukewarm and slothful elders, are imbued with their depraved habits and thereafter are never restored to the integrity of holy fervor. Therefore I say to you elders: be, by good works and chaste and always modest speech, a model of life for the young, so that whenever they are corrected for their offenses, they may not defend themselves by the examples of the elders. For it is most shameful that elders should be guilty in those things for which the younger are deservedly reproved. Live, I pray, old men, in such a way that in your presence the younger may presume neither to say nor to do anything that seems blameworthy.

Let them fear you as judges of evils, not as acting the part of patrons, since as many as sin by your example are reckoned to have perished by your teaching. Let no one among you become lukewarm or negligent, since desires kill the lazy man, and the vanity of all things destroys the idle monk. Let there be among you no talkative man, no wandering monk, no roving idler, murmuring and restless, since whoever delights in such pursuits both ruins himself by evil conduct and kills his brother by his examples. Let there be among you no mocker of the simple, no despiser of the humble, nor any rash censurer, since he who is quick to mock will be consumed in his foolishness and will not be glorious. He opens his mouth against the humble, is always seeking quarrels, and rejoices that he is talkative about the deeds of others.

He will not prosper in his counsel; and if he is raised to some honor, he will quickly fall into the depth. His pride is hateful to God, since, although he is stupid and foolish, he boasts that he is learned and wise. Soon his foolishness will be laid bare, and a grievous destruction will seize him.

Folio XXVI.

His heart meditates folly, and there is no peace around him. He will be hateful to those near him and to his neighbors, and no faithful friend will accompany him. He leads his life in hypocrisy, having assumed a pretense of dissimulation, and by his foolishness he will draw many into aversion. He hates peace and loves discord; he will be caught in the sloth of his mind, and there will be no one to grieve with him. He will be crushed by a double affliction, because he did not permit peace to those who had it. The devil has made a nest in his tongue, and Satan has fixed his dwelling in his mind. Therefore there is no love of the brethren in his heart, since he sows discord between the shepherd and the sheep. He boasts that he is a friend of God and accepts no one as his equal in regular observance, but he does not understand humility, the greatest ornament of a monk.

He does not open his mouth for words of spiritual edification, and from his heart nothing but vanity proceeds. All day long, dissolved in mind and wandering in body, he runs about in the monastery; he gives himself to useless and utterly idle speech; he thinks nothing of the salvation of his soul; he cares for his belly as God. Guard your mind from his speech, and do not set your foot in the way of his words.

Whoever desires to show himself a monk and minister of God, whoever truly loves the Lord Jesus with his whole heart, be cautious and watchful in all your works, and always flee the companionship of those in whose life nothing of heavenly doctrine is seen. Be the companion of humble monks seeking perfection and [unclear], who yields, shaken, to every wind; but strengthen your soul in a good purpose [unclear] to love, or be deceived by the counsel of the depraved. For it is best that the heart be established by grace; and the one who instructs by example toward the good, love and venerate as a father. Have no commerce of familiarity with a restless brother, lest at some time, strengthened by his depraved example, you fall into the rebellion of the proud. Let no angry and murmuring monk full of [unclear] be at your side; and with him who

49
De fugiendo praevarorum consortio. maioribus recalcitrat nunquam arbitres anmicum. Quiem videris sine benedictione senioris canonae violare ieiunii et hostem fuge salutis: qui loquacitate vel est non cristente causa subvertit pacem et suscitat lites. Quasi a facie colubri fuge monachum rebellem et inobedientem se mitibus: quoniam veneno malitie plen? estuat: et in elatione mentis perdidit animam suam. Qui non obediit mandato senioris perueris est: qui corruptus nobi inilitur apostata. Qui fratri suo detractens obloquitur: nō sit in colloquio tuo: quomam longe est fur et dexter. Quiem omni studio in observantia regulari vivendi sollicitum: ut patrem amabis et veneraberis et amantissimi preceptorem. Huius familiaritate confidenter vitaris: cuius amicitia semper in dei amore te faciat meliorem. Tiros totum studio imitare bonos: et illorum sequere mores: qui vivunt monastice perfectioni conformes. Fratrem bone voluntatis habe amicu: ab eo autem duri cordis est auerte aures tuas. Qui lenis est animo et moribus dissolutus: sit tibi quasi homo qui sepes in agro dissipat. Noli socius esse illius qui reguam et silentium contemnit: qui loca non discernit nec tempora: qui sine benedictione prioris ubiqus et multiplicat. Monachum vino et potationibus communiem monasterii canonem crebrius excedentem et fomentum luxurie et scaturiginei dei ta omnium vitiorum. Monachus qui consilio capitis sui contra seminosis mandati innititur perditioni est proximus: et festivus ambulat in periculo aniesue. Ne communicaveris operibus monachi pertinacis: et habeas illius amicitia: qui sua te meritate maioris factis cachinnans ob loquitur. In medio disciplinatorum esto continuus: et libenter cum humilibi ambulet anima tua. Qui enim viris coniungitur bonis: virtutem illorum participat: et qui cum malis graditur cadet in foueam. Monachus autem peruerse voluntatis seducitur plurimos: et qui contemnit obedientiam: niquae exaltabitur. Qui vocelquens extollit et clamat in altum vociferans: stultitia cordis sui non potest abscondere: et in vanitate sua gloriatur. Amicitia bonorum virorum firma salus est amicis et in societate praevarorum simplicius innocetia corruptitur. Societas illorum est optima: ma quorum dei timor confirmavit bonorum operum exempla. Aibil precesius amico timenti deum: et nihil periculosis socii qui praeve est voluntatis. Frater timens deum in toto corde suo: pro muro fortitudinis erit annco suo: et tali cui sanctitate mentis coniugitur: benedictione dei spiritus omni tempore sanctificatur. Quin medio timenti deum gratatur: quasi muro in circuio fortissimo ne deficiat sustentatur. Ex verbis suis cognoscitur seruus altissimi: et monachum bonum opera indicant sanctitatis. Omne verbum turpe scurile: et ocius ab ore timenti domini non egreditur: et qui verus amator est iecu: nihil quod offendat bonitate operatur. In ore monachorum amantis semper christus resonat: et qui verus est dei culor: sermonem iusticie in ore simul et in opere demonstrat. Qui timet deum consiliarius est optimus: et qui ad canonem ambulat iudex est prudens cogitationum. Senior timens deum et in observantia regulari multo tempore probatus et experitus director est iuuenum: et qui nō habet in vestre maculam bonus in stitutor: sit novitio: um. Qui divinarum est intelligens doctor et explanator scripturarum custodiens in humilitate animas suas: omnia verba eius sine rea libenter excipe: quoniam nervos habet et soliditatem future felicitatis eterne. Qui vere docet et infirmanti copa titur: et qui iecum diligit: fluentem animo ad fortitudinem cohoratatur. Qui cum homine verboso graditur: non evadet contentione: et qui delectatur mendacio: nun quae erit sapientie amicus. Qui assiduus est in externis: non erit proficiens: et sine causa gloriatur se monachum. Cito propositu sanctitatis coarputur: quando monachus extra cellam cui desiderio frequenterius evagatur. Qui secretum celle suae sine mandato senioris deserit: ad perfectum sancti propositi nō cotendit. Bonorum virorum ac deum timenti pulchra societas: et qui coluerit habitare cum eis non sentiet confusionem. Tabula mundi est coi monachi iuuenis: in qua seniorus conversatio nuncup delenda inscribitur. Cordis pulchri scriptor est pessimus: senior qui turpia coizam iuueni vel agit: et loquitur. Qui sermone teuerario iuueni inficit: quasi herodes impius qui

On fleeing the company of transgressors.

...kicks against his superiors, never consider him a friend. Whomever you see violating the canon of fasting without the blessing of an elder, flee as an enemy of salvation; likewise the man who by talkativeness, or for a [unclear] reason, overturns peace and stirs up quarrels. As from the face of a snake, flee the monk who is rebellious and disobedient to his elders, since he seethes full of the poison of malice and, in the pride of his mind, has lost his soul. He who does not obey the command of an elder is perverse; he who, corrupted, [unclear] is an apostate. Let not the man who speaks slanderously against his brother be in conversation with you, because [unclear] is far off and [unclear].

Whomever you find wholly solicitous in every zeal to live in regular observance, love and venerate as a father and a most beloved teacher. With confidence enjoy the familiarity of him whose friendship always makes you better in the love of God. With all zeal imitate good men, and follow the conduct of those who live in conformity with monastic perfection. Have as a friend the brother of good will; but turn your ears away from him who is of hard heart. Let the man who is soft in spirit and dissolute in conduct be to you like a man who breaks down hedges in a field. Do not be the companion of him who despises the rule and silence, who distinguishes neither places nor times, who without the prior’s blessing everywhere [unclear] and multiplies [unclear]. The monk who, given to wine and drinking, rather often exceeds the common canon of the monastery is the fuel of lust and the spring [unclear] of all vices.

The monk who relies on the counsel of his own head against the [unclear] command is close to perdition, and walks festively in danger of his soul. Do not share in the works of an obstinate monk, nor have friendship with the man who, laughing at the deserved deeds of his superior, speaks against them. Be continually in the midst of disciplined men, and let your soul gladly walk with the humble. For he who is joined to good men shares in their virtue, and he who walks with the wicked will fall into a pit. But a monk of perverse will leads very many astray; and he who despises obedience will never be exalted. He who lifts up his voice and cries out with loud shouting cannot hide the foolishness of his heart, and glories in his vanity.

The friendship of good men is firm salvation for friends, and in the company of transgressors simple innocence is corrupted. The company of those men is best in whom the fear of God has confirmed examples of good works. Nothing is more precious than a friend who fears God, and nothing more dangerous than a companion who is of perverse will. A brother who fears God with all his heart will be a wall of strength for his friend; and the man joined to such a one in holiness of mind is sanctified at all times by the blessing of the Spirit of God. He who rejoices in the midst of those who fear God is sustained, lest he fail, as if by a very strong wall around him.

From his words the servant of the Most High is known, and works of holiness reveal the good monk. No foul or scurrilous word comes quickly from the mouth of one who fears the Lord; and he who is a true lover of Jesus does nothing that offends goodness. In the mouth of monks who love [God], Christ always resounds; and he who is a true worshipper of God demonstrates the discourse of righteousness both in his mouth and in his work. He who fears God is the best counsellor; and he who walks according to the canon is a prudent judge of thoughts. An elder who fears God and has long been proved and experienced in regular observance is a director of the young; and he who has no stain in his garment should be a good instructor for novices. He who is an understanding teacher and expounder of the divine scriptures, guarding his soul in humility: receive all his words gladly without [unclear], since he has the sinews and solidity of future eternal happiness.

He who teaches truly also suffers with the infirm; and he who loves Jesus encourages the wavering spirit to strength. He who walks with a verbose man will not escape contention; and he who delights in falsehood will never be a friend of wisdom. He who is assiduous in external things will not make progress, and boasts without cause that he is a monk. The purpose of holiness is quickly corrupted when a monk wanders outside his cell rather too often through [unclear] desire. He who abandons the secrecy of his cell without the command of an elder does not strive toward the perfection of the holy purpose. Beautiful is the company of good men and of those who fear God; and he who has chosen to live with them will not feel confusion.

The heart of a young monk is the tablet of the world, on which the conduct of elders is now inscribed, [unclear] to be erased. The worst writer of a beautiful heart is the elder who either does or says shameful things [unclear] before a young man. He who infects a young man with reckless speech is like the impious Herod who

Omelia XII: pueros interfecit. Paluz quod iuuenis a senex stulto et negligente recipit:etā pre/ sbyter facrus non emēdabit. Omne vas quod impletur a ceto corrupcitur:et mo/ nachus qui in noviātu negligentur: cum senuerit nō emendatur. Daledict? senex cuius mala conversatione percunt iuuenes: quoniam qui sequentibus relinquit mala vestigia: quasi qui cecum sua manu precipitauit in foveam. Apud internum iudicez tot quisq moritib? dign? est:quot innocentes pravo exemplo eius perierit Senem vite moderatorem tue requiritu inuenis.nou qui multos cōpleuit annos in sua conversatione dissoluta et tepida.sz quem timor domini et scripturarū dei sci/ entia cōmendat. Deliz? est societas mo/ nachī adolescentis qui timet dominum: quā senex doctoris contubernium cuius vita non habet lumen amoris divini: & re/ gularis obseruannie integritatez. Ŝener moribus incompōsitus indigens mundi/ cia mentis et carens disciplina: quasi qui Iesus in tibia claudus ducitur ad sepul/ chrum. Monachus senex et dissolutus:si nilis est homini fatuo qui nesciens fines cum latronibus in convivio potantium capitur. Senex sine maturitate: quasi fi/ stula sambuci contrita pedibus ludentiū Gane gloriatur se multis diebus eritisse monachū:qui conversationis interne nō percepit inicium. Qui cordis sui munditi am siligit: consortio indisciplinatoz sratrum se omni tempore custodit. Sicur adherens vestibus saltantiuz macula pi/ cis contristat virginitātis qui bon? est in uenis ad turpia verba senioruz crubescit: Aascius sermo non est hominis deum timentis:quoniam ex abundātia cordis os loquitur: & qui turpia profert eloquia: nō est mundus coram altissimo. Si odirete ceperint peccatores propter timorem dei non contristeris:qua nīl malis displicēas bonozum perfectionē non apprehendes Dalis enim displicere propter iustiāni laudabile est: & divini amoris manifestuz inditiū Si diligis alaz tua fuge ssilia in disciplinatoy. & cu derisorib ne cōmuni/ caueris. Cum bonis ambula: & qui timet dominum fiat consiliarius tuus. Demonachis in viā directis. Omelia: Fo.XXVII, Monachorum est mundi fugere:et hominuz turbas amore solitudinis quam- tum prevalent omnitem pore declinare. A solitudi- ne monach? dicitur:licue ab unicate unus nominatur. Donach? essenon potest qui frequentiam lectatur populorum:et qui delectatur in sribibus monasticam nec duz gustavit dulcedinē. Qui monachus es cenobī solitudinem sine causa rationabili non debes defercere et qui obligaris ad silētiu noli colloquyis oblectari mūdan orū. Quisquis amat va gos in viāe discursus conscientiaz suam deseruit. & qui frequens est extra monaste rium suī puritate interni profectus non custodit. Qui domos parentum circum epulis delectatur proximorum se non co/ fiderat monachum: & qui pergit ad coi uia potātiu interficit animā suā Qui doz mit in domo cognati sui querit solatia:et qui declinat religiosorum convuentus. p/ niciosam sequitur libertatem. Donach? in domo patris et matris quasi agnus in medio luporum: & quasi lepus qui vena/ torum circumdatus est canibus. Hi mo/ nach? es. Si dei servus et miles:quid facis in domo parētu:aut quid requiris in me/ dio populo? Monachus extra cenobiun dīu manens in medio secularium:quasi homo qui sub aquarum profundo sepelitū ynigenitum suum. Nam sicuti piscibus non est vita in arido:ita mona/ chis non est salus animē in seculo. Extra flumen piscis moritur: & monachi consci entie puritas cito extra monasterium vi/ latur. Monachorum vita in cenobio:et mores animozum in medio secularium. Dagna virtus animi est tur/ bas hominum fugere.aut quibus inter- esse fuerit omnino necessarium mente ta/ men declinare. Compellimur necessitate iter nonnuquam per mundum agere:sed tanto minus er homini soccursu puritas conscientie polluitnr:quanto mentis de/ fiderium a celle secreto minus elongatur Monēdus igitur nobis est monachus quisq bonus:vt quotiens pro cuiusq rei necessitate precepto senioris in viam di/ gitur:nunquam foris animē euagetur. Qui sensus suos nō custodit. obiecto ma/ li cito corrumpitur: & qui timorem domi/ ni abūcit,ad monāsteriuz impurus necel

Homily XII

He killed the boys. The evil that a young man receives from a foolish and negligent old man, even when he has been made a priest, he will not amend. Every vessel that is filled with filth is corrupted; and a monk who is negligent in the novitiate, when he has grown old, is not amended. Cursed is the old man by whose evil manner of life young men perish, because he who leaves evil tracks for those who follow is like one who with his own hand has cast a blind man headlong into a pit. Before the eternal Judge each man is worthy of as many deaths as there are innocents who have perished by his wicked example.

Young man, seek an old man as the guide of your life: not one who has completed many years in a lax and lukewarm manner of life, but one whom the fear of the Lord and knowledge of the divine Scriptures commend. Better is the company of a young monk who fears the Lord than the fellowship of an aged teacher whose life does not have the light of divine love and the integrity of regular observance. An old man disordered in morals, lacking purity of mind and without discipline, is like [unclear], lame in the leg, being led to the grave. An old and lax monk is like a foolish man who, not knowing the boundaries, is captured with robbers at a drinking banquet. An old man without maturity is like an elder-wood pipe crushed under the feet of players.

Vainly does he boast that he has been a monk for many days, if he has not grasped the beginning of inward conduct. He who loves the purity of his heart guards himself at all times from the company of undisciplined brothers. Just as a stain of pitch clinging to the garments of dancers grieves virginity, so a good young man blushes at the filthy words of elders. Lascivious speech does not belong to a man who fears God, because out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks; and he who utters filthy words is not clean before the Most High. If sinners begin to hate you because of the fear of God, do not be saddened, because unless you displease the wicked you will not attain the perfection of the good. For to displease the wicked on account of justice is praiseworthy, and a manifest sign of divine love. If you love your soul, flee the counsels of the undisciplined, and do not keep company with mockers. Walk with the good, and let him who fears the Lord be your counselor.

Concerning monks sent on the road. Homily.

Folio XXVII

It belongs to monks to flee the world, and, for love of solitude, to avoid the crowds of men at all times as much as they can. A monk is named from solitude, although he is called one from unity. He cannot be a monk who delights in the throng of peoples; and he who delights in cities has not yet tasted monastic sweetness. If you are a monk, you must not leave the solitude of the monastery without reasonable cause; and if you are bound to silence, do not delight in the conversations of worldly people. Whoever loves wandering excursions on the road has abandoned his conscience; and he who is often outside the monastery does not preserve the purity of his inward progress.

He who goes about the houses of his parents and delights in the feasts of neighbors does not consider himself a monk; and he who goes to the banquets of drinkers kills his own soul. He who sleeps in the house of his kinsman seeks comforts; and he who avoids the assemblies of the religious follows a destructive freedom. A monk in the house of father and mother is like a lamb in the midst of wolves, and like a hare surrounded by the dogs of hunters. If you are a monk, if you are God’s servant and soldier, what are you doing in the house of your parents, or what are you seeking in the midst of the people? A monk remaining long outside the monastery among secular people is like a man who buries his only son beneath the depth of waters. For just as there is no life for fish on dry land, so there is no salvation of soul for monks in the world. Outside the river the fish dies; and the purity of a monk’s conscience is quickly violated outside the monastery. The life of monks is in the monastery, and the [death?] of souls is in the midst of secular people.

It is a great virtue of the soul to flee the crowds of men, or, when it is entirely necessary to be among them, nevertheless to avoid them in mind. We are sometimes compelled by necessity to make a journey through the world; but the less the desire of the mind is drawn away from the secrecy of the cell, the less the purity of conscience is polluted by meeting men. Therefore every good monk must be admonished by us that, whenever by order of his senior he is sent on the road because of the necessity of any matter, his soul should never wander outward. He who does not guard his senses is quickly corrupted when evil is set before him; and he who casts away the fear of the Lord, [unclear] impure to the monastery

Aum efluit renus.limo¬ sitate sua pulchritudinem patentiū in cir cuitu pratorum commiaculat:et dum fa¬ bulis secularium intendit monachus pu ritatem conscientie deturpat.Antequam ergo de monasterio ponas pedem tuum sanctis te orationibus munias:et priusqƺ egrediaris viam domino precibus com¬ mendare non obmittas.Deinde quod le¬ gillator mandauit exequere:et orationibꝰ tam abbatis quam fratrum omnium tu endum te cōmitte.Canonem seueritatis obseruantie regularis tibi met ip̄i prescri¬ bito:sub cuius memoria stabili.ab omni animum defluxu occurrentium custodi¬ as vanitatum.De cenobio nusquam pro¬ grediaris sine benedictiōe abbatīs:quia cum debeas esse mortuus atqƺ sepultus huic seculo.non licebit tibi quicquam vl¬ terius absqƺ senioris imperio.Militeʒ te¬ regis iesu christi agnoscito:tuum impera¬ torem sequaris oportet:sine quo nō est sa¬ lus.Ille cruci affixus.non suis sed alioꝝ manibus deponitur:et tu si cupis saluari necesse est tua voluntas abbatis imperio gubernetur.Monachus enim qui ceno¬ bium sine permissione abbatis quoquā egreditur:quasi ouicula in tenebris que domus incendio cōcrematur.Verus au¬ tem christi monachus etiam extra ceno¬ bium existens corpore.in claustro mētis remanet:et non minus est solus cum mul¬ tis:quam in cella consueuit esse solitariꝰ. Amator christi etiam in medio multitudi¬ nis iesum cogitat:et qui verꝰ est operatoꝛ virtutū:in omni loco cor siuʒ in dei timo¬ re solidum conseruat.Nam et si corpoꝛe non fit in monasterio:corde tam propter vigoreʒ animi semper constitit stabilisqƺ¬ si solus iu claustro.Corpoꝛis motu spūs non polluitur:quādo mentis solitudo cu¬ stoditur.Eadem tibi sanctitate viuendū est in itinere o monache qua cōuersari iu¬ beris in cenobio:et maiore quadam gra¬ diendum cautela:ne quempiam remissio¬ re scandalizes exemplo:vbi tot monacho¬ rum sunt indices:quot inspectores adesse videntur.Omniū oculi seculariū in mo¬ nachos suspiciunt:et sanctitatē quā illos audiunt professos in operibus exquirūt. Plus offendit monachus in vno temera¬ rio verbo:quam homo seculo deditus in decem milibus.Quantūlibet enim leuis et scurrilis homo videatur mundanꝰ mo¬ nachorum tamen insolentiam equanimi¬ ter tolerare non didicit:quoniam omnes claustrales non quales sunt sed quales es¬ se deberēt.rustica simplicitate credit.Un¬ de malum verbum aut factuʒ apud illos monacho ad dānationē ascribitur:quod mundano homini ad veniam imputatur Nęc immerito.Monachus enim qui sā¬ ctum et approbatum canonem professus est.omnem conatum suum tenetur ad ꝑ¬ fectionem dirigere:et conuersationem ho¬ minum secularium verbo et opere in om¬ ni puritate mentis et corpoꝛis longe supe¬ rare.Verbum etenīʒ leue seu ociosū quod secularibus ad veniam conceditur:clati¬ stralibus ad interitum estimatur.Omni¬ bus metallis aurum preciosius est et am¬ plius a mortalibus cōcupiscitur:et in nul¬ lo citius macula vel corruptio falsitatis accusatur.Et viciū quod in auro iudicia¬ ria seueritate discernitur:in ceteris metal¬ lis pro vilitate nature dissimulatur.Aurū sua pulchritudine letificat oculos:et cōfor¬ tat in virtute sua precordia vite.Aurum conflatuʒ in igne non minuitur:et verus dei monachus in tribulatione persecute¬ nis a sanctitatis proposito non mutatur. Concerning monks sent on a journey.

[unclear] will return. A stream flowing out, by its muddiness, stains the beauty of the meadows lying open round about; and when a monk gives attention to the tales of secular people, he defiles the purity of his conscience. Therefore, before you set your foot out of the monastery, arm yourself with holy prayers; and before you go out on the road, do not neglect to commend your way to the Lord with prayers. Then carry out what the lawgiver has commanded, and entrust yourself to be protected by the prayers both of the abbot and of all the brothers. Prescribe for yourself the canon of the severity of regular observance, and, with a stable remembrance of it, guard your mind from every outflow of vanities that meet you.

Do not go anywhere out of the cenobium without the abbot’s blessing, because, since you ought to be dead and buried to this world, it will not be lawful for you to do anything further without the command of your elder. Recognize yourself as a soldier of King Jesus Christ: you must follow your emperor, without whom there is no salvation. He, fixed to the cross, is taken down not by his own hands but by the hands of others; and you, if you desire to be saved, must have your will governed by the abbot’s command. For the monk who goes out anywhere from the cenobium without the abbot’s permission is like a little sheep in the darkness that is burned up in the fire of the house. But the true monk of Christ, even when he is outside the cenobium in body, remains in the cloister of the mind; and he is no less alone among many than he is accustomed to be solitary in his cell.

The lover of Christ thinks of Jesus even in the midst of a crowd; and he who is a true worker of virtues keeps his heart firm in the fear of God in every place. For even if he is not in the monastery in body, yet in heart, because of the vigor of his spirit, he has always stood firm and stable, as if alone in the cloister. The spirit is not polluted by the movement of the body, when the solitude of the mind is preserved. You must live with the same holiness on the road, O monk, with which you are commanded to conduct yourself in the cenobium, and you must walk with a certain greater caution, lest you scandalize anyone by a more lax example, where there are as many judges of monks as there seem to be onlookers present.

The eyes of all secular people look up to monks, and they seek in their works the holiness which they hear them to have professed. A monk gives more offense by one rash word than a man given to the world does by ten thousand. For however light and buffoonish a worldly man may seem, nevertheless he has not learned to tolerate the insolence of monks with an even mind, because in his rustic simplicity he believes all cloistered men to be not such as they are, but such as they ought to be. Hence an evil word or deed among them is ascribed to the monk for damnation, whereas it is imputed to the worldly man for pardon. Nor without reason. For the monk who has professed a holy and approved canon is bound to direct his whole effort toward perfection, and in word and deed, in all purity of mind and body, far to surpass the conduct of secular people. For a light or idle word, which is granted to secular people for pardon, is judged for destruction in cloistered men.

Gold is more precious than all metals and is more desired by mortals, and in no other is a stain or corruption of falsity more quickly charged. And the flaw which is discerned in gold with judicial severity is passed over in the other metals because of the baseness of their nature. Gold gladdens the eyes by its beauty and strengthens the innermost parts of life by its virtue. Gold, when smelted in the fire, is not diminished; and the true monk of God is not changed from the purpose of holiness in the tribulation of persecution. A small [unclear] in a golden vessel is very displeasing in the sight of a powerful man; if an earthen vessel is crooked, no one detests it. When a monk offends in small matters, a great outcry of many people rises against him, because his conduct is compared to gold. The canonical life of monks is gold, a mirror. Gold in the midst of mud receives no stain of its nature, but preserves all its beauty inviolate.

So too the true monk, a lover of Christ, remains among men, when sent on a journey, just as he has learned to conduct himself in the secrecy of his little cell, because he walks pure in mind as well as in body before the Lord. For if he is a true monk, he is not polluted by the dust of another’s manner of life, nor does [unclear] delight him away from the rectitude of [unclear]. He who is secure in heart is not divided even in the midst of those making a tumult. Therefore, monk, you who desire to be good, gather your mind back to yourself; and before you leave your cell for the journey, dispose your heart. Let the fear of the Lord always be the companion of your journey.

Homily XII.

And let the guardianship of monastic discipline never depart from your side. Stop your ears with the remembrance of the last things, lest the hearing of vain speech pollute the integrity of your mind. Humbly cast your eyes down to the earth, lest they look upon what it does not befit a servant of God to desire. Do not take part in the conversations of carnal men; if you cannot avoid their presence, beware lest you lend them your mind. Even in the midst of ribald men, do not transgress your rule, and do not abandon your accustomed gravity. Do not fear the insults and reproaches of [unclear], and let your heart not be troubled by the words of men of darkness. The observance of monastic discipline is justice; and those who despise the simple pursue the innocent with laughter. Preserve your holy purpose in all things, and the Most High will avenge the injury.

Do not say in your heart, “I suffer violence,” nor be ashamed at the words of those who mock you. The glory of a monk is to endure insult, and the crown of beauty is to rejoice in reproaches. He who is patient under injuries is stronger than Atlas, and he who is not saddened when mocked is greater than all. If you have fixed your desire in heaven, nothing on earth will disturb you; and if you are a true monk, your heart will exult at injuries. There is a judge in heaven who knows all things, and there is the Most High God who cares for all things. He is the just rewarder of merits, and he will remember his poor. The more deeply you cast down your soul now in this life, for love of God, into the depth of humiliation, the more in future glory you will be exalted above the rest.

For by patience heaven is ascended, and through humility one comes to the kingdom. For it was also necessary for Christ himself to suffer, and so to enter into his glory. A delicate soldier is he who seeks pleasures while his emperor patiently endures insults and mockeries, and while he hangs on the gibbet of the cross for his army, he follows after pleasures. A soldier who goes forth naked to battle without arms, and a monk who disdains to embrace patience and humility amid insults: for both there is swift destruction. The monk who is a sincere lover of Christ is not angered by injuries, does not threaten those who inflict insult, stands fixed in his holy purpose, and, however much the wicked rush upon him, is not moved. As timely rain increases the hay in the meadows, so merit grows for the monk from the humble endurance of injuries. Humility is the sinew of all virtues, and constant patience under injuries for the love of God is the mine of good works.

Therefore, when you are about to go out from the monastery onto the road, prepare your heart for the endurance of injuries, and strengthen your mind against the insolences of mockers. When misty fellows shout after your back, repeating the name “monk,” remember Christ, mocked and spat upon before the governor, who did not answer a word, but silently preserved patience. Imitate him as your leader, O monk; always listen to him as your teacher, for he was meek and humble of heart. Do not answer a word to those who mock you; do not turn your face backward, but say with the prophet: “Those who sought evils for me spoke vanities, and meditated deceits all day long. But I, like a deaf man, did not hear; and like a mute man not opening his mouth. And I became like a man who does not hear, and has no rebukes in his mouth.” This Christ did; this Jesus taught; this the king of all commanded. If you wish to be his disciple, you must always be ready for all injuries.

When you are set upon the road, do not neglect to say your canonical prayers with whatever devotion you can; and always turn over something good with you in your mind, either by praying or by meditating. The Lord walks with you, and his holy angels accompany you as you walk. And therefore preserve a clean heart in all things, lest you offend the majesty of so many and such companions. The Lord is all eye and ear; from his knowledge nothing is hidden. Keep constant guard over your words, and let deliberation of the heart precede every word of your mouth, so that you speak nothing at all of which you could repent. A monk will speak both few words and reasonable ones, and his lips never exceed measure in speech. All his conversation is directed to the edification of his neighbors; and he who teaches very many by his conduct, even when silent, speaks useful things. He who is a true lover of God walks most humbly on the road; and he who fears the Most High restrains his mouth from laughter. In all your life, think yourself mortal, and live dying, as one who is already sending forth his last breath. Happy the kingdom and rich before God the province in which monks rise up with Boötes, since where there is no fear of God, the theaters are filled with cloistered men. A monk on the road

53
De monachis in viam directis. Qui deum habet amicum: facile homi- num contemnit familiaritatem: et qui cū angelis loquitur: mortalium colloquijs minime delectatur. Quotieus in via si¬ gnuꝫ dominice passionis aut crucifixi cō¬ spexeris: non pretereas nisi dicas. Ago tibi gratias domine iesu christe pro dolo¬ re vulnerū tuoruꝫ: pro sanctissimi sangui¬ nis tui effusione: et pro morte tua innocē¬ tissimia quam in ara crucis sustinuiti pro nobis: et rogo te per amaram passionem tuam. miserere mei nunc et in tremenda hora mortis mee. Hanc orationem bre¬ uissimam sepius inter eundum replica: et nunquam pretereas imaginem crucifixi: nisi gratias egeris saluatori. Non contē¬ das cum eo qui tecum in via graditur. ne contra te reuersus ad monasteriuꝫ ma¬ li quicquam mentiatur. Qui socium iti¬ neris ad impatientiaꝫ ꝓuocat. quasi qui canem furiosum verbere compellit ad la¬ tranduꝫ. Mansuetudine vincitur impro¬ bus: et qui humilis est corde mitigat ani¬ mo concitatum. In medio secularium ho¬ minum non effundas sermonem: ne forte contra te sumat irrisionem. Despoliū loqui bona concedimus inter iuuenes: qui autem minor est ordine audiat illum. Arator lassus festinat ad requiem: et mo¬ nachus integer animo. currens devia ad cellam suam cū defiderio reuertitur. Cō¬ primatur in ore verbum donec ratio sen¬ tentiam equitatis proferat: et sermo qui potest instruere audientes non absconda¬ tur. Non credideris carminibus palpo¬ num: quoniam enꝫ exbalistauerint inno¬ centem. aures mulcent sermonibus incō¬ positis: Dencipiti similis est monachꝰ. qui contentionebus alitur: et quasi bo¬ mo spaticus qui sub nomine religionis iurgia suscitat. Coram eruditis non adij¬ cias loqui. ne forsitan cum nō intēligis parabolam irridearis a circumstantibus. Qui monachuꝫ se recognoscit profundo sermone novytitur: et qui docet paruulos enodem facit questioneꝫ. Aumvadis ad homines proposito tuo dissimiles nō glo¬ rieris iu aliquo: sed si fueris interrogatꝰ paucis responde humiliter. Constitutus in itinere semper deum cogita: et senioris tui reuerentiam existima comitanteꝫ. Ni¬ hil facias omnino quod illi velis non ef¬ fe manifestum; quoniam vt sacer inquit

Concerning monks sent on the road.

He who has God as his friend easily disdains familiarity with men; and he who speaks with angels takes very little delight in the conversations of mortals. Whenever on the road you see a sign of the Lord’s Passion or of the Crucified One, do not pass by unless you say: “I give you thanks, Lord Jesus Christ, for the pain of your wounds, for the shedding of your most holy blood, and for your most innocent death, which you endured for us on the altar of the cross; and I beseech you, by your bitter Passion, have mercy on me now and in the dread hour of my death.” Repeat this very brief prayer often as you go, and never pass by an image of the Crucified One unless you have given thanks to the Savior.

Do not contend with him who walks with you on the road, lest, when he has returned to the monastery, he lie about some evil thing against you. He who provokes the companion of his journey to impatience is like one who drives a mad dog with a blow to bark. A wicked man is overcome by gentleness; and he who is humble in heart calms a soul that has been stirred up. In the midst of secular men do not pour out speech, lest perhaps he take up mockery against you. We allow good things to be spoken [unclear] among young men; but let the one who is lesser in rank listen to him. The weary ploughman hastens to rest; and the monk whole in spirit, running the byways, returns with longing to his cell. Let the word be restrained in the mouth until reason brings forth a judgment of fairness; and let speech that can instruct hearers not be hidden.

Do not put trust in the songs of flatterers, since [unclear] they have shot down the innocent; they soothe the ears with ill-composed speeches. A monk who is nourished on contentions is like [unclear], and like a [spastic?] man who, under the name of religion, stirs up quarrels. In the presence of the learned do not add to the speaking, lest perhaps, when you do not understand the parable, you be laughed at by those standing around. He who recognizes himself as a monk is [unclear] by profound speech; and he who teaches little ones makes [unclear] the question. When you go to men unlike you in purpose, do not boast in anything; but if you are questioned, answer humbly in few words. When set upon a journey, always think of God, and regard the reverence of your elder as accompanying you. Do absolutely nothing that you would not wish to be made known to him; since, as the sacred [writer] says

De quotidiana peccatorum expia tione. Omnia.xiiij. On All Things, XII.

The servant of Christ is believed to act in Christ’s stead in the monastery, and therefore he is deservedly honored by all. Therefore live as though you always had him present before your eyes; and whatever you would not presume to do or say while he was looking on, do not attempt in any way when he is absent. For it is foolish consolation, when conscience is biting with guilt, for sin to be hidden from men and to flee the judgment of the pastor, when one knows oneself to be sick unto death. The monk who does an evil which he wishes to be hidden from his prelate has violated the integrity of the monastic canon, and has gravely sinned against the fifth degree of humility. For thus it commands: The fifth degree of humility is this: if he has not concealed from his abbot, by humble confession, all evil thoughts coming into his heart and evil deeds done by him in secret. These are the admonitions of father Benedict; these are the holy teachings of monastic instruction. If you, monk, despise or neglect them, you will be convicted of forgetfulness of your own salvation.

It is a sure sign of humility if a monk does not refuse to open his heart to his elder, and does not wish any of the evils he has committed to be hidden from his pastor. He who confesses his fault with humility will be strengthened against the adversary of his salvation; and he who hides his thoughts will make progress in evil. For there is no thought of evils so small that it does not gradually grow if neglected; and no vice so slight that it does not gain strength if it has been dissembled. Therefore evil thoughts must be repelled immediately at the beginning, because when a depraved thought is not suddenly extinguished it produces delight; delight produces consent; consent casts one headlong into action. Then an action of evil, often repeated, begets habit; habit begets necessity; necessity brings in despair; despair contempt; contempt obstinacy; and that brings forth the eternal death of the soul. For Scripture says: When the impious man has come into the depth of evils, he despises.

Is not your abbot, O monk, the pastor and physician of your soul? Are not I, my dearest brothers, after God, the one who feeds your mortal bodies with necessary nourishment? Am I not compelled to minister the word of salvation to you? If you sheep flee the pastor, what are the pastures of the spirit which you expect from us? The sick man who flees the physician despises his own salvation and willingly kills his own soul. Therefore the monk who walks in the way of malice and turns aside from the paths of justice is near to death; and he slips so much the more deeply into the depth of vices, the less he reveres the judgment of those who correct him. But he is truly a monk who keeps his soul from every iniquity and does nothing at all which he would wish his pastor not to know. He who conceals his way is not pure; and he who flees the presence of the judge increases suspicion. Like a sheep walking in the desert, which is seized by the wolf, so the negligent and impure monk who withdraws himself from the knowledge of his pastor is devoured by demons. The sick man running to destruction, and the monk hiding every sin: there is no salvation for them unless they return to the physician.

Monks returning from a journey should immediately on that very day, according to the monastic canon, prostrate themselves in the sight of all the brothers, so that whatever has been committed on the road through negligence may be expiated by the common prayers. For the common prayer of many avails much for washing away sins, if it has been poured out to the Lord with the fervor of devotion.

Here ends On All Things, XII: On Monks Sent on a Journey.

On the Daily Expiation of Sins.

On All Things, XIV.

As long as we are placed in this corruptible life, dearest brothers, we offend daily in many things; and however holy our conduct may seem

On the daily expiation of sins.

We are not without sin. For the body that is corrupted weighs down the soul, and the earthly habitation depresses the mind that thinks many things. For Scripture says: “There is no righteous man on earth who does good and does not sin.” Likewise the holy evangelist John says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.” Indeed, through commerce with the flesh, which is too much delighted, the soul sins, and the strength of the spirit is diminished by despair. For the mind is deceived by the presentation of sensible things, and readiness to sin is strengthened by long habit. The weakness of the flesh enfeebles the fervor of the spirit, and the frailty of the will resists the holy purpose of the mind. Hence Solomon, the most wise king, says in the book of Proverbs: “Seven times in a day the righteous man will fall and rise again; but the impious will fall into evil.” By the testimony of this saying we are admonished not to grow slack in the purpose of holiness, even if it should happen that we have fallen seven times in a day.

As often, O monk, as you have fallen through sin from the purpose of holiness, so often rise again to your former fervor, not with sloth. It belongs to human frailty to fall, but to diabolical obstinacy to remain cast down in the mire of crime. The demons sinned once, and in their obstinacy they were made hardened and pertinacious, never thereafter to return to repentance. But men, as often as they have fallen, can always rise again to repentance, and by tears and prayers obtain the grace of God which they had lost by sinning. For the heart of man is flexible and can be moved in either direction, because no man in the flesh is to be believed able to become so evil that he cannot, if he wishes, recover from his malice and, with God granting it, reform his mind toward goodness. Conversely, no one becomes so good in this mortal life that he cannot become evil, if he misuses the grace of the Lord.

Since these things are so, my brothers, you must be admonished by my exhortation today to walk carefully: so that he who, with conscience as witness, is already advancing on the paths of righteousness may persevere in them by progressing daily, and he who understands himself to be guilty before the Lord may amend his life as quickly as possible. If human frailty daily impels you, or, to speak more properly, casts you down and makes you sin, let the love of God and of your own salvation also incite you daily to expiate your fault humbly through true contrition. Thus also the righteous man falls seven times in a day and rises again, because although he slips through human frailty, nevertheless, always persevering in the purpose of holiness, he is strengthened more and more in spirit in the love of God. For while he keeps his conscience free from grave sins, he is unwillingly stained by daily negligences; and when he sees that he cannot live without faults, he groans the more, humbly recognizing his weakness. But if he has even been overtaken by a graver fault, he soon rises again to amendment through repentance.

Therefore, considering the condition of human frailty, the ancient moderators of monastic discipline established various kinds of expiation, by which both monks of good will might daily advance toward better things and the wicked might be compelled to the observance of the regular life. For in the Rule the holy father Benedict commands thus, saying: “With all solicitude let the abbot take care concerning delinquent brothers, because the physician is not needed by the healthy, but by those who are ill.” For this reason the first leaders of regular observance established by prudent consideration that daily after Prime a chapter of faults should be held in the appointed place, in which, with the abbot or prior presiding [unclear], the actions of all the brothers should be brought into the open with fair examination.

This place, my brothers, bears the type of the purgatory of souls, because here not only are past sins expiated, but we are also fortified by expiatory repentance [unclear]. For in this place, which we call the chapter room, whatever you have committed openly is corrected and expiated through salutary repentance. Here each day, with the paraphrast pronouncing it, you learn your monastic law, according to the integrity of which you promised to live; here every day you hear the exhortatory word of salvation; you listen to the briefly recited victories of Christ’s martyrs and their manifold sufferings for the orthodox faith. This is the school of monks, necessary for the consideration of regular discipline, in which all that is commanded to be observed by cloistered men is learned. There are two things, my most beloved brothers, which this place requires of you: the first, that in correction [you be] always humble

Omelia.xiii. Fo.xxx. teneatis patientiam: alterum vero vt no- stram qualēcumqꝫ libenter suscipiatis exhortationem. Ad primum cupientes vos esse paratos sancti legislatores nostri. fortia martyrum gesta quorum imitatores fieri debeatis legenda precipiunt: ac deinde vt sitis dociles animo passum ex regulavnum subiūgere mandauerunt. Itaqꝫ vt sitis imitatione sanctorum martyrrum fortes et patientes ad increpationes necessarias. series passionis eorum in auribus vestris hic legitur: et quatinus adsalutarem doctrinaʒ preparatis animos. lectio vobis de regula quam profitemini vna recitare. Sancti martyres christi expemplo vos suo cōbortantur ad patientiam: et vt sitis etiam ad iniuria parati diuus vos admonet benedictus per doctrinam. Nemo igitur vestruʒ amantissimi fratres in hoc loco penitentiam recuset ꝓsuis negligentijs quotidie humiliter su/scipere: nemo dedignetur. Hic locus est publicum expiandi peccatum: in quo sic iudicij temperatur seueritas: vt pietas discretionis non violetur. Uedicus enim esse cupio animarum vestrarum non peremptor. idcirco ad iudicij nostri examen securi accedite: et vosmertipsos de commissis in aperto negligentijs humiliter proclamate. Nolo vos grauare supra regulam: vt secretissima conscientie delicta de confessione sacramentali ad publicū trāseram exꝑamen culparuʒ. quod nouimus fecisse q̄dam in graue animarum doctrinam suorum subditorum. Sic enim dicit legifer noster benedictus in regula. Si vero anime peccati causa fuerit latens. tantum abbati aut spiritualibus senioribus patet faciat. qui sciāt curare sua et aliena non detegere vulnera seu publi/care. Duo sunt in monasterio loca exꝑationis peccati: alter eorum que sunt manifesta: et alter eorum que sunt occulta. Da nifesta enīʒ peccata in proclamatione culpa parum quotidiana publlice coram omnibus expienda sunt: occulta vero et quoꝛū manifestatio scandalizaret infirmos ad confessionem remittenda. Nam cuius peccatum est manifestum oportet vtpublice quoqꝫ puniatur: et qui deliquit in occulto etiam in secreto emendetur. Sũtquidam claustralium rectores qui laten/ria subditorum peccata ad publicum examen referre non verentur: qui iuditio quidem meo non satis prudenter iura prelationis exequuntur fue. dum subditis viāprecludūt salutis: et confessionem libera/rimaqꝫ constringunt sub vinculo male voluntatis: quod quam sit periculosum, nemmo vel mediocriter sapiens qui non intel ligat. Danc enim pastoris temeritatem sanctus institutor monachoruʒ ita redarguit dicens. Magnopere sollicitudinem gerat abbas. et omni sagacitate et industria curet: ne aliquam de ouibus sibi creditisperdat. Nouerit se infirmarum curam suscepisse animarum: non super sanas tyrannidē. Ordinauimus vobis ex seniorebus quattuor spirituales confessores: vt si quis vestrum aliqua fuerit occulta temptatione preoccupatus? et nostram habuerit inexpertam inuentum su/spectaquead illos pro consolatione sui securus possethabere recursum. Quanuis nemessinota tota congregatione hactenus inuenerimus ista. quem nobis fidem tam in confessione quam extra detraxisse notauerimus. Omnes enim cognoscitur et aperte videtis: quod nihil in vobis ampliusque/ro: nihil plus desidero. quam vestram salutem: et spiritualis profectus quotidia/nus incrementum. Uos enim corona mea. vos honor meus. vos gaudiuʒ meūquia tunc me felicem existimo: cum uosin dei profecisse amore cognosco. Da/gnam proficiendi oportunitatei conseqcuti estis fratres charissimi: quoniam et locus in quo militamus domino ab omnistrepitu remotus est: et quotidiana vos admonitione ad meliora prouere noꝑcesfamus. Quotiens vero qui spiam vestruʒin aliquod peccatum per humanam fragilitateʒ ceciderit: iacere in deiectione animi diutius non permittitur: vbi alter abaltero in vera charitate fraterna pro suisnegligentijs quotidie proclamatūr. Hic locus est purgatorijterrestris: in quo monachus pro suis negligētijs discrete corrige: et ꝓ humilē patientia ꝓ christi amore quotidie lōgo martyrio creatori suo īmolatū. Arm est fratresinhoc cōsistorio culparū proclamatos discretorecipe: vestrum est omnia patientissime e iiij

Homily XIII. Folio XXX.

that you maintain patience; the other, that you willingly receive our exhortation, such as it is. For the first purpose, our holy lawgivers, wishing you to be ready, command that the brave deeds of the martyrs, whose imitators you ought to become, be read; and then, so that you may be teachable in spirit, they ordered one passage from the Rule to be added. And so, that by imitation of the holy martyrs you may be strong and patient under necessary rebukes, the sequence of their passion is read here in your ears; and, in order that you may prepare your minds for saving doctrine, a reading from the Rule which you profess is recited to you together with it. The holy martyrs of Christ encourage you to patience by their example; and the blessed Benedict admonishes you by his teaching that you should also be ready for injuries.

Therefore let none of you, most beloved brothers, in this place refuse humbly to receive penance daily for his negligences; let no one disdain it. This place is the public place for expiating sin, in which the severity of judgment is so tempered that the kindness of discretion is not violated. For I wish to be the physician of your souls, not their destroyer. Therefore come securely to the examination of our judgment, and humbly proclaim yourselves openly concerning negligences committed. I do not wish to burden you beyond the Rule, so as to transfer the most secret offenses of conscience from sacramental confession to the public examination of faults, which we know that certain men have done, to the grave [unclear] of the souls of their subjects. For thus our lawgiver Benedict says in the Rule: But if the cause of the soul’s sin has been hidden, let him make it known only to the abbot or to spiritual elders, who know how to heal their own wounds and those of others, not to disclose or publish them.

There are two places in the monastery for the expiation of sin: one for those sins that are manifest, and the other for those that are hidden. For manifest sins must be expiated publicly before all in the daily proclamation of faults; but hidden sins, and those whose disclosure would scandalize the weak, must be referred to confession. For he whose sin is manifest must also be punished publicly; and he who has offended in secret must also be corrected in secret. There are certain rulers of cloistered men who do not fear to bring the hidden sins of their subjects to public examination; and in my judgment they do not execute the rights of prelacy prudently enough, since they close off from their subjects the way of salvation and bind their confession, most free though it is, under the bond of ill will. How dangerous this is, there is no one even moderately wise who does not understand. For the holy founder of monks rebukes this rashness of a pastor, saying: Let the abbot exercise solicitude with great care, and with all sagacity and industry take care not to lose any of the sheep entrusted to him. Let him know that he has undertaken the care of sick souls, not tyranny over healthy ones.

We have appointed for you four spiritual confessors from among the seniors, so that if any one of you has been seized beforehand by some hidden temptation, and has found our [unclear] inexperienced or suspect, he may securely have recourse to them for his consolation. Although we have found these things hitherto known to the whole congregation [unclear], whom we have observed to have withdrawn trust from us both in confession and outside it. For all know, and you plainly see, that I seek nothing more in you, desire nothing more, than your salvation and the daily increase of spiritual progress. For you are my crown, you my honor, you my joy, because then I consider myself happy when I know that you have made progress in the love of God.

You have obtained a great opportunity for making progress, dearest brothers, since the place in which we serve the Lord as soldiers is removed from all tumult, and we do not cease to advance you toward better things by daily admonition. But whenever any one of you has fallen into some sin through human frailty, he is not permitted to lie long in dejection of spirit, where one is daily proclaimed by another in true fraternal charity for his negligences. This is a workshop of salvation, in which the mind is fed with the nourishment of heavenly doctrine, and the soul is daily cleansed from the stains of offenses by public satisfaction. This place is an earthly purgatory, in which the monk is corrected with discretion for his negligences, and through humble patience, for the love of Christ, is daily offered to his Creator in a long martyrdom. [unclear] brothers, in this assembly, receive with discretion those proclaimed for faults; it is yours to endure all things most patiently

On the Daily Expiation of Sins.

to suffer. For it is necessary that we make satisfaction for our sins; but if we neglect to do this in this life, in the life to come, compelled, we shall necessarily do it. There are some among you who take corrections very hard. To them we declare what we have often said, that in the future they must endure very grievous things, they who refuse to endure small and light things here. But I, considering their weakness and ignorance, am gravely tormented within myself, because I see their minds wounded, and yet I am afraid to apply the necessary medicines. For if I apply remedies suited to the diseases, I fear lest, made fainthearted, they fall into despair, or certainly, given over to a reprobate mind, withdraw entirely from their holy purpose. Therefore I use as much discretion as I can, as all of you will bear witness for me, preferring to send the weak through patience with charity to purgatory rather than, from just severity, to have the despairing descend into hell.

For who in this mortality could ever make satisfaction for sins who did not apply a good will to penitence? For good will alone commends the works of penitents. But although many are punished unwillingly, they are still far removed from perfect satisfaction. Believe me, my most beloved brothers, that satisfaction for sins is commended more by suffering than by acting. For even the Lord and Savior of us all, Jesus, by suffering expiated the sin of the whole world on the altar of the cross. Would that you knew how effective a medicine it is for the soul wounded by sins to receive proclamations and corrections with humble patience, and also, for the increase of perfect satisfaction, to bear injuries and insults with equanimity. I am certain that humble patience in adversity far surpasses every kind of satisfaction; and the readier the mind has been to bear insults and injuries for the love of Christ, the more easily and quickly it will obtain from the Lord pardon for all its sins and a fuller indulgence.

For this place in which we now speak is the workshop of purgation and expiation, in which zeal for regular discipline holds primacy, discretion presides over examination, charity directs and completes all things. Hence in this very place patience is very necessary for you; without its presence no satisfaction will be consummated. The monk who is a zealous lover of his salvation loves this place as a workshop of expiation, and never goes forth from it without having been made better than himself. For this place is to be feared and dreaded by demons, but dear and greatly venerable to the holy angels of God; in it the fault of humble monks is washed away, and whatever is committed openly is also expiated publicly before all. But if any hidden fault has been committed by any of you, the secret confession of the penitent will likewise purge it away. In both cases pure confession with humility is required, and both here and there patience is judged necessary for you.

Therefore, whoever you are, monk, who desire to be good, prepare your soul in all patience, so that you may hold the tranquility of mind most constant as much in adversities as in prosperities. When you have been proclaimed by some brother for your negligences, patiently [unclear] the rebukes from the senior, you who offend daily in many things. He endured countless injuries most patiently for your salvation, and why should you not suffer humbly for your sins? Bear patiently with all humility, faithfully bringing to mind how innocently the mighty Son of God was accused. For if he, just and innocent, who committed no sin, suffered insults, why should you not patiently bear rebuke with tolerance in satisfaction for sins? But if you did not deserve the proclamation in judgment, nevertheless endure it patiently for the love of Christ; now it will be reckoned to you not only as satisfaction for preceding sins, but much more as justification. Therefore whether a monk is proclaimed justly or unjustly, he has no ground for just defense, because if he has sinned he suffers according to his desert; but if he is innocent, he is the more bound to patience. For no one unless patient and humble will be able to imitate Christ. But since the monk is especially bound to be a disciple and imitator of Christ, it is especially fitting for him to be patient. Homily XIII.

Fol. XXXI.

[Without?] sword and fire a monk can be a martyr, if for love of God he has kept true [unclear] patience in his soul. For the true monk is neither puffed up by praises nor saddened by blame; he shows himself patient under injuries; at insults and reproaches he is glad and humbly keeps silent. No one is stronger than the patient man who knows how to conquer himself and humbly to endure adversities for love of God with a tranquil mind.

But the hard, impatient man is proud and arrogant, since he does not follow Jesus, the teacher of humility; and therefore he is indignant at just rebukes and [unclear]. As the furnace tests gold, so insults and injuries test a monk, whether he truly loves Christ. Humility and patience in adversity are the true badges of monks; whoever is not clothed in their adornment glories vainly in the name. He who is not humble cannot truly be a monk; he who does not keep patience in adversities cannot be a true disciple of Christ.

Hence king Solomon says in the book of Proverbs: “The patient man is better than the strong, and he who rules his own spirit than one who storms cities.” For a man’s teaching is known through patience, and his glory is to pass over wrongs. The furnace tests the potter’s vessels, and the trial of tribulation tests men among us. The monk who follows Christ in truth and who is a meditator on the Lord’s passion is patient under all injuries, not forgetful; amid insults he exults in spirit and rejoices. For, as blessed [Christopher?] says, all who have wished to live piously in Christ Jesus suffer persecution, and whatever evil befalls them they overcome with the greatest constancy.

And although patience is necessary for a monk in every place and time, nevertheless in the daily examination of faults it must be guarded with especially diligent attention: there correction of morals is carried out, and whatever has been committed against the standard of monastic purity is amended in each one by the senior. Therefore before we enter this place, all should think in the morning, and the mind should be strengthened against those things that can happen, so that if perhaps a rather harsh rebuke occurs, it may not overturn the mind from the state of tranquillity. For even if we have resolved to bring insult upon none of you, nor to do injury, nevertheless we do not deny that it can happen, so far as can be, that someone who has been corrected may think himself rebuked beyond his desert, since he weighs our paternal corrections by the words rather than by the intention.

As God knows, we seek your salvation in all things, and nothing else: to cut away vices by the roots, according to the ordinances of our religion. We sincerely intend to injure no one. We cannot please everyone in all things, but we are especially compelled to displease those who, while sinning against the rule each day, promise themselves impunity for their crimes. Of these king Solomon said: “An evil teaching belongs to those who abandon the way of life, and he who hates rebukes shall die.” The pestilent man does not love him who corrects him, nor does he go to the wise. He who does evil deliberately flees the light and hates correction because he is foolish; but he who is sensible in spirit gives thanks to his corrector.

Therefore in this matter I do not fear the hatred or murmuring of subjects, knowing that I have taken on the care of sick sheep, to whom, whether willing or unwilling, I am bound to apply the remedies of salvation. If it could be done, brothers, I would very much wish to disturb none of you in anything, even slightly, but to live among you with the greatest tranquillity and cheerfully to serve the Lord our God in peace of mind and body. But because not all of you truly seek the things that are God’s, I must rebuke and sometimes disturb the restless, lest impunity for smaller crimes provide boldness for graver ones. For I know what necessity I suffer through the danger of pastoral care; and therefore I neither can nor ought to be silent when you sin, lest I be judged somewhere as consenting. I gladly endure it if, for this reason, it happens that I am hated, because this cannot be done without the gravest danger to your souls.

We ask you through our Lord Jesus Christ, crucified for us, that for love of God and for the remission of your sins you endure our paternal and necessary rebukes at all times patiently and with true humility. Let each one consider in himself that there is no day on which he does good and does not offend in some respect; and let him know that he will receive in this world the reward of his works: good things for good, and for evil things [unclear]. Therefore let him strive, as much as he can, in this life to make satisfaction for his offenses

Hubium non expectet crastinuz salus hodierna: z qui debitum potest cu gratia in libertate solnere: non se patiatur ad carcerem trahi cum tortura. De vera penitentia

On the Daily Expiation of Sins

[unclear], and humbly to expiate all their iniquities by the daily chastisement of the body. Know, my brothers, that there is no sin so small that the justice of almighty God lets it go unpunished. And therefore, since there is none of us who has not offended in many things, arm yourselves, I beg you, with patience and humility, so that whenever you are corrected for your sins, you may bear it with all gentleness. For in this time of free choice you can, with a small expiation, make sufficient satisfaction for many debts, for which after death in purgatory the soul will be tormented, even for small ones, for a long time and most grievously.

Indeed voluntary satisfaction is of great value; but that which is done from necessity earns less toward grace. Altogether, brothers, it is fitting and necessary for the soul to be cleansed from fault, if it is to reign in heaven and rejoice with Christ. But the soul that has neglected the cleansing of its faults in the present life will be heavily punished in the life to come. Let none of you say, my dearest brothers, what many ignorant people have been accustomed to say: “It is enough for me if my soul has undergone the pains of purgatory.” Believe me, brothers, whoever says this word from the heart does not consider what purgatory is to be. For he does not know what he is asking for, who desires purgatory. Just as a man is foolish who, when he could pay his debt free, scorns to do so and willingly goes to prison, so he deserves to be judged the most foolish of all men who, when he can make satisfaction to God for his sins in this life, puts it off to the future.

In this life repentance is fruitful, and voluntary satisfaction avails much by merit; but after death there will be no place for repentance, but each one will then receive according as he has done in his body, whether good or evil. Think on these things, brothers, while you live in health, lest, overtaken by the command of death, you at last grieve too late. Let the salvation of today not wait for the morrow, and let the man who can pay his debt with grace while at liberty not allow himself to be dragged to prison with torture. As much as each one can in his whole life, so much let him take care to make satisfaction for his sins, since the spirit returns securely to the Lord if, while still existing in the body, it is daily purified by the fire of divine love.

Here you have a place in which daily expiation is made for public guilt: if you kept true and humble patience in your mind, you would without doubt obtain certain remission of all. But what you ought to do for secret and hidden sins, not only the rule admonishes you, but also daily sacramental confession instructs you in all things. At the altar we are accustomed every day, each one devoutly, to offer the Son of God’s majesty; and none of us approaches that holy washing and mystery unless he has first confessed according to custom, since the highest purity is required where, through the Mass, the salvation of the whole world is renewed.

Who among us, dearest brothers, amid these things does not daily make progress in the love of God, unless he shamefully and wholly lays aside every desire for progress? For I dare to say that the monk who does not make progress in this holy congregation is utterly convicted of having forgotten his own salvation. Believe me, brothers: God will save no one against his will. If you neglect your own progress, nothing but yourselves will be blamed. For God is the intellectual light that enlightens every man coming into this world, as John, the eagle that soars aloft, says; but those who do not receive the light will necessarily remain in darkness. He who turns his mind away from the faith that is in the Son of God remains in darkness; and for him who does not do the works of light, nothing that he sees will profit him for salvation. Outside the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ there is no salvation, and he who thinks otherwise is not a Christian.

Let not a foolish consideration of piety seduce you, O man, so that you believe anyone outside the faith of Christ, in any religion whatever, is to be saved, however innocently he may live or according to the law of nature; for just as outside Noah’s ark there was no life for men, so outside the Christian faith there is salvation for no one unto eternal life. For Christ, the only Son of God, is the one and only Savior of the world; whoever does not believe in him, the wrath of God remains upon him, and he will be condemned with the devil. But you, my brothers, who now believe in our Lord Jesus Christ, I beg you henceforth to live in such a way that, Christian in name and in deed, you may be able to come to his fellowship: who lives and reigns with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, through all ages of ages.

On True Repentance

60
Om̄elia.xiiij. monachorum.Omelia.xiij; ¶ Fo.xxxii. QUamuis tota cōuersatio nr̄a fr̄es mei charissimi recte pnīa nominari possit:qͥppe qͥ et nob̓ mortui et mundo iā sepulti vide/ mur:quia tamen carne mortali sumꝰ circūdati et peregrinamur in medio nationis peccatricis.fieri nō potest quin fragilitatꝭ proprie impulsu quo/ tidie in aliquo delinquamus:pro cuius expiatione non solum generaliter sed etiā specialiter fuerit penitendo satis faciendū Est em̄ penitentia cunctis mortalibꝰ neccessaria:qua et cōmissa mala deplangāt cum emendationis proposito:et deinceps quantum fieri potest.viuere statuat sine peccato. Monachorū est proprium sine intermiffione penitentiam agere:et tam pro suis quam pro alienis peccatis iugiter orare.Non enim docentis officiuꝫ habet monachus:vt facer hieronymus inquiret:sed plangentis:qui vl̓se lugeat infirmus:vel mundū perfectus:et domini pauidus prestoletur aduentū.Si ꝑfectꝰ es monachus penitentiam agito pro peccatis alienis:si vero infirmꝰ oportet vt animipliꝰ peniteas pro proprijs.Temp̄ itaqƺ penitendū est monacho:qui non foluꝫ psuis sed etiam pro delictis aliorum inter/ cessor ad deuꝫ constituitur.Sed quis in vobis est fratres qui proprio non grauet̉ delicto?Quis inquā est vestrū qͥ nō indigeat penitentia?Video vos in multis qͦtidie offendere et doleo:cerno quam preteteritorum negligatis penitentiam et contremisco.Nnūquid non agnoscitis vos essemortales?Et quare vocabulo monachi non satis facitis:vt penitentiam intēpore necessariam agatis?Mementote quesocomminantis scripture dicentis. Ne tardes conuerti ad dominū et ne differas dedie in diem.Subito enim veniet ira illiꝰ et in tempore vindicte disperdet te.Non enim preteribitis mortem que vobis o senes in ianua ē:et iunioribꝰ latet in infidijs sed quādo minus cogitatis d̓ corpore cōpulsus exierit spūs.Vnde si vos esse peccatores recognoscitis:si venire ad dei miseretiam precor assumite:et mores vestros in omnibus secundū regule puritateꝫ emendate.Satis fit hactenus veram neglexi se penitentiam:et nimis tepidam tanto continuasse tempore conuersationem.Deus etenim qui diffimulat pctā hominū propter penitentiam:differentibus penitere non promisit vite prolongationem.Considerate longanimitem dei qui vos pec cantes quotidie taꝫ diu misericorditer distultit et agite penitentiam:quatinus opta tam inueniatis remiffionem.Dicit enim dominus per prophetam.Nolo mortem impij sed vt conuertatur a via sua mala et viuat.In sācto quoqƺ euāgelio dicit.Penetentiā agite:appropriq̄bit eī regnū celorum.Magnū est bonū penitentia mortalibus:que sordidas purgat animas:etmētes ab interitu reuocat oͤstinato.Hicdiuus dicit augustinus.
