De patientia et mansuetudine lerantie metas custodire volueris: opor- tebit in primis contumeliam adesse infe- rentem. Si fuissem inquit monachus pi- ger et animalis in diebus martyrum, nul- la penaruʒ genera subire pro christi amo- re timuissem: corpus voluntarie obiecif- sem tortoribus: vt coronam martyrij re- portassim. Magna stultitie temeritas. Perbum pro dei amore patienter sufferre numquam potuisti: et constantiam san- ctorum martyruʒ polliceris? Leuem cor- reptionem metuis: qui corpus te daturuʒ pro christo promittis. Si martyriū te de- lectat: audi quid beatissimus papa gre- gorius dicat. Si adiuuante nos christo virtutem patientie seruare contendimus et in pace ecclesie vitimus: et martyrij pal- inam tenemus. Naʒ sino ferro et flamma martyres esse possumus: si patientiam in animo veraciter custodimus. Mori a ꝑ sequente martyrium in aperto opere est: ferre autem contumelias et odientem dili- gere: martyriuʒ est in occulta cogitatione Patientia vero est aliena mala equanimi- ter perpeti: et contra eum qui malum intu- lit nullo dolore morderi. Quid nunc pi- ger dices o monache: qui martyriuʒ ver- borum sufferre leuissimum impotens: de constantia fundendi sanguinis tam pro- terue gloriaris? Disce miser in leuibꝰ ha- bere patientiam: et considera quoniam di- cēte scriptura qui in modico infidelis est: ei quod maius est quis crederet? Ad om- nia que fiunt in cenobio murmuras: increpatus quantumlibet leniter pro graui bus delictis et negligentijs tuis impatien- tissime toleras: nemo tibi recte in mona- sterio graditur: nemo preter te in tua esti- matione religiose conuerfatur. Tu quan- tum tibi videtur solus in cenobio sanctꝰ. tu omnium doctissimus neminem scire cōsentis quod tu solus ignoras. Super omnes te honoribus cuuctis existimas dignum: quia non solum patientia cares sed neqʒ humilitatem veram neqʒ obedi- entiam retines. Non est hec via per quā itur ad regnum celorum: quando in scho la humilitatis superbit monachus: et mo ribus christo viuit contrarius christianꝰ. Monachus autem iesu christi solemni- ter iuratus minister: vt dominum possit imitari suum non debet esse superbus sed humilis: obedines non rebellis: mansue tus non crudelis: neqʒ proteruus sed mi- tis. Monachus vero superbus iracun- dus contentiosus et proprie voluntatis a mator, quales prob dolor vt frequenter sunt in temporalibꝰ constituti, quos apud nos cellarios secundum regulam nuncu pamus. quorum elatio multis viam ad interituʒ fecit. Compellit me dolor ad lo- quendum et prohibet verecundia: quam uis casum noueritis omnes quo nos in fratre diabolus pridem confudit. Quis il- lo in tota congregatione nostra superbi- or? quis maiore proternua plenꝰ inecessit? Quia vero maiores inter nos reruʒ teni poralium experientiam habere videbatur cunctis ob id se prestantiorē existima- uit. Permisit omnipotēs vt caderet: qua tenus qui suam infirmitatem reputatus agnoscere noluit: confusus tandem non sine multorum scandalo aduersarium in telligeret deum superborum. Doleovehe menter et plus quam dici potest culpa ru entis mihi grauior videtur: quoniam il- lo ruente confundimur omnes. Det illi deus penitentiam agere veram: vt qui eiꝰ lapsu schandalizati fuerant: satisfactione corauʒ deo et hominibus edificentur. Fē- per monachis perniciosa fuit elatio: et mē tem hominis quam semel iniuaferit: in fo ueami vitiorum omniuʒ demergit. Cauc- te superbiam fratres mei quoniam ipsa ē omnis peccati exordium: ipsa est que per inuidiam diaboli mortem introduxit in orbem terrarum. Superbia virtutuʒ est mors omniuʒ: et cunctoruʒ fons et scaturi go vitiorum. Humilitas autem virtutū nutrix maxime decet monachos: quoniā et nites facit et mansuetos. Omnis enim sup erbus impatiens? et omnis arrogans mansuetudinis inimicus. Qui humilis est corde habet in aduerfis pro dei amo- re patientiā: et qui ad iniurias animo trā- quillus est: duplicem meretur coronam. Uir patiens in aduerfis deo fit proximus qui autem superbus et impaticus est leti ficat inimicos. Dicit naqʒ scriptura. De lior est patiens viro forti: et qui domina- tur animo suo expugnatore vrbium. Sā ctus quoqʒ presul augustinus. Paratus debʒ esse hō iustus et pius. patientes eoꝝ malitiaʒ sustinere. quos fieri bonos cupit vt potiꝰ īnumerꝰ crescat bonoꝝ: et n̄ pari malitia seqͥs numero addat maloꝝ Est ē nobis patiētia ml̓tū neccīa frēs: vt volū tatē dei faciētes factauʒ ī xp̄o reportenius

On patience and meekness

If you wish to keep the bounds of tolerance, there must first of all be someone present who inflicts insult. “If I had been,” says the lazy and unspiritual monk, “in the days of the martyrs, I would have feared no kinds of punishments to undergo for the love of Christ; I would voluntarily have exposed my body to the torturers, so that I might carry away the crown of martyrdom.” Great rashness of folly. You have never been able to endure a word patiently for the love of God, and you promise the steadfastness of the holy martyrs? You fear a slight correction, you who promise that you will give your body for Christ.

If martyrdom delights you, hear what the most blessed Pope Gregory says: “If, with Christ helping us, we strive to preserve the virtue of patience, and live in the peace of the Church, we also hold the palm of martyrdom. For without sword and flame we can be martyrs, if we truly keep patience in the soul. To die at the hands of a persecutor is martyrdom in open deed; but to bear insults and to love one who hates us is martyrdom in hidden thought.” Patience, indeed, is to suffer another’s evils with equanimity, and to be gnawed by no grief against him who has inflicted the evil.

What now will you say, lazy monk, who, unable to endure the very slight martyrdom of words, boast so insolently of steadfastness in shedding blood? Learn, wretched man, to have patience in light matters, and consider that, as Scripture says, “he who is unfaithful in a little thing, who would entrust him with what is greater?” You murmur at everything that is done in the monastery; when reproved, however gently, for your grave faults and negligences, you endure it most impatiently. No one in the monastery walks rightly for you; no one except you, in your estimation, conducts himself religiously. As it seems to you, you alone are holy in the community; you, the most learned of all, allow no one to know what you alone are ignorant of. You think yourself worthy of all honors above everyone, because you not only lack patience but retain neither true humility nor obedience.

This is not the road by which one goes to the kingdom of heaven: when a monk is proud in the school of humility, and a Christian lives in his conduct contrary to Christ. But a monk, a minister solemnly sworn to Jesus Christ, in order that he may imitate his Lord, ought not to be proud but humble, obedient not rebellious, gentle not cruel, nor insolent but mild.

A monk, however, who is proud, wrathful, contentious, and a lover of his own will, such as, alas, those set over temporal affairs often are, whom among us according to the Rule we call cellarers, their pride has made for many the road to destruction. Grief compels me to speak, and shame forbids me, although you all know the fall by which the devil lately put us to shame in a brother. Who in our whole congregation was prouder than he? Who went about filled with greater insolence? Because he seemed among us to have more experience of temporal affairs than all the rest, for that reason he thought himself more excellent. The Almighty permitted him to fall, so that he who [unclear] refused to recognize his own weakness might at last, confounded and not without the scandal of many, understand that God is the adversary of the proud.

I grieve vehemently, and more than can be said. The fault of the one who fell seems to me the heavier, because when he fell we are all put to shame. May God grant him to do true penance, so that those who had been scandalized by his fall may be edified by his satisfaction before God and men.

Pride has always been destructive to monks, and the mind of a man which it has once invaded it plunges into the pit of all vices. Beware pride, my brothers, because it is the beginning of every sin; it is what, through the envy of the devil, introduced death into the world. Pride is the death of all virtues and the source and spring of all vices. But humility, the nurse of virtues, especially befits monks, because it makes them both mild and meek. For every proud man is impatient, and every arrogant man is an enemy of meekness. He who is humble of heart has patience in adversities for the love of God; and he who is tranquil in soul before injuries merits a double crown. A patient man in adversities becomes very near to God; but he who is proud and impatient gladdens his enemies. For Scripture says: “Better is the patient man than the strong man, and he who rules his own spirit than the conqueror of cities.” Likewise the holy bishop Augustine: “A just and pious man ought to be ready to sustain patiently the malice of those whom he desires to become good, so that rather the number of the good may increase, and he may not by like malice add himself to the number of the wicked.” For patience is very necessary to us, brothers, so that, doing the will of God, we may receive [unclear] in Christ.

Si boni homines et iusti in hoc mundo sunt diuites:eoruʒ non fortitudini sed infirmitatī per dei prouidentiam cõsulitur:vt beneficijs ad meliora prouocentur.Iunior fui dicit propheta et senui.et non vidi iustum derelictum:nec semen eius mendi cans.Jacta inquit cogitatum tuuʒ in domino et ipse te enutriet:non dabit ineternum fluctuationem iusto.Nouit dominus iesus quid ynicuiqꝫ seruulorum suorum ad salutem conueniat:et ideo munera presentis vite pro captu singulorũ inequaliter dispen̄at.Non enim omnibus omnia conueniunt:propterca iustorum in hoc mundo rebus temporalibus alij sunt pauperes:alij vero locupletes.De pauperibus dominus iesus in sãcto euã gelo dicit.Beati pauperes spirituriquoniam ipsorum est regnũ celorum.Et per prophetam loquitur dicens.Exce excoxit seđ non quasi argentum: elegi te in camino paupertatis.Non enim conducit ad eternam salutem omnibus huius mũ di possidere diuitias:sed quosdam expedites:prout dominus vniuersorum cuiqꝫ prouidit esse vtilius. De iustis et bonis diuitibꝰ salomon dicit in libro prouerbio ruʒ.Benedictio domini diuites facit:necessiabitur ei afflictio.Si autem mali et reprobi diuitijs abundauerint in hoc seculo non debet bonos mouere ad indignationem:sed magis timeant eum qui nullum bonum dimittit irremuneratum et nullum malum impunitum.Malos enim quos propter iniquitatem eorum remunerare in celis non potest.pro eorum bonis in hac vita remunerat:et bonis q̃s hic in paupertate nutrit pro iustitia merito eterna in celis premia conferuat.Ve rum sicut non omnes in hoc mundo pau peres sunt iusti et boni:ita non omnes rerum temporalium diuites in hac vita sũtmali.Malorum remuneratio in terris merito sine indignatione ferenda est:quãnon amor dei sed iustitia voluit esse presen̄tem.Unde sicut mali nihil habent in celo:ita vos qui monasticam paupertatem est professo nibil habere deberis interra:sed spe illius boni ad quod tenditis quicꝫid in via contigerit aduersi tolerare patientissime debesis.Naz vt sanctuschristi amator paulus ait:non sunt condigne passiones huius temporis ad superuenturam gloriam que reuelabitur in nobis.Qui diuites sunt in christo coniungant humilitati misericordiam:qui verosunt transitorijs curat.Ita qui verus est monachus nec laudibus extollitur:nec vituperatione frangitur:intumescit necessariarum rerumaffluentia.nec contrahitur paupertatem.ta simul contentnit et Homily XVIII. Fol. XLIII.

promise. Adversities are present to us every day, by which we may be exercised; therefore, just as the cause for endurance is never lacking, so, I pray, may necessary patience always be present. We are oppressed by want and poverty of necessary things; we are burdened by the commerce of weak flesh; moreover the world tempts us in order to entice us; the devil tempts us in order to lead us astray. Among so many adversaries of our salvation, brothers, it is necessary that we keep watch in all patience and humility, since in this pilgrimage, as long as we live, we are placed, so to speak, in the midst of evils.

Our poverty ought to suffice us, because it is not the part of monastic religion to be exalted in temporal things, but rather to be humbled, so that monks, poor and imitating Christ, who was made poor for us, may deserve to glory with him forever in heaven. What if we see certain wicked men and sinners in the world abounding in riches? If good and just men are rich in this world, provision is made by God’s providence not for their strength but for their weakness, so that by benefits they may be summoned to better things. “I was young,” says the prophet, “and I have grown old, and I have not seen the just man forsaken, nor his seed begging.” “Cast,” he says, “your thought upon the Lord, and he will nourish you; he will not allow the just man to waver forever.”

The Lord Jesus knows what is fitting for the salvation of each one of his little servants, and therefore he distributes the gifts of the present life unequally according to the capacity of individuals. For not all things are fitting for all people; therefore, among the just in this world, with respect to temporal goods, some are poor, while others are wealthy. Concerning the poor the Lord Jesus says in the holy Gospel: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” And he speaks through the prophet, saying: “Behold, I have refined you, but not as silver; I have chosen you in the furnace of poverty.” For it is not conducive to eternal salvation for all men to possess the riches of this world, but it is advantageous for certain persons, according as the Lord of all has foreseen to be more useful for each.

Concerning just and good rich men Solomon says in the book of Proverbs: “The blessing of the Lord makes men rich; affliction shall not be joined to it.” But if the wicked and reprobate abound in riches in this age, this ought not to move the good to indignation; rather, let them fear him who leaves no good unrewarded and no evil unpunished. For the wicked, whom he cannot reward in heaven because of their iniquity, he rewards in this life for their good deeds; and for the good, whom he nourishes here in poverty for righteousness’ sake, he preserves eternal rewards in heaven. But just as not all the poor in this world are just and good, so not all who are rich in temporal things in this life are wicked. The reward of the wicked on earth must rightly be borne without indignation, since not the love of God but justice has willed it to be present.

Therefore, just as the wicked have nothing in heaven, so you who have professed monastic poverty ought to have nothing on earth, but, in hope of that good toward which you are striving, you ought to endure most patiently whatever adversity befalls on the way. For, as Paul, the holy lover of Christ, says: “The sufferings of this time are not worthy to be compared with the glory to come, which shall be revealed in us.” Those who are rich in Christ should join mercy to humility; but those who are poor should take up patience, with innocence, for the love of God. The delight [unclear] of Christ is cast down neither by poverty nor raised up by riches, but, standing firm in himself, he rules his spirit calmly and cares nothing for transitory things. Thus he who is a true monk is neither lifted up by praises nor broken by reproach; he does not swell with an abundance of necessary things, nor is he contracted by poverty. He despises both joyful and sad things alike, since, as the prophet had said, “the sun shall not burn him by day, nor the moon by night.”

But we, dearest brothers, should make a virtue and a good will out of necessity, and from the hardship of poverty which we necessarily suffer we should obtain for ourselves a good and a great advantage; and this can happen only if, for the love of God, we bear this very poverty manfully and with a tranquil spirit. The deformed way of life of our predecessors has brought upon this monastery the want that we suffer; if we keep his commandments with a perfect heart, the mercy of almighty God will in time, without doubt, relieve it. From almost two hundred years back, as a similar conjecture follows.

On patience and meekness

[unclear]: the purity of monastic institution in this monastery of Sponheim, as also in almost all the others, failed; and the disorder of the monks’ life utterly dissipated the whole substance of earthly goods.

Indeed, when in the year of the Christians one thousand four hundred and sixty-one, Frederick, count palatine and duke of Bavaria, a most Christian man, who was residing at [Simmeren?], held the depraved life of monks in his principality in great hatred, he reformed three monasteries, expelling the deformed monks, and introduced men excellently trained from other monasteries. First, indeed, he brought two monasteries of regular canons of Saint Augustine back to the observance of regular discipline: Rebdorf, that is, among the [unclear], and Schwabenheim among the [Stauronesians?] in the district of the [Nagavienses?]. Finally, in the aforesaid year of the Lord, he also renewed this present monastery of ours, Sponheim, for reform of the order; and, after removing the abbot with five monks, he restored four others in their place for observance, setting over them my predecessor Johannes of Kolenhusen, now serving as abbot in Seligenstadt.

They found the place so oppressed by poverty and burdened with debt that there was no one who believed it could be restored, since all the annual revenues had either been sold or alienated under title of redemption; indeed, nothing at all was left on which they might live. Brother Heinrich, one of the first four reformers sent from Mainz, is present as narrator and witness of the things we say; from his mouth you will know all things more fully. And behold, the seventeenth year is now underway since this place began to be restored under the chapter of the reformed union of Bursfelde, and still we are tortured by no small poverty.

Therefore I have said these things, brothers, so that you may know that we do not bear alone the want that we suffer, since those four men who first reformed the monastery endured heavier things; beans and peas filled their bellies, and a thin pear-drink supplied them drink in measure. The mercy of God has called us to this place, in which through patience we may overcome the [antidicuus?] of our salvation, so that, according to the counsel of the divine Apostle, having scant food and clothing with which we may be covered, being content and giving thanks to the Lord in cheerfulness of mind, we may [serve?]. For we have not been called to feasts of the flesh, nor to the delights of this world, not to pleasures nor to the consolations of the present life, but to serve as soldiers for our Lord and emperor Jesus Christ in abstinence from all the delectable things of this age, in pure conscience and humility of heart.

Attend now therefore to your calling, O monks, and do not [unclear] the purpose [unclear] you desire to attain. Woe to you, faithless monk, who, having become a despiser of your calling and a transgressor of your vow, do not live monastically in the monastery; you who were called to endure tribulation patiently for the love of God, and [unclear] concerning refreshment. For your profession commands you to go humbly content in every usefulness and extremity of garments, and you do not fear to apply zeal to the fastidiousness of clothing. You have been called to thirst, and you, not content to drink water, delight in drinking wine to satiety, contrary to the monastic canon. You were made a monk to fight strongly against the adversary of your salvation, and you, having cast away from yourself the courage of the virtues, go about sluggish, [unclear], and naked; indeed, what is graver, accompanied by a band of vices. You were invited to keep watch in holy prayers, and you are dissolved in inert sleep and shameful sloth. You were called into the subjection of humble obedience, and you, swollen with pride, scorn to obey the precepts of your elders. You have been called into charity, and you do not fear to carry hatred in your breast against your brother. You have been called into weeping and tears, and [unclear] laughter with disordered deep guffawing. The Lord called you in the monastery to repentance, and you, dissolved into wantonness, join sin to sin. You were called to meditate day and night on the law of our Lord Christ, and you, walking after vanities, devote yourself to tales and perishable things. You have been called to heaven, and you, loving the world, pursue earthly things. The Lord called you, humbled, into meekness, and you go about full of rancor and pride. You were called by the Lord to the perfection of the purest monastic manner of life, and you rot like a beast in the dung of vanity and negligence. To the observance of

¶ Omelía.xviii. datoruꝫ dei vocatus es: et tu voluptatibꝰ carnis deditus nihil minus quam chri¬ stum cogitas. Ad amandum dominum iesū suꝑ oīa iuuitatꝰ es: et tu ambulas pꝰ desideria cordis tui mala īgratū te exhi¬ bēs redēptori tuo. Qui spū viuere ḋbue¬ ras trena sapis et õnia spũalis ꝯuersatio¬ nis sancta exercitia submersus in suꝑbia contemnis. Et quid in illa die iudicij re¬ sponsurus es iudicii qui ingratissimo tibi dicturus est. Ego qui dominus sum vni uersortim propter te humiliaui in emetip sum formam serui accipiens et habitu in¬ ventus vt homo: sanguinem pro te meuꝫ effudi: pro te verbera sustinui: et mortem pro te nimis amaram spontaneavolunta te subiui. Ego te o monache in toto corde meo dilexi: ego te in sanguine meo d̓ mor te perpetua redemi: ego te si mandata cu stodiuisses mea ad celeste regnū ex amo¬ re vocavi. Tu autēvixisti preceptis meis contrarius: et quod grauius est in vetba mea iuratus cum esses apostatam et im¬ pium te traditorem contra me dominum tauꝫ exhibere non timuisti. Nunc igitur da rationem villicationis tue. Quid tunc responsurus es o monache piger et deses qui tempus nunc acceptabile tam infru¬ ctuose consumis: et viuere in vera purita/ te monastica secundum regulam contemnis? Quid inquā respondebis? Negabis ne prauitatis opera que cōmisisti. ostensu rus per fallaciā bona que nunc operarri spernis: quatens mendacio circũuenias iudicem sicqꝫ debitam euadas tuis demeritis penā? Sed ignorare non debes quoniam omnia que fecisti dixisti vel cogitasti per omnem vitam tuaꝫ bona et ma la in conspectu iudicis sunt manifesta: et nihil eū latere potest: qui solus omnia no uit. Omnia enim in libro dei scripta sunt et conscientia tua omniū aduersum te malegestorū apertum ꝑhibebit testimoniuz ita quod nec minima quidē cogitatio poterit latere. Dicit enim ad deum scriptura prophetarum. Quoniaꝫ cogitatio hominis confitebitur tibi. Ad tribunal omnia scientis iudicandus es: ante cuius terribile iudicium omnis creatura cum metunimio et tremore stabit: vbi nulla penitus admittitur excusatio: sed singuli recepturi sunt debitā suis meritis semota appellatione sententiam. Milia milia sanctorum spirituum ¶ Fo.xliiii. assistent ei: et tu mendacio te fallere iudice posse confidis. Sed audi consilium me¬ um et surgens ab inertia tua perniciosa tādem expergiscere: et per veram penitentiā ad dei misericordiaꝫ in tempore a iustitia recurre. Non differas de die in dieꝫ: quo niam nimis est periculosum in peccatis manenti confidere: et salutis remedium quod offertur refutare. Memento quo¬ niam moriturus es: et quando non cogitas ad iudicium vocaberis. Logita p̄cor dubium viuendi tempus quemodo labitur: et omnia que mortalia sunt quamci¬ to corrumpuntur. Nihil in humanis sta¬ bile: nihil fixum. nihil firmum: sed omnia que cernimus corruptibilia sunt: et cum tēpore mutantur. Considera etiam vbi naꝫ sunt fratres nostri valentinus martinus et ioannes qui anno presenti nobiscumvi uentes sani incolumes ac leti fuerunt: no biscum pariter loquebantur, māducabāt bibebant et laborabant: nihil minus quā hoc anno se morituros cogitantes. Ecce quando non putabāt venit mors rapuit eos: statuitqꝫ animas eorum ad tribunal tremendi iudicis: qui reddidit vnicuiqꝫ secunduꝫ opera manuū suarum. Ecce nūc iam disce fratrũ tuorũ exemplo quo¬ niam et tu moriturus es: et forsitan multo transibus ab hoc mundo citius quam poteris estimare. Resipiscito miser quādo ia potes: age penitentiam in tempore sanita¬ tis tue quando iudex pollicetur misericordiam: et noli differre bonum hodiernum in dubium ex astrum. Consurge vel nūc sero tandem ab ignauia negligentioris transacte conuersatiōis in qua hactenus turpiter computruisti: et expurga consciētiam tuā ab omni macula peccati: lachrymis exterge quod commisisti malum: et iam deinceps viue innocenter vt condere cet monachum. Perfectum emendationis capesce propositum: et intellige quo¬ niam non incipientibus bonum sed perfeuerantibus vsqꝫ in finem repromittur regnum celorum. Scito etiam quod nōperuenitur inertia et torpor ad caelum: sqlabore magno: conatu voluntatis proficiendi maximo: et studio exercitiij spiritualis indefesso. Uolēs igitur domino seruiri ac placere in veritate: semper consiste apud temetipsum pauidus in timore: et prepara animā tuā ad tēptationē. Resistēdū ē fortit̉ īordinatꝭ motibꝰ et ꝯcupiscētijs

Homily XVIII.

You have been called to the [choir?] of God, and you, given over to the pleasures of the flesh, think of Christ least of all. You have been invited to love the Lord Jesus above all things, and you walk after the evil desires of your heart; you show yourself ungrateful to your Redeemer. You who ought to live by the Spirit savor earthly things, and, sunk in pride, despise all the holy exercises of spiritual conduct. And what will you answer on that day of judgment to the Judge, who will say to you in your utter ingratitude: “I, who am Lord of all, humbled myself for your sake, taking the form of a servant, and being found in fashion as a man. I poured out my blood for you; for you I endured blows; and for you I underwent a most bitter death by my own willing choice. I loved you, O monk, with my whole heart; I redeemed you by my blood from perpetual death; I, out of love, called you to the heavenly kingdom, if you had kept my commandments. But you lived in opposition to my precepts; and, what is more serious, though you had been sworn to my words, you did not fear to show yourself against me, your Lord, as an apostate, impious traitor. Now therefore render an account of your stewardship.”

What then will you answer, O lazy and idle monk, who now consume this acceptable time so fruitlessly, and despise living in true monastic purity according to the Rule? What, I ask, will you answer? Will you deny the works of wickedness which you have committed, and through deceit display the good works which you now scorn to perform, so that by lying you may circumvent the Judge and thus escape the penalty owed to your demerits? But you must not be unaware that all things you have done, said, or thought throughout your whole life, good and evil, are manifest in the sight of the Judge; and nothing can be hidden from him, who alone knows all things. For all things are written in the book of God, and your conscience will bear open testimony against you concerning all the evil things you have done, so that not even the smallest thought will be able to lie hidden. For the Scripture of the prophets says to God: “For the thought of man will confess to you.” You are to be judged before the tribunal of the One who knows all things; before whose terrible judgment every creature will stand with very great fear and trembling, where no excuse at all is admitted, but each person, with appeal set aside, will receive the sentence owed to his merits. Thousands upon thousands of holy spirits

Folio xliiii.

will stand beside him; and do you trust that you can deceive yourself by lying while he is judge? But hear my counsel, and, rising from your destructive sloth, at last awaken, and in due time flee from justice to the mercy of God through true repentance. Do not put it off from day to day, because it is very dangerous for one who remains in sins to be confident, and to refuse the remedy of salvation that is offered. Remember that you are going to die, and that when you do not expect it you will be called to judgment. Consider, I beg you, how the uncertain span of life slips away, and how quickly all mortal things decay. Nothing among human things is stable, nothing fixed, nothing firm; but all things that we see are corruptible, and change with time. Consider also where our brothers Valentinus, Martinus, and Ioannes now are, who in the present year were living with us, healthy, unharmed, and joyful; they spoke with us, ate, drank, and worked together with us, thinking least of all that they would die this year. Behold, when they did not think it, death came and snatched them away, and set their souls before the tribunal of the dread Judge, who rendered to each according to the works of his hands. Behold, now learn from the example of your brothers that you too are going to die, and perhaps you will pass from this world much sooner than you can estimate.

Come to your senses, wretched man, while you still can; do penance in the time of your health, when the Judge promises mercy, and do not defer today’s good to the uncertain [tomorrow?]. Rise up, even now, late though it is, from the sloth of your more negligent past conduct, in which until now you have shamefully rotted, and purge your conscience of every stain of sin; wipe away with tears the evil you have committed; and henceforth live innocently, as befits a monk. Take hold of the perfect purpose of amendment, and understand that the kingdom of heaven is promised not to those who begin the good, but to those who persevere to the end. Know also that one does not arrive at heaven by sloth and torpor, but by great labor, by the very greatest effort of a will to make progress, and by unwearied zeal in spiritual exercise. Therefore, wishing to serve the Lord and to please him in truth, always remain within yourself, fearful in awe, and prepare your soul for temptation. One must resist with strength the disordered movements and desires

On Patience and Meekness

of the flesh: one must struggle with a most steadfast mind against all the enticements and vanities of the world; by prayers and greatness of spirit the devil, the adversary of our salvation, must be put to flight. No drowsy, lazy, and slothful man will ever have come to the kingdom of God; no one without continual labor and many sweats has obtained heaven. For the Lord says in the holy Gospel: “The kingdom of God suffers violence, and the violent,” that is, those who have learned steadfastly to resist the evil desires of the flesh, “seize it.”

Turn over the deeds of all the saints, and nowhere will you find anyone sanctified without great and continual labor. For even if no one becomes holy by his own powers, nevertheless the gracious mercy of the almighty Lord, which grants to those who strive both the will to do good and the strength, sanctifies no one without the works of a good and right will. Since, therefore, God wills all men to be saved and none to perish, we, my brothers, must take the greatest care not to receive his grace in vain, but rather strive with all our strength so that, like fertile ground, we may always answer the free gifts of so great a sower with fitting fruits from the works of good will.

Let us therefore arm ourselves with the shield of faith and put on the breastplate of constancy and saving patience, so that, prepared against all things that can befall us, through humility and the fervor of the Holy Spirit, with our Lord Jesus Christ helping us, we may overcome. In all these things patience is very necessary for us; without its support there never was, nor could there be, any perseverance in good and holy works. For there was no other way to heaven for the saints than patience; nor could he ever be sanctified who cast patience aside.

Indeed, all who pleased almighty God from the beginning of the world down to this our age triumphed over the prince of the world in no other way than through patience. Hence they could all most rightly say that saying of the psalmist: “For your sake we are put to death all the day; we are counted as sheep for slaughter.” The most holy apostle of Christ, Paul, also, recalling the patience of the saints of old, says among other things: “They went about in sheepskins, in goatskins, needy, distressed, afflicted; the world was not worthy of them; wandering in deserts, in mountains, in caves and in the caverns of the earth.” For all who wish to live piously in Christ will suffer persecution, since, as the prophet says, many are the tribulations of the just, and from all these the Lord will deliver them.

Patience, therefore, is necessary for all mortals, and especially befits cloistered persons, since, just as adversities are never lacking to the just in this world, so no one will be justified without patience. Now the chief degrees of patience, as the diligence of the ancients distinguished them, are three. The first and lowest is that of those men who neither seek adversities nor willingly endure them; but when they happen, they are weighed down in spirit and cast down with grief. They also sometimes complain and murmur for a time against those who inflict them; but after the inflamed agitation of the mind has passed, they return to themselves, and are seen patiently to endure the insult inflicted without revenge.

Yet the patience of these men, not of great virtue, is always very close to a fault of the mind, and for that reason must often be reckoned of no merit, and sometimes of lesser merit. And although such persons in our times are said to be distinguished by the virtue of patience, nevertheless, compared with the ancient saints, they do not deserve this venerable name of Christian long-suffering and endurance. For that does not seem to be true patience which has been darkened by bitterness and indignation of an agitated mind.

The second degree of patience is said to belong to those men who, although they do not seek to endure evils, nevertheless when they come, receive them willingly and kindly, and embrace them most patiently as a gift sent by God. And such persons are truly to be called patient: those who, kindled by divine love, bear with equanimity whatever adversity occurs, and preserve in tribulation the same tranquillity of mind that they previously had in prosperity. I would not doubt that that most holy Job the Idumean was of their number: he not only, struck by extreme adversity, patiently bore all things, but even, placed in a whirlpool of evils, gave thanks and blessed the Lord. “The Lord [unclear] gave; the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has been done; blessed be the name of the Lord.”

All Christians should preserve this degree of patience, and before others especially cloistered persons. For the wise man says: “The teaching of a man [unclear]

...is recognized by patience. For the more each person has been instructed in the law of the Lord and in knowledge of the teaching of rational nature, the more patient he will be in adversities. What if I speak more boldly, as a lover of truth: adversities profit us more than prosperity, if we are learned and not forgetful [unclear] of our proper condition.

But a third degree of patience remains, certainly the highest and most perfect, rightly granted to those who not only, when there is need, bear contrary things calmly for the love of God and the usefulness of the brethren, but also, more fervent and inflamed with the spirit of charity, hasten gladly to expose themselves to receive insults and injuries. And this kind of patience is divided into two parts, just as a twofold class of martyrs is found. For some, although they could have hidden when persecution of believers was raging, with Christ’s charity burning in them, and with no one compelling them, but by their own free will, presented themselves before the tribunals of the persecutors, publicly confessing Jesus, the Redeemer of the world, and received the torments inflicted on them with joy. Others, although they did not thrust themselves forward unbidden, nevertheless joyfully accepted martyrdom when it was offered, always prepared to endure for the faith of Christ whatever the cruelty of tyrants might have thought to inflict.

To these most illustrious confessors rightly obtain a neighboring degree: if the cruelty of the impious, by persecuting them, did not remove them from this world, nevertheless they in no way lost the glory of martyrdom. For, crucifying their flesh in this world for the name of Christ, they endured both a voluntary and a daily martyrdom; they were made glorious through abstinence and humility, always steadfast in mind and most patient, and most ready to accept bodily martyrdom. You also, O monks, should take care to be [unclear] with all your powers; and although enemies who kill the body for Christ are now lacking, by resisting the desires of the flesh and patiently sustaining adversities for the love of God, you should show yourselves martyrs in mind and spirit. In the peace of the saints, the best kind of martyrdom is to afflict the flesh by abstinence for the name of God, to desire nothing in this world, to advance always in good works, and, if any evil occurs, to bear it in all things gladly and patiently with cheerfulness of mind. To this new [unclear] of patience, dearest brothers, henceforth...

...lives, if you desire to reign with Christ forever. Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ: so that what each person desires to be done for himself, he should also cheerfully bestow upon his brother.

On True Humility

Homily Nineteen.

It is the opinion of nearly all learned men, dearest brothers, that the highest and chief virtue of monks is none other than humility, because it is the mother and nurse of all virtues. Humility indeed makes the monk; pride destroys and corrupts him. The Lord says through Isaiah: “To whom shall I look, if not to the poor little one, and the contrite in spirit, and the one trembling at my words?” For God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble; because the beginning of every sin is pride, and without true humility no one can attain salvation. Since this is so, I think it necessary for me, brothers, to exhort you without interruption that, fleeing pride, you should always preserve deep humility in all your works. Indeed, no good work is believed to please the Lord God when it is presented without the seasoning of humility.

For humility is a most healthful medicine for the souls of the faithful, because it aids all: it presses down the swollen ulcers of the spirit; it restores what is wasting away; it corrects what is depraved; it removes what has grown out excessively. Humility is the mother and parent of all virtues: you strengthen patience; you arouse compunction; you illuminate charity; you adorn chastity; you make prayer fruitful; you commend fasting and abstinence. O holy humility, truly beloved of God: through penitence you justify the impious; you preserve the just in their purpose of holiness; you powerfully open heaven to your lovers; you close hell to penitents. O humility, venerable and exceedingly pleasing to God: you compelled the Son of the eternal Father to descend from heaven into the womb of most chaste Mary, the perpetual virgin; you made him appear visible to us; you caused him, wrapped in poor cloths, to be laid in a manger, so that he might adorn us in heaven with the ornaments of perpetual happiness. You [unclear] the Son of God with the circumcision of the flesh...

On the True Humility of Monks.

Omnis qui se exeat humiliabitur: & qui se humilitat exaltabitur. & rege celoz do cuius quisvis iniuratoribus dicit. Discite a me quia mitis fuz et humilis corde: & inuenietis requie animabus velris. Beatissima quoz genetrix intacta virgo maria: in suo catico laudis dulcissimo de oño deo sic loquit. De posuit poetes de sedibus: & extrauit humiles. & prophetas dicit in psalmo. You impelled [us] to undertake it, so that, [circumcised?] in mind, we might be able to enter the promised inheritance of the saints. And great is the humility of power, which made the king of heaven and earth withdraw from the face of one most vile man, and dwell for a seven-year exile in the land of the Egyptians. You compelled Christ Jesus, the only-begotten Son of God, to assume a human body for our salvation, and made him undergo also the most bitter passion and death by his own voluntary will. And great is your dominion, O venerable humility of holiness, since the kingdom of heaven is promised to you, to whose worshippers the gift of everlasting blessedness is granted; and whoever keeps to your footprints is raised up to the height of the angels, as Christ says in the holy Gospel: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted.” And the king of heaven says to certain [unclear]: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls.” The most blessed mother also, the untouched Virgin Mary, in her sweetest canticle of praise, speaks thus of Almighty God: “He has put down the mighty from their seats, and has exalted the humble.” And the prophet says in the psalm: “The Lord has looked upon the prayers of the humble, and has not despised their petitions.” For the prayer of the humble penetrates the clouds, and until it draws near it will not be comforted, and it will not depart until the Most High looks upon it. Humility makes the monk who is pure in his conscience most pleasing to God; and the more he casts himself down by humbling himself for God’s honor, the more glorious he will appear in the kingdom. The monk who truly humbles himself becomes a son of the Most High through participation in grace, and with the king of heaven, Jesus Christ, he will rejoice forever. He who truly desires to imitate Christ should also take up true humility; clothed and fortified with it as with a breastplate of strength, he may do great things, and, thinking only lowly things of himself, may not incur the stain of vainglory. For this is the true perfection of monks: always humbly to recognize one’s own imperfection, and to consider rather what good is lacking to him than what he has in the world. For true humility always stretches forward to what lies ahead through the desire of charity, and, carefully mindful of things past lest it lose the merits it has gained, and desiring to acquire through the zeal of devotion the things not yet possessed, in the fervor of holiness

Et nobis cõfidimus quod sepius dicere solemus ad salutem nostram conducere pauper¬ tatem: dum causam humiliatis habe¬ mus magnam: elationis vero et superbie materiam nullam inuenimus. Alij conti¬ nua exercitatione virtutum et memoria mortis quã breui necessario sunt passuri ad magnã humiliatẽ peruenerunt. Quẽ¬ nõ etiã superbissimum humiliaret intẽta me¬ ditatio mortis? Aut quis tam ferox anīo qui nõ demittat paulatim tumorẽ: si dili¬ gentius cogitauerit in breui se moriturũ? Proinde conscientia monachi nunq́ꝫ de¬ bet memoriam a se mortis future depellere quatenus et humilis permaneat et tristis vt consistens in humilitate nõ superbia h ij

Homily XIX. Folio XLVI.

[unclear] is raised up; it is sustained by the rock of humility alone. For truly, if true humility is lacking, the gathering together of all the other virtues will be nothing other than a kind of collapse of a house built without a foundation on sand. For in the spiritual building humility lays the stable foundation; charity orders the breadth of that house; the wall is raised on high by the continuation of good works in fervor of spirit; the roof is placed at the summit in faith in our Lord Jesus Christ and in firm hope of the promise of eternal protection and happiness; and its length is arranged in the long-suffering of patience with most beautiful ordering.

Therefore, my brothers, again and again I admonish, adjure, and beseech you to take care to found the building of spiritual exercise in the depth of humility, because no good work is pleasing to God if it has been offered apart from true humility. Now there are many things which have been wont to move the servants of God toward true humility. For consideration of their own worthlessness humbles some within themselves before God, because, when they consider that by experience they have already often found themselves wretched and weak, being humbled they place all their hope and confidence in God. Others, weighing carefully the multitude of God’s benefits toward them, fear the judgment of ingratitude; and therefore in the sight of God, with great fear and reverence of gratitude, they always go forward humble. And who among us is there, brothers, to whom the compassion of almighty God has not also granted many benefits, even individually? If we wish to be grateful for them, we must above all be humble.

Others, after a multitude of sins, converted to penitence by divine kindness, diligently recall to memory how many evils they have committed against the law of the Almighty; and for these, humbled in bitterness of spirit, they detest their impieties with horror. But we offend in many things; whence it is necessary that we humble ourselves always in mind and heart, and even in body, so that grace may abound where sin formerly abounded. Often, moreover, the providence of divine compassion permits certain persons to sin enormously for a time, so that afterward, converted to penitence, they may learn to remain inwardly humble. Better is a humble penitent than a proud man who has not sinned, because humility justifies penitents, while pride condemns the arrogant eternally, even if they have done nothing else evil than this alone, that they are proud.

Others, carrying in their heart by daily meditation the bitter passion of Jesus Christ, humble themselves the more, the more they know that they are greatly indebted for such and so wonderful benefits of that same Redeemer of theirs. The Son of God humbled himself, having been made man for us; and, filled with many reproaches, he voluntarily underwent the most shameful death of the cross, that he might free us from the destruction of perpetual death. What Christian man, and especially what monk, will not humble his soul greatly before God, when he has recalled to memory such humility of his Creator and Redeemer? For truly, the man whom the humility of Christ does not move to meekness will profit from no admonitions of men. In vain do we say that we are monks, unless we have followed Christ humbly according to our powers. For this reason he said in the holy Gospel that he himself is the way, so that we might imitate his humility, and so that the conduct of so great a master might become the spiritual form of the disciple.

Therefore, brothers, as much as we can, let us strive with all our strength that all that pride has made swollen in us may be leveled, renewed, and reformed by humility conceived from meditation on the most bitter passion of Jesus Christ. O how fitting it is for us to humble our souls for love of Jesus Christ, my brothers, since God himself and the Creator of all, made [unclear] of humility, cast himself down for us into such great humility. Therefore the supreme medicine for inducing true humility in a servant of God is for him daily, and often, to recall to memory the most bitter passion of Christ Jesus.

Tribulations also, adversities, and infirmities, together with poverty or want, have made many humble, who perhaps in prosperous and favorable circumstances would have perished, puffed up. And we trust that what we often customarily say is conducive to our salvation: poverty, since we have a great cause of humility, while we find no material for exaltation and pride. Others, by continual exercise of virtues and by memory of the death which shortly they must necessarily suffer, have come to great humility. Whom would not even the attentive meditation of death humble, however proud? Or who is so fierce in spirit that he would not gradually put down his swelling pride, if he reflected more diligently that he is soon to die? Accordingly the conscience of a monk ought never to drive away from itself the memory of future death, so that he may remain both humble and sorrowful, and, standing firm in humility, not [unclear].

De vera humilitate monachorum. De vero continuus omnem cordi lasciui¬ am interdicat. Nōnullos etiam gratuita dei miseratio preuenit: et spiritꝰ sancti co¬ habitatione humiles facit. Om̄is qui spi ritu dei agitur: superbiā summe detestat̉. Qui seipsum in veritate cognoscit sapiē¬ tissimus est: et non potest ab humili tatis mansuetudine facere discessum. Omnis aūt superbus et arrogans ignarus est: eti ain si magnus inter mortales et inclitus videatur. Uera em̄ sapiēta in domicilio requiscet sancte humilitatis: et ipsa ꝑ pati entie documentū clariorꝫ ostēditur. Ex co gnitione dei et suijpsius humilitas nasciṫ. et hec vera sapientia merito nuncupatur Qui seipsum cognouit veraciter iā nō ha bet vnde superbiat: qm̄ sciens vilitatem suam nihil altū cogitat: sed in merore ani mi positus ad dominuʒ clamat. Ubi fuerit humilitas ibi paxest vera et summa tranquillitas: vbi autēdominatur superbia: ibi rācor: ira: turba¬tio et discordia sine intermissione confun¬dunt vniuersa. Iauete igitur fratres meīsuperbiā: quoniaʒ si angelos de celo pro¬iect elatos: pauperes quando non dam¬naret claustrales. Demones fecit ex an¬gelis: et socios demonum proculdubio

On the true humility of monks.

But the continual [fear?] of God forbids every wantonness to the heart. The free compassion of God also forestalls some, and makes them humble by the indwelling of the Holy Spirit. Everyone who is led by the Spirit of God utterly detests pride.

He who truly knows himself is most wise, and cannot depart from the meekness of humility. But every proud and arrogant man is ignorant, even if he seems great and famous among mortals. For true wisdom will rest in the dwelling-place of holy humility, and it is itself shown more clearly through the lesson of patience. Humility is born from knowledge of God and of oneself, and this is rightly called true wisdom.

He who has truly known himself now has nothing for which to be proud, since, knowing his own vileness, he thinks nothing lofty, but, placed in sorrow of soul, cries to the Lord: What is man, that you are mindful of him, or the son of man, that you account him? Man has been made like vanity; his days, as it is written, [unclear] under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in the time of visitation.

For humility with chaste fear greatly pleases the Lord God in his servants, since he approves no virtue of a man unto salvation without it. Therefore, if we desire to climb to the lofty threshold of the kingdom of heaven, we must be very humble, because there is no other road to heaven except that of the deepest humility, by which both the Son of God himself and all the saints ascended. But all who have tried to enter the kingdom by another gate, their head of pride having been struck back on the threshold of humility, could by no means enter. For the gate of humility does not admit the proud, and the narrow road of meekness does not receive lovers of greed and self-exaltation.

Therefore whoever has [unclear] to come to the height of the heavenly [unclear], let him ascend by the steps of humility; without these, whoever begins to ascend undoubtedly falls into the depth of perdition and death. For humility is the ladder of heaven, beautifully distinguished by twelve rungs; concerning its ascent our lawgiver, blessed Benedict, says in the Rule: If we wish to reach the highest summit of humility, and swiftly to arrive at that heavenly exaltation, we must set up for ourselves that ladder which appeared to Jacob in dreams, by which angels were shown to him ascending and descending. Without doubt that descent and ascent is understood by us to be nothing other than to descend by exaltation and to ascend by humility, as divine Scripture tells us: Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and he who humbles himself will be exalted.

The ladder itself, set upright, is our life in this world, which is raised up to heaven by the Lord when the heart has been humbled. For we say that the sides of the same ladder are our body and soul. Into these sides the divine calling has inserted the different steps of humility and discipline that are to be ascended. Thereafter, indeed, he enumerates those twelve steps in order with a sufficiently beautiful arrangement; since they are all very well known to you, it would be superfluous to spend longer on reviewing them on this occasion.

For it is enough in this place to remember the holy canon, upon the words of which you all long ago willingly swore, so that you may know that humility is no less necessary for salvation for you than love of God and, at the same time, of neighbor. For humility is said to be the monk’s greatest virtue, and it is so necessary to his profession that without it he cannot be saved. A monk exalted in mind and proud is not the bondman of Christ, but of the devil; he will have no share with the Son of God in heaven, but will be tormented without end with the demons in hell.

For Christ, the teacher and instructor of humility, detests all the proud, and admits into his company only the humble, the gentle, and the meek. But the devil is the head and inventor of pride, whose servants and disciples are all who follow his pride and self-exaltation. For he himself, the king of the proud, cannot bear the humble; he flees the gentle, and does not dare to stand in the sight of the meek in heart. For Christ dwells in the assembly of the humble servants of God; but in the midst of the proud the devil stirs up the contentions and quarrels of those at discord.

Where there is humility, there is true peace and the highest tranquillity; but where pride rules, there rancor, anger, disturbance, and discord confuse everything without ceasing. Therefore, my brothers, avoid pride, since if it cast down the exalted angels from heaven, when would it not condemn poor cloistered men? It made demons from angels, and, without doubt, [unclear] companions of demons

Humilitas peccatores iustificat: supbia vero suos se ctatoꝛes damnat. Humilitas deo facit ꝓ ximū: supbia aūt a gr̄a dei efficit alienuꝫ. Fo. XLVII. b iij

Homily XIX.

At all times, with all your strength and as much as you can, flee all pride and ostentation, since unless you greatly humble your souls, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven. Walk always before the Lord Jesus in the simplicity of your heart, having a pure conscience in all things, lest your humility become bestial; for it contributes nothing to salvation for a sinner to acknowledge himself publicly and, by persevering in evil, not to amend his fault. For the true servant of Christ sanctifies his humility by good works, and amends all the guilt of his past life by continual penitence. Daily he recalls to memory the evil that he remembers having committed, and groans deeply that he has offended the Lord. He walks very cautiously, and so laments past offenses that he by no means commits further things to be lamented. The monk who is truly humble follows the fasting Lord in a pure conscience, and fears nothing more in this world than to offend the teacher whom he imitates. Whatever he does and wherever he goes, he always thinks of the Lord Jesus as present, and by continual meditation examines how he may please him alone. For this is truly Christian humility, and humble Christianity: to [unclear] sin in true compunction, and to preserve the conscience in all purity at all times, not only from fear of punishments but rather from love of Christ. The true humility of monks continually does whatever good it can for the honor of God, and thinks that it will do nothing that it knows displeases Christ. True humility of monks [unclear] human [unclear], and, serving the Lord in the fervor of charity, is a companion of the holy angels, a friend to the citizens of heaven, and very formidable to demons. For demons fear and flee nothing more than the humility of the servants of Jesus Christ, because, since they themselves are most proud by their vicious will, they are most violently tormented by humble devotion. For where true humility is, demons cannot remain; for as ice is dissolved by fire, so malignant spirits are scattered from the presence of a humble monk. O humility, venerable mother and preserver of all virtues: yours is the kingdom, yours the power; you confer the kingdom upon the humble; you bestow the glory of eternal happiness upon the meek; without your guidance no one comes to heaven; whoever follows you does not fear hell. Whoever gathers works of virtues without you is like one who carries dust into the wind. You are the seasoning of all good works; for just as food in the mouth of the eater is not savory without salt, so without your companionship no one will be established as a friend of God. Humility made the Son of God man; humility will make the servant of Christ equal to a holy angel. An angel, through pride by his own choice, became the devil; and a Christian man through humility becomes an angel. Humility opens heaven to the meek servants of God, and pride plunges arrogant men down to hell. Humility makes friends of God, and pride makes companions of demons. Humility enlightens the mind to true wisdom, and pride blinds the understanding of the one whom it possesses. Humility purges the man whom it possesses from all disordered affections; and pride fills its worshipper with all crimes and filthiness. Humility makes its lover a servant of God; pride, however, makes him a slave of the devil. Humility makes one wise in the law of the Lord; pride, however, renders man foolish, away from the knowledge of the Most High. Humility brings the poor man into the fellowship of God; and pride makes the rich man a member of the devil. Humility is the mother and nurse of all virtues; and pride is the [source?] of all vices. Humility, with charity as mediator, covers a multitude of sins; pride, however, by itself introduces the fullness of all vices. Humility makes a monk’s good works most pleasing to God; pride, however, renders idle the endeavors of the proud before the Creator. Humility receives from the Lord whatever it has asked; but almighty God resists the prayers of the proud. Humility always has, in the Lord’s mercies, a pious confidence with cheerfulness of mind; pride, however, with the sting of despair, begets disturbance in man. Humility always has joy of spirit in the love of Christ; pride, however, is always occupied by pernicious fear. Humility, the [support?] of good works, neglects none of the spiritual exercises; pride, however, despises all pursuits of salvation. Humility justifies sinners; pride, however, condemns its followers. Humility makes one near to God; pride, however, makes one alien from the grace of God.

De vera humilitate monachorum. Humilitas mandatis dei placida volun- tate studiosa obsequitur: superbia preceptis altissimi reluctatur. Humilitas merita sempiterne felicitatis accumulat: su- perbia autem sibi grauissima inferni tormenta parat. Humilitas securitatem prestat in mortis articulo: superbia vero horribilem metum et calamitatem affert morituro. Dumilitas animam sui cultoris in tremendo dei iudicio ab omni angustia liberat: supuria aute omnes elatos quos decepit in mundo coram iudice accusat. Humilitas dei seruos iudicis locabit ad dexteram: superbia vero damnandos constituet ad si nistrum. Humilitas causam aget pro suis et obtinebit in iudicio: superbia autem nimirum confusa tradet elatos diabolo. Humilitas premium eterne felicitatis suis rependet amicis: superbia veto tormentam perpe tue damnationis omnibus dabit elatis. Dumilitas in celo sine fine coronabitur: supuria autem apud inferos estimabilem cruciatum cum demonibꝰ perpetuo patietur. Dumilitas coronata cum christo regnant in celis: et superbia contemptacum dilecto cruciabitur in penis: Dumilitas leta et gloriosa in eternum sedebit ad dextera mundi: superbia autem tristis et ignominiosa sine iacebit in tormentis inferno. Tunc humiles exultabunt in gloria: et superbi omnes pre nimio dolore perpetuis temporibus clamabunt in pena. Ibi istambunt humiles in conspectu dei et sanctorumomni in leticia magna et exultatiom semipiterna: recipientes pro volutaria huius vite inopia divitias immarcescibles: promansuetudine regnum: pro triestitia gaudiomundi et carnis maceratione spontaneacelum. Uidentes auct superbi et arrogantes in inferno constituti tantam gloriam humilium quos in mundo despexerunt miserabuntur in taum subita mutatione faucitorum turbabunturque timore horribili premimia spiritus angustia gementes et dicentes in furore superbie. Hi sunt monachipauperes et humiles quondam vilibus induti: se questrati ab hominibꝰ: ab essu carminium et omnispurcicia carnis abstinentes: quos habuimus aliquem in derisum et similitudinem improperij: nos insensatiori vitam illorem estimabamus insaniam: et finem illorum fine honorem. Ecce quem inter filios dei computatis sunt: et intersauctos fors illorum test. Ergo errauimus via veritatis: et iustitiennobis lumen non illuxit: et sol intelligentienon est ortus nobis. Quid nobis iam pdestsuperbia qua tunc instati contempsinushumiles: et quid nobis confert habita inseculo diuitiarum iactantia? Preterierunt omnia: et nos per continua cõtumacia inter demones computati sumus: quam humilitatem odiosemper habuimus: ac semine patimur iestimabilem cruciatus. Humiles autem in perpetuum viuent: et apud dominum est merceseorum: et cogitatio illorum apud altissimum. Hec fratres mei semper precogitate: quam dubitanter ita futura sunt: veraque propter ea mētis humilitatem assumite: per eum omne sugite: conscienciam puram consciencia tenere et ereniepmia vite mereamini obtinere. Amen. De monachorum obedientia vera: Omelia. xx. Umilitas monachorum si- vera et perfecta fuerit: omnene plenitudinem sanctarumvirtutum parit. Quod si virtutum splendorem caruerit: vera in mente humili- tas nunquam fuit. In primis etenim veramparit obedientiam: et profundum in cunctispro dei amore subiectionum.Monachusemin qui vere humilis peregrinatur in carne:saluatoris nostri iesus christi studiosumse in omnibus prebet discernim: pro cuiusamore omni vilitate et extremitate contenus: abbati suo in cunctis obediens se gloriaritur subiectum. Magna virtus est humilismonacho celum aperit: et infernum sua fortitudine claudit. Obedientia viam para- dyssi reparam: et pacem inter deum et hominemreformat. Nec monachus est dicendumus fed meadax et fallacissimus apostataqui scquis ī cenobio vivit et continua servat sine hu

On the True Humility of Monks.

Humility eagerly obeys the commandments of God with a willing disposition pleasing to him; pride resists the precepts of the Most High. Humility heaps up the merits of everlasting blessedness; pride, however, prepares for itself the most grievous torments of hell. Humility provides security at the point of death; pride brings horrible fear and calamity to the dying man. Humility frees the soul of its devotee from every distress in the dread judgment of God; pride, however, accuses before the judge all the haughty whom it deceived in the world. Humility will place the servants of God at the judge’s right hand; pride will set those to be damned at the left. Humility will plead the cause for its own and will prevail in judgment; pride, surely confounded, will hand the haughty over to the devil. Humility will repay the reward of eternal blessedness to its friends; pride, however, will give the torment of perpetual damnation to all the haughty. Humility will be crowned without end in heaven; pride, however, will suffer immeasurable torment with the demons forever in the lower regions.

Humility, crowned with Christ, reigns in the heavens; and pride, despised, will be tormented with [unclear] in punishments. Humility, joyful and glorious, will sit forever at the right hand of [unclear]; pride, however, sorrowful and ignominious, will lie without end in the torments of hell. Then the humble will exult in glory, and all the proud, because of excessive pain, will cry out in punishment for all ages. There the humble will stand in the sight of God and of all the saints in great joy and everlasting exultation, receiving, for the voluntary poverty of this life, unfading riches; for meekness, a kingdom; for sorrow [unclear], and for the spontaneous mortification of the flesh, heaven. But the proud and arrogant, placed in hell, seeing such great glory of the humble whom they despised in the world, will lament in so sudden a change of [unclear], and will be troubled with horrible fear, groaning under the very great anguish of spirit and saying in the fury of pride: These are the poor and humble monks, once clothed in vile garments, separated from men, abstaining from the eating of meats and from every filthiness of the flesh, whom we held at one time in derision and as a likeness of reproach; senseless as we were, we judged their life madness, and their end without honor. Behold how they are counted among the sons of God, and their lot is among the saints.

Therefore we have strayed from the way of truth, and the light of justice has not shone upon us, and the sun of understanding has not risen for us. What does pride now profit us, by which, when we were then puffed up, we despised the humble? And what does the boastfulness of riches possessed in the world bring us? All things have passed away, and through continual contumacy we have been counted among the demons; because we always had humility in hatred, we now suffer immeasurable torments. But the humble will live forever, and their reward is with the Lord, and the care of them is with the Most High. These things, my brothers, always think upon beforehand, because without doubt they are thus to be; and therefore assume humility of mind, flee every [unclear] through it, keep a pure conscience, and may you deserve to obtain the rewards of eternal life. Amen.

On the True Obedience of Monks: Homily XX.

If the humility of monks has been true and perfect, it brings forth the whole fullness of the holy virtues. But if it has lacked the splendor of the virtues, true humility was never in the mind. For first it brings forth true obedience, and a profound subjection in all things for the love of God. For the monk who truly lives as a pilgrim in the flesh shows himself in all things an eager [disciple?] of our Savior Jesus Christ; for love of him, despising every vileness and extremity, he glories in being subject to his abbot, obedient in all things. Obedience is a great virtue: it opens heaven to the humble monk and by its strength closes hell. Obedience restores the way of paradise and reforms peace between God and man. This, however, is true monastic obedience: that which is rendered to the commands of superiors not from servile fear but from an inward affection of charity, which, persevering until death not through fear of punishment but through love of justice, works good in cheerfulness of mind. There are two most beautiful wings of the mind by which the monk flies from earth to heaven; one of these is called humility, the other is known as the obedience of subjection. The monk who has not been adorned with these wings has entirely lost both the name and the merit of his dignity. Nor is he to be called a monk, but a deceitful and most false apostate, who [unclear] lives in the monastery and continually observes without hu

Homily 20. Folio XLVIII.

the obedience of humble subjection. For a monk without obedience is a monster of the devil; and he who resists the commands of his superior will inherit the punishments of hell. The disobedience of the first man lost the life of eternal happiness from the beginning; the obedience of Jesus Christ restored it. For he was made obedient to the Father for us even unto death, and by his most innocent passion he restored to us the happiness that had been lost. Therefore the path to salvation is humble obedience, as our holy lawgiver, blessed Benedict, cries out in the Rule: “Listen, O son, to the precepts of the master, and incline the ear of your heart, and willingly receive and effectively fulfill the admonition of a loving father, so that by the labor of obedience you may return to him from whom you had withdrawn through the sloth of disobedience.”

Obedience is the tree of eternal salvation, which grows in the garden of monastic humility. Obedience is the dwelling-place of the Holy Spirit and the quiet tomb of one’s own will. Obedience is the merit of heavenly happiness and the one lesson of monastic discipline. Obedience is the extermination of all self-exaltation and pride, and the persecutor of all vices. Obedience overcomes wickedness and extinguishes every disordered pleasure of the flesh. Obedience makes the conscience pure and clean, and preserves true humility in the mind. Obedience is the remedy of the wounded soul and the foundation of the whole monastic observance. Obedience is the faithful custody of all good works and the discipline of a sincere mind. Obedience is the beginning of mortification and the glorious ornament of the monk. Obedience is the preserver of peace and concord; without it the vigor of monastic discipline perishes. Obedience always directs the keen edge of the mind toward God; and he who has truly been mortified in spirit despises all the consolations of this world. Obedience makes the monk near to God and far removed from all the filth of the soul. Obedience is the adornment of holiness and the garment of beauty; without it no one would come to the kingdom of eternal glory. Obedience is the mother of victory, and he who knows how, for the honor of God, to be humbly subject will obtain the crown of martyrdom in heaven. Obedience separates the monk from the world, and whoever follows it with his whole heart will be great before the Most High. Obedience is the consummation of Christian perfection; in its humble workshop, the more a monk advances, the holier he becomes. Obedience is sure security at the hour of death; for the more ready the monk was for obedience to commands, the more securely he will fly away when he departs from here. Obedience is the rewarder of humility and the chief mark of merits. Obedience is the rule of Christian gentleness and the strongest nourishment of inward charity. Obedience is the shelter of chastity and the purest ornament of innocence. Obedience is [unclear] voluntary mortification; its merit is of such dignity that he who is rebellious and proud wears the monastic habit without cause. Obedience is the voluntary mortification of the members; its merit is of such dignity that man has nothing greater to offer in honor of God.

Let each one offer, for love of God, what he can: without doubt that man has offered more than all who has, because of God, killed his own will through obedience. It is indeed a great good to distribute one’s possessions, for love of Christ, to the use of the poor, and to relieve the want of the needy with alms. But as much as the whole outweighs the part, as much as the free choice of the will is nobler than necessity, as much as heaven is distant from earth, so much more has that man offered who, out of love for God, has by a spontaneous will denied himself forever. For whatever temporal substance you have offered to God is not yours but another’s, and is of less value than your own, both in estimation and in reward. You have one thing of your own which, offered above all things, is pleasing to God. What is this, unless the free will which the almighty Creator has placed in your power? A good will, however, is greater than all riches, because nothing richer is offered to God, nothing is consecrated more acceptably. This most precious gift to God, my brothers, you once offered when, denying yourselves and all worldly things for his honor, you put on the monastic habit.

Remember, I beg you, the words of your holy profession, and let that solemn promise never depart from memory, which each one of you uttered in the sight of God before us, saying: “I, brother Johannes, promise stability, conversion of my morals, and obedience according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, before God and his saints, in this monastery, which has been built in honor of blessed Martin, in the presence of lord Johannes, abbot.” Behold the bond by which we have voluntarily bound ourselves to obedience; behold [unclear] four
