Nihil em̄ amāti difficile: sed oīma duꝛra: omnia grauia et ardua: ardens faciliãfacit amor. Que fit ordinatio vi-te monastice bona: Sermo secundus. Egminus institutionē sanctissimi patris nostri Bn̄dicti qua vsitato vocabulo religionem siue ordinarō appellamꝰ: in pͥncipio fundatiōis sue claruisse scissimā: et ꝑ totā latinorū ecclesiam valdemultipliciter fuisse dilatatā. Unde annisqͣꝫ plurimis in hoc ipso ordo multi clariuerū viri sapiētes eruditi atqꝫ sanctissimique sunt Lautet in om̄ibꝰ amba/

Sermon I.

The monk, therefore, who is strong with true virtue neither dares rashly nor fears without counsel. For courage and constancy together are the royal road, from which the rash and stubborn man turns aside to the right, but the fearful, faint-hearted, and timid man to the left. The monk, constant and strong in spirit, never withdraws from the purpose of holiness, but is neither cast down by adversities nor lifted up by prosperities. Hence also the most holy bishop Ambrose says: “The fool changes like the moon. But the wise man is not broken by fear, is not changed by power, is not exalted by prosperities, is not sunk by sorrows.” For where wisdom and virtue are, there is constancy and strength of spirit. Therefore the wise man is always the same in spirit; he is neither diminished nor increased by changes of circumstances, nor does he, like a little child, waver so as to be carried about by every wind of doctrine, but remains perfect in Christ, founded in charity and rooted in the perfection of faith.

Finally, my dearest brothers, perseverance is necessary for you in every good and virtuous work; without it no one ever comes to the crown of glory. For the Lord says in the holy Gospel: “He who perseveres to the end will be saved.” Take away perseverance, and neither will virtue have a reward, nor service a recompense, nor a benefit merit grace. For perseverance alone in good works deserves to receive the crown of praise; without it, it profits nothing to have begun a good thing. No virtue has merit if perseverance is not brought to its increase. The kingdom of eternal happiness is promised not to those who begin the good, but to those who persevere in the good until death, because the denarius will be paid to the laborers in the vineyard not in the morning or at midday, but when evening has come.

For he who began well is not to be praised, but he who continued well to the end is to be honored. Therefore, my brothers, I am accustomed diligently to admonish you, and I ought never to cease, that you carefully attend to your calling and walk cautiously in all religion and holiness, as you know you have sworn. Seek the Lord while he can be found.

Let the life of Christ the Savior be your imitation; by the foundation of your institution you are bound to follow him according to your strength, not by steps of the feet but by likeness of affections. But in all things walk [unclear]; always place the fear of God, in true humility, before the gaze of the mind. For you have need of great purity, you who in mind and body have consented to the holy warfare of Christ. It now belongs to you, O brothers, to despise the world and all things that are in the world for God’s sake with perpetual courage; to overcome all motions of carnal pleasures; to flee sin; to occupy yourselves constantly in good and holy works. Your life also, so far as human weakness allows, ought to imitate angelic purity and to flee and detest all depravity. The holy angels are never idle, but are always, without weariness or [unclear], diligent in the praises of God. The holy angels love God above all things, and do not withdraw even for a moment from his charity. In imitation of them the monk ought to be assiduous in the service of Christ, and always occupied in good works according to the Gospel and the Rule.

The monk ought to have the charity of God most fervently, and true [charity] of neighbor [unclear]. The monk ought to have the charity of God most fervently: he who does not wish to become idle should love; how much more strongly does the most chaste love of God impel the mind it possesses toward arduous things. For fervent love toward God perfects the monk and does not allow him to be idle. For the most holy Pope Gregory says: “The love of God is never idle. For it works great things if it exists; but if it refuses to work, it was never true love of God.” For if the mad poet spoke truly of carnal love, “he who does not wish to become idle loves,” how much more strongly does the most chaste love of God impel the mind it possesses toward arduous things. Love God, brothers, with your whole heart, as far as the strength of desire can extend itself, and you will be able most easily to observe all the things that have been commanded you.

For nothing is difficult to one who loves; but all hard things, all heavy and arduous things, burning love makes easy.

What Is the Good Ordering of the Monastic Life: Sermon Two.

We have read that the institution of our most holy father Benedict, which in common usage we call religion or order, shone forth as most holy at the beginning of its foundation, and that throughout the whole church of the Latins it was very widely extended in many ways. Hence for very many years in this very order there flourished many men who were wise, learned, and most holy, and

117
¶ Que sit ordinatio vite monastice bona. qui omnē magnifice illustrauerunt ecclesiā. Sunt em̄ qui scribāt ex hac monasti¬ca religione nostra sanctorū cathalogo insertos taꝫ viros qͣ moniales quinde cim milia sexcentos. Dorū nobis multitudo sanctorū in ordine fratres ad imitationē proponit̉: nō ad vane gloriādū. Quid eo¬rū ultitudo nobis ad salutē nostrā pōt cōducere: si cōuersatione qua precesserūt nō imitatur: Quotiēs ordinis nostri vi¬ros sācissimos laudare vt iliter cupimꝰ: ad eorū consortiū venire sanctis moribꝰ festinemus. Tūc etenim de multitudine sanctorum ordinis nostri fructuose glorio¬abimus: si recte viueātes eorū numerū au gere sedulo conemut. Propterea nanqꝫ tantā vobis multitudinē sanctorū ꝓponimus: vt cū vicisse mūdū et carnē multos ante vos in hoc ipso ordine cōspicitis: de vestra tandē cōuersatione tepida resurga tis. Uirtutē quā illis dei miseratio contu lit: vobis in vera charitate petentibꝰ non negabit. Vicerūt illi mundū qꝛ christū to ta deuotione dilexerūt: oīa pro eius amo¬re cōtemnentes. Cōtempserunt om̄ia: et dn̄s iesus ꝓuidit illis quecūqꝫ videbant̉ eis ad sustētationē vite necessaria. Dura¬uit hic fernor diuotionis monachorum post primā ordinis institutionē pluribus annis in magna constantia: et multoꝝ mi liū hominū anīas conuertit ad dn̄m. Sʒ nihil stabile in humanis: nihil perpetuuꝫ in caducis. Cōtulit monachis religio sācta diuitias: donec matrē filia ex tempo¬re suffocauit. Nam vt scriptura dicit: omnes qui volunt diuites fieri: incidunt in tentationes diaboli. Incrassatus est dilectus et recalcitravit: impinguatus et dila tatus terrenis possessionibꝰ: dereliquit institutionis prime sancta studia: abijt post vanitates et insanias falsas: quē copia rerū temporaliū: diuitijs spiritualibꝰ inopē et uiserū fecit. Hec ordinis nostri misera¬da deformitas cepit post diui patris Benedicti transitū annis ferme ducentis: et magis ac magis cū tēpore creuit: quo iusqꝫ randē ꝑ totū ordinē noxiū virꝰ sese dif¬fudit. Hec aūt deformitas ordine non subito sed per multorū successuꝫ annoꝛū tādē pene totū occupauit: qͣuis om̄ipotens deꝰ bonis eū viris in toto nuncqͣꝫ destitue rit: sʒ reliquit sibi semꝑ aliquos. qͥ genua sua an̄ baal minime curuauerint. Surrexerunt em̄ viri misericordie quoꝝ iustitie nuncqͣꝫ tradētur obliuioni qͥ ruine ordinis compatientes humerum submisere labo ri: et euꝫ largiente domino suffragium in multis locis restaurarunt. Sulte quidē varie reformationes in ordine particula res multociens diuersis temporibus vi¬guerūt: sed nulla fuit vnqͣꝫ generalis que totū ordine ad integritatem regularis obseruantie reduceret. Deniqꝫ particula¬res instaurationes quas plures fuīsse diximus: quasi omnes collapsas iterum videmus. Nouissime autē eo videlicet quo anno christianoꝝ millesimo quadringentesimo atqꝫ vicesmo concilū generale celebrabatur in constantia noua quedam et hactenꝰ vltima reformatio particularis in alemania sumpsit exordiuꝫ: que a quodam cenobio in saxonie partibus tūc qui de omnū paupertimo quod burẜfeldia nuncupatur appellatiōis sue foritur volum. Primus vero auctor et princeps huius reformationis sanctissime fuit io¬ānes rode abbas insignis monasterij sanctri mathie apud treuiros: qui generalis visitator ordinis constiturus a prefato cōstanciensi concilio: ne alijs predicans ipse iudicaretur reprobus: reformationē pri¬mum exhibuit in semetipso. Reformavit enim et se in primis et monachos memo¬rati monasterij: confirmationē edidit conformes regulę: confirmationē sancti ope¬ris impetravit sedis apostolice. Int̓ omnia vero cenobia ordinis burẜfeldia monasteriū humile atqꝫ pauperculū hac re¬formationē primo succepit: quā postea inreinhausen et ī pauca saxonie monasteria sibi vicina dilarauit. Mortuo tādē ioāne rode abbate scī mathe: pͥncipe reforma¬tiōis nr̄e cū ī eodē loco nō inueniret̉ ꝓ di latatiōe īcepti negocij: successor idoneꝰ: io¬ānes de hagen abbas burẜfeldensis qͥ iā certa monasteria reformauerat vir sanctꝰ et multū zelosus ꝓ ordīe instāte archiepiscopo treuiroꝛū iacobo electus fuit. Qui sua paupertate ꝯtētꝰ burẜfeldiā nō ꝯsensit dimittere: ne diuitias paupertati videret̉ p̄posuisse. Mansit igit̉ in suo monasterio et aliꝰ in locū primi reformatoris ordinatus fuit. Qui cuꝫ neqꝫ doctrina neqꝫ zelosanessori suo yideretur cōparandus: parum pro continuatione inchoati negocij potuit efficere: nec reformationē ī multos anpliare. Cōtigit intea nicolaū eusanū sā¬cte romane ecclesie presbyterū cardinalē

What constitutes the good ordering of monastic life.

who splendidly illuminated the whole Church. For there are those who write that from this our monastic religion fifteen thousand six hundred, both men and nuns, have been entered in the catalogue of the saints. This multitude of saints in the order, brothers, is set before us for imitation, not for vain boasting. How can their multitude conduce to our salvation, if we do not imitate the manner of life in which they went before us? Whenever we desire usefully to praise the most holy men of our order, let us hasten by holy conduct to come into their company. For then we shall glory fruitfully in the multitude of saints of our order, if, by living rightly, we diligently strive to increase their number. For this reason we set before you so great a multitude of saints: so that, when you see that many before you in this very order conquered the world and the flesh, you may at last rise up from your lukewarm manner of life. The virtue which God’s compassion bestowed on them he will not deny to you if you ask in true charity. They conquered the world because they loved Christ with total devotion, despising all things for love of him. They despised all things, and the Lord Jesus provided for them whatever seemed necessary for the sustenance of life.

This fervor of the monks’ devotion endured for many years after the first foundation of the order in great constancy, and converted the souls of many thousands of men to the Lord. But nothing is stable among human things, and nothing lasting among perishable things. Holy religion bestowed riches on the monks, until in time the daughter suffocated the mother. For, as Scripture says, all who wish to become rich fall into the temptations of the devil. The beloved grew fat and kicked back; made corpulent and enlarged by earthly possessions, he abandoned the holy pursuits of the first institution; he went after vanities and false follies, and abundance of temporal things made him poor and wretched in spiritual riches. This lamentable deformity of our order began about two hundred years after the passing of the divine father Benedict, and grew more and more with time, until at last the harmful poison spread itself through the whole order. Yet this deformity did not occupy the order suddenly, but at last, through the succession of many years, almost the whole of it; although almighty God never wholly deprived it of good men, but always left for himself some who had by no means bent their knees before Baal. For men of mercy arose, whose righteous deeds will never be handed over to oblivion; taking pity on the ruin of the order, they put their shoulder beneath the labor, and, with the Lord generously granting aid, restored it in many places.

To be sure, many varied particular reforms flourished in the order many times and at different periods, but there was never any general reform that brought the whole order back to the integrity of regular observance. Finally, however, we see that the particular restorations, which we have said were numerous, have almost all collapsed again. Most recently, namely in the year of the Christians 1420, when the general council was being celebrated at Constance, a certain new and hitherto latest particular reform took its beginning in Germany; from a certain monastery in the parts of Saxony, then indeed the poorest of all, called Bursfelde, it [unclear] the [unclear] of its name.

The first author and leader of this most holy reform was Johannes Rode, abbot of the distinguished monastery of Saint Matthias at Trier, who, being appointed general visitor of the order by the aforesaid Council of Constance, first exhibited reform in himself, lest, while preaching to others, he himself should be judged reprobate. For he first reformed both himself and the monks of the mentioned monastery; he issued a confirmation in conformity with the Rule; he obtained from the Apostolic See confirmation of the holy work. Among all the monasteries of the order, however, Bursfelde, a humble and poor little monastery, first received this reform, which afterward spread to Reinhausen and to a few monasteries of Saxony neighboring it.

At length, when Johannes Rode, abbot of Saint Matthias and leader of our reform, had died, since no suitable successor for the enlargement of the enterprise begun could be found in that same place, Johannes de Hagen, abbot of Bursfelde, who had already reformed certain monasteries, a holy man and very zealous for the order, was elected at the urging of Jakob, archbishop of Trier. Content with his poverty, he did not consent to leave Bursfelde, lest he seem to have preferred riches to poverty. Therefore he remained in his own monastery, and another was appointed in the place of the first reformer. Since this man seemed comparable to his predecessor neither in learning nor in zeal, he could accomplish little for the continuation of the enterprise begun, nor expand the reform among many. Meanwhile it happened that Nicholas of Cusa, priest-cardinal of the holy Roman Church

Primus aūt burẜfeldie abbas in refor- mationis fuit ioannes monachus de rein- bausen institutus:secundus ioannes de hageniam dictus:tertius vero theoderi- cus quē vidimus:et quartus ioānes qui nūc est in regimine nouiter institutꝰ.Re- formationis nostre origineꝫ fratres cha- rissimi propterea breuiter perstrinximus vt quāto ceperit labore cognoscatis: et vs- qꝫ ad mortē in sancta obseruantia regula- ri constantes perseceretis. Inter omnes em̄ reformationes ordinis nostri que pre- cesserunt nulla fuit vnqͣꝫ regule diui p̄a- tris benedicti magis cōformis et consen- tanca:et a peregrinis adinuentionibꝰ ma- gis aliena.Omnii aliarū pene reformati- onū statuta legimus:sed nulla plus quā nostra cōsentance regule ad puritatē intē- tionis benedicti existimamus.Hec est re- formatio burẜfeldensis in ordine sanctis- sima:que verā et docet obedientiā et custo- dit in humilitate subiectionem.Viuūt in hac sancta religiōe pauꝑes et sine peculio monachit:vivūt humiles:vivūt obedien- tes.veneranda monacho- rū vnio:in qͦ charitas gemiata imꝑat:ohe- dientia militat:humilitas obtēperat:ora- tio vigilat:p̄seuerātia pugnat:caltatas sā- cta triumphat. Hec est schola discipline regularis:institutrix christiane humilita- tis:q̃ mores ad rectitudinē dirigit:et car- nis vicia restringit.Nemo in hac virtutū palestra voluntatē ꝓpriā sequi cōtra regu- laꝫ ꝑmittit̉:nemo bn̄facere prohibet̉.Ad puritatē regule in hac sancta vnione viui- tur:et si quispiaꝫ a semitarectudinis de- uiare ceperit:senioꝝ industria mox ad ob- serantiā iustitie reuocat̉.Regula sa nctis- simi patris bn̄dicti ter publice in anno le- git̉:vt nemo sub ignorantie typo se de ob- seruātia excusare moliat̉.Duo sūt q̄ mihi spē magnā de p̄seuerantia huiꝰ sancte re- formatiōis pollicent̉:annale viꝫ capitulū et biēnal̓ diligēs visitatio monachoꝝ.Al- terū si qd̓libꝫ istorū inter mittit̉:mox refor- matio periclitat̉.Cogitate nuncigił fr̄es charissimi et quātū potestis diligētissime curate:m hoc diui p̄sulis martini cenobi- um sub tā venerāde reformatiōis titulo inutiliter occupetis:qm̄ nisi scd̓m regulā et ordinis statuta:pure:sancte et inculpatē vixeritis:frustra d̓ noīe ꝯfiditis.Dicemꝰ vobis pauca salutis vr̄e monita:ꝑ quorū studiosam obseruantiā reformatiōis nr̄e burẜfeldine et nomē habebitꝭ merito et di- gnitatē.In primis an̄ oīa conatū vrm̄ totꝭ desiderijs ī monasticā ꝑfectionē diri- gite:quē quotiens tepescentē senseritis: mox ꝑ dn̄ice passiōis et mortis innocētissi- me intentā memoria̓ renouate.Nā et si es- se pfecti nō teneamur de necessitate saluti tenemur tm̄ ad ꝑfectionē conari desideri- is totis. Vox em̄ vt monachꝰ conatū ꝓ- ficiēdi abijcit in fouea̓ defectionis cadit. Secundū qd̓ vobis custodieidū sctā cō- suetudo reformatiōis nr̄e istituit:conatū ꝓficiendi in ꝯcepto desiderio fortiter cu- stodit.Hane igit̉ qn̄ suscitati ad primas ꝯsurgitis:ista in secreto faciatis.Cursuꝫ instātis diei futurū examinādo discutite:et qͥd agendū vtiliter infltet prudēter cogita- te.Quā caute velitis viuere diētotū ī cor- dibꝰ vr̄is ꝓponite et anīos cōtra oīa q̄ ad- uersa possent accedere ꝑ pacietiā armate. Quicqd agitis ī feruoꝛe charitatis ꝑfici- te:et oīa verba et facta semꝑ ad dei laudeꝫ ordinate.Tertiū vobis iudicamꝰ vtile et necessariū:vt ꝑ deuotissimas or̄ones au- xiliū in oībꝰ semp̄ studeatis implorare di- uinū.Et valde nobis videt̉ cōueniēs qd̓ sepe diximꝰ et semp̄ admonemꝰ:vt qͦsqꝫ ve- strū admīnꝰ? semel in die dn̄ice passionis agat memoria̓:et ꝓ multis a deo ꝑceptis hn̄ficijs vl̓ vna vice dicat gratiaꝝ actio- ne.Od̓ ut fieri possit ab vnocqͥꝫ vestrū vni- formiter:formā hāc breue̓ quā ordinaui- mus auscultate:et si vultis ꝓ vobis rescri- bite.Adoro:laudo:benedico et glorifico te dn̄e iesu chr̄e fili dei viui saluator et vi- uificatoꝛ omniū fideliū animarū:et ago ti- bi gr̄as ex intimo cordis mei Que sit ordinatio vite monastice bona.

Sermon II. Fol. LXII.

...the legate of the apostolic see to come into Germany; and since he burned with great zeal for our order, he established and introduced many things for its reform. Hearing, moreover, of the good reputation and most fervent purpose for regular discipline of the aforesaid abbot in Bursfeld, he summoned him to himself and appointed him general reformer of the order, and through his diligence reformed several monasteries. On this occasion at last he instituted an annual chapter for the preservation of the reform; he transferred the presidency from St. Matthias to Bursfeld; he obtained from the apostolic see the confirmation of all the things that he had instituted for the good of the reform.

The first abbot of Bursfeld in the reform was John, a monk from Reinhausen, duly appointed; the second was John called of Hagen; the third was Theodoric, whom we have seen; and the fourth is John, who is now newly appointed in governance. Therefore, dearest brothers, we have briefly touched upon the origin of our reform so that you may know with how much labor it began, and so that you may persevere constant in holy regular observance even unto death. For among all the reforms of our order that have preceded, none was ever more conformable and consonant to the Rule of the divine father Benedict, and more alien from foreign inventions. We have read the statutes of nearly all the other reforms, but we judge none more consonant than ours to the Rule and to the purity of Benedict's intention.

This is the Bursfeld reform, most holy in the order, which both teaches true obedience and preserves subjection in humility. In this holy religious life monks live poor and without private property; they live humble; they live obedient. O venerable union of monks, in which twin charity commands, obedience serves, humility complies, prayer keeps watch, perseverance fights, holy chastity triumphs. This is the school of regular discipline, the instructress of Christian humility, which directs conduct toward rectitude and restrains the vices of the flesh. In this arena of virtues no one is permitted to follow his own will against the Rule; no one is forbidden to do good. In this holy union life is lived according to the purity of the Rule, and if anyone begins to stray from the path of rectitude, he is at once recalled to the observance of justice by the diligence of the seniors. The Rule of the most holy father Benedict is read publicly three times a year, so that no one may attempt to excuse himself from observance under the pretext of ignorance.

There are two things that promise me great hope for the perseverance of this holy reform: namely, the annual chapter and the diligent biennial visitation of the monks. If either of these is interrupted in any way, the reform is at once endangered. Consider now, therefore, dearest brothers, and take the most diligent care you can, lest you occupy this monastery of the divine bishop Martin uselessly under the title of so venerable a reform; for unless you live purely, holily, and blamelessly according to the Rule and the statutes of the order, you trust in the name in vain.

We shall speak to you a few admonitions for your salvation; by zealous observance of them you will deservedly have both the name and the dignity of our Bursfeld reform. First of all, before all else, direct your effort with all desires toward monastic perfection; whenever you sense it growing lukewarm, renew it at once by attentive remembrance of the Lord's passion and most innocent death. For even if we are not bound by necessity of salvation to be perfect, nevertheless we are bound to strive toward perfection with all our desires. For as soon as a monk casts away the effort to advance, he falls into the pit of falling away.

The second thing that the holy custom of our reform has established for you to keep strongly preserves the effort of advancing in the desire once conceived. Therefore, when you rise, having been awakened for Prime, do these things in secret. Examine and discuss the future course of the coming day, and prudently consider what useful thing must be undertaken. Set before your hearts how cautiously you wish to live throughout the whole day, and arm your spirits with patience against all things that could come upon you as adversities. Whatever you do, complete it in the fervor of charity, and always order all words and deeds to the praise of God.

A third thing we judge useful and necessary for you: that through most devout prayers you should always strive to implore divine assistance in all things. And it seems very fitting to us, as we have often said and always admonish, that each one of you should at least once a day keep remembrance of the Lord's passion, and for the many benefits received from God should at least once offer thanksgiving. In order that this may be done uniformly by each of you, listen to this brief form that we have arranged, and if you wish, write it down for yourselves: I adore, praise, bless, and glorify you, Lord Jesus Christ, Son of the living God, savior and giver of life to the souls of all the faithful, and I give you thanks from the depths of my heart

for your [return?] afterward into the land of your temporal birth. I give thanks to you, sweetest Lord Jesus; I praise, bless, and adore you for all your labors, journeys, and wearinesses; for hunger, thirst, cold, nakedness, poverty, and want; and for the necessities, injuries, insults, mockeries, and slanders which you sustained throughout your whole life for us, voluntarily and not under compulsion. And as often as you moved your hand to work, your foot to walk, or as often as you opened your mouth to speak, so often do I bless, praise, glorify, and humbly adore you, and with all the powers of my heart I always give thanks to you, mediator of God and human beings, sweetest Jesus Christ. I give thanks to you, Lord Jesus Christ, most merciful king of the heavens, for your most holy teaching, for the establishment of your faith and of the evangelical sacraments, for the calling of the nations, for the justification of sinners, and for all your wonders and powers, and for all your benefits, which you have bestowed either on me in particular or on all others together with me in general. I give thanks to you, Lord Jesus Christ, most kindly savior, for your charity which you had toward the human race, and for your whole most bitter Passion and all the pains which you sustained for us wretched ones. I give thanks to you, Lord Jesus; I praise, bless, and adore you for the sorrow and sadness of your most innocent heart, which, when the time of the Passion was at hand, you sustained for us, when you said to your disciples following you:

“My soul is sorrowful even unto death.” I beseech you, through this sadness of your heart, O Lord God, have mercy on me now and at the hour of my death, and take from me all melancholy and disordered sorrow, granting me at all times a salutary sadness for my sins. I give thanks to you for the sorrow of your most holy heart when, placed in agony, you prayed to the Father as many as three times that he would transfer from you the chalice of the Passion, and, with sweat poured forth in wondrous anguish, you wholly resigned yourself to his will for us. I give thanks to you, O king of heaven and earth, for your captivity, for the insults, injuries, and mockeries which you sustained throughout the whole time of the Passion for our salvation and that of all. I give thanks to you

with immeasurable grief. I adore you, Lord Jesus Christ, crowned with thorns, and I give thanks to you for the piercings and pains of your most holy head, for the blows, spittings, and all the mockeries cruelly inflicted by the impious upon your majesty. I adore you, Christ Jesus, Son of the living God, bearing the very heavy weight of your cross; I adore you, stripped before the multitude looking on; I adore you, stretched out by hands and feet and very cruelly fastened to the cross with iron nails. I adore you, Jesus Christ, eternal king, hanging and dying on the cross for me; and I give thanks for the pains of your wounds, I give thanks for the pouring forth of your most precious blood, I give thanks for your most innocent death, which you voluntarily sustained for our sins and for those of the whole world. I give thanks for your immeasurable goodness, because you called me from fear to faith, because you caused me to be baptized in the name of the Holy Trinity, and because you deigned to call me away from the vanity of the world to serve you in true tranquility of mind, into this holy congregation. I beseech you through your most holy

name, O sweetest Jesus, mediator of God and human beings; I beseech you through the pain of your wounds and through the merit of your most bitter Passion; I beseech you through the pouring forth of your most holy blood and through the power of your most innocent death: grant me pardon for all my sins; pour into my heart the sweetness of your most fervent love; give me

gratiarum actio post matutinas q̄ temporis orandi aprīsimũ est: q̄ deuotione plueuit augere nocturne quietis silētiũ. Dico enim q̄ verū testātur experti: nullas orātiōnes ad impetrādũ efficaciores: q̄ illas q̄ cui dīnice passionis memoria et gratitudine deo patri offerunt. Quartũ q̄ vobis p̄ regulari obseruantiā indicāuimus necessāriũ est: vt in custodia sensuũ vigiletis et teriōũ: q̄ nemo ciuitāte cordis sui bene custodire sufficit: q̄ portas claudere contēnit. Amate silentiũ: q̄ fugite omnes huius seculi tumultũ. Prudentiā sancta cūctis adhibete q̄que facitis: q̄ secretũ amate qui eritis. Monachus enim q̄ publicũ q̄ vagos discursus diligit: verũs obseruantiā amator nunq̄ fuit. Quintũ monēnus vt p̄ sūciōsum animi fugiatis ocii: q̄in hoc pe stiferũ virũ graviũm nutrit vicia: q̄ sē per imundas parit cogitationes. Quicũ q̄igitur virtūtũ amator: propriā salutem diligit: quicũs peruenire ad eternā felicitāte concupiscit: quasi a facie diaboli fu giat ocii: si cupit declinare peccātũ. Se pro ad puritāte obseruantiā regularis de salutis necessāritate requiritur: verũp̄e tatiũ abdicatione vtũb ad mortẽb omnibũ inuiolata custodiātur. Monachus enim babēs peculiũ: iter sibi parat ad infernũ. Qui aut pecūniās recipit q̄ exponit in ce nobio minister sit publicũ: nemo id pre sumere audeat privātũ. Divitiāri pos sēsio nō decet monachōũ: qui dũm iēsũ in paupertāte spiritus imitāri iubentur. Audiamus sanctũ christi apostolũ dicen tẽ: Habentes vicũt ţ amictum his contẽtisũmus. Providemus vobis deo miserante necessaria: non quantũ postulat in ordinate voluptatis cōcupiscientia: q̄ũ in cōtentā paucis requirit natura. Itaç sīcuit vobis habere aliquid sine consensu abbatis non est licitũ: itaç cum ministremus omnia nec necessāriũ. Septimũ q̄od facit monachũ: est humilis obediēntia p̄ ceptoriũ. Nonem verũs monachũ esse po test qui cōtenmit obediēntiā: q̄ negat su perioriũs suis quũ promīsit humilẽ subie ctionẽ. Dic inobediēntiē morbus ex ela tionẽ q̄ superbia mentis oritur quẽadmo duex malo vlcere saniēs generat. Sed q̄ũa scriptura: Adibilis corũ deo q̄ hominũbũ est superbia: q̄ omnis transgressio nis initiũ. Dilitta monachōũ est imita tio christi: qui patri obediuit vtũb ad mo tem, Q̄etavum locũ exornat virũ pul cherrium castritas: qua cōtemta necesse iã est regularis vt omis naufragetur integ ritas. Monachus em de necessāritate sal utis sue vtũb ad mortẽb iubetur caste vi vere: q̄ ab omni pollutione venerea p̄ tuo abstineere. Decem tria sunt vorta mon astice cōuerstationis principalia: contra q̄ ru obseruantiā vivere monachōũ est dũ natio certa. Monachōũ etenim profes sio sub eterne damnationis sententia p̄ ci pit eos vinere sine proprio: sub obediēntiā pastoris: q̄ in perpetua castitate. Uno ex tri bus his ablato: integritas monastica vi o lata est: q̄ damnat transgressio cōtenmen te. Q̄ nono igitur locũ admonemus omi ne hominẽ deo dicatiũ quatenq̄ tantũ ser pentẽ venenosũ: propriā semper cauēat voluntāte: q̄ũ nifi ca omi temporẽ suspe stũ habuerit: facile in fouẽ damnationis cadit. Attendite regulũ: q̄ monachis nec corporis nec voluntatis prũe puniētivũ luntāte. Nemo peccat inuitus. Si volũ ratẽtu deo q̄ abbati tuo in omnibũ perfe cte submisēris: peccātũ facile declinabũs. Decimũ q̄od integritāte obseruantiā regularis cōseruare p̄t in vobis frātres mei charissimũ: est vt in omnibũ aduer sũs ţ contrariũs pacientiā babeatis cōstanti simũ prũp̄or tẽ amorẽ dei. Ast emi paciēntiā virtũs magna q̄ũ tolerantiā alio nomi e vocamus: sine qua nemo tentationũ sua rũ victor euadet. Prũp̄or tẽ dũcit in san ctũ euāgelio dũs. In paciēntiā vestra pos sidebitis animas vestras. Qũid est paci entiā nisi q̄ suas ţ fuouũ inuuriũs ţ cerera queç aduersa pro dei reuerentia ţ amori re eq̄uimũter tolerare? Areditẽ mihi frā tres sententiā apostolũ dicũ: pacientiā vo bũs est valde necessāria: vt voluntāte dei facientes reprotetis reprimiũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũũ

Sermon II. Folio LXIII.

thanksgiving after Matins, which is the most suitable time for prayer, because the silence of the night’s quiet is wont to increase devotion. For I say what experienced men attest to be true: no prayers are more effective for obtaining what is sought than those which they offer to God the Father with remembrance of the Lord’s Passion and with gratitude.

The fourth thing which we have indicated to you as necessary for regular observance is this: that you keep watch in guarding the outer senses, because no one can adequately guard the city of his own heart who neglects to close the gates. Love silence, and flee all the tumult of this world. Apply holy prudence in all things that you do, and love retirement wherever you are. For a monk who loves publicity and wandering excursions was never a true lover of observance.

Fifth, we admonish you to flee the pernicious idleness of the soul; for this pestiferous [unclear] nourishes grave vices and always gives birth to unclean thoughts. Therefore whoever is a lover of virtues and loves his own salvation, whoever desires to come to eternal happiness, let him flee idleness as from the face of the devil, if he desires to avoid sin.

Sixth, for the purity of regular observance, by necessity of salvation, it is required that the renunciation of private property be kept inviolate by all until death. For a monk who has private property prepares for himself a road to hell. But the one who receives and spends money in the monastery should be a public minister; let no private person dare presume to do this. Possession of riches does not befit monks, since they are commanded to imitate Jesus in poverty of spirit. Let us hear the holy Apostle of Christ saying: Having food and clothing, with these let us be content. By God’s mercy we provide you with necessary things: not as much as the disordered desire of pleasure demands, but what nature, content with few things, requires. And so, just as it is not lawful for you to have anything without the abbot’s consent, so, since we supply everything, it is not necessary either.

The seventh thing that makes a monk is humble obedience to preceptors. No one can be a true monk who scorns obedience and denies to his superiors the humble subjection which he promised. This disease of disobedience arises from elation and pride of mind, just as pus is generated from a bad ulcer. But, as Scripture says: pride is hateful before God and men, and the beginning of every transgression. The delight of monks is the imitation of Christ, who obeyed the Father even unto death.

The most beautiful virtue, chastity, adorns the eighth place; when it is scorned, all the integrity of regular life is necessarily shipwrecked. For a monk, by necessity of his salvation, is commanded to live chastely until death and perpetually to abstain from every venereal pollution. There are three principal vows of monastic life; for monks to live contrary to their observance is certain damnation. For the profession of monks, under sentence of eternal damnation, commands them to live without property, under obedience to the pastor, and in perpetual chastity. When one of these three is taken away, monastic integrity is violated, and transgression condemns the contemner.

In the ninth place, therefore, we admonish every person dedicated to God always to beware of so great a venomous serpent: his own will. Unless he holds it suspect at every time, he easily falls into the pit of damnation. Attend to the Rule: for monks are not permitted to have either their bodies or their wills in their own power. No one sins unwillingly. If you have perfectly submitted your will to God and to your abbot in all things, you will easily avoid sin.

The tenth thing which can preserve in you the integrity of regular observance, my dearest brothers, is that in all adversities and contradictions you have most steadfast patience for the love of God. For patience is a great virtue, which by another name we call endurance; without it no one will come away victor over his temptations. Therefore the Lord says in the holy Gospel: In your patience you shall possess your souls. What is patience, if not to bear calmly one’s own injuries and those of one’s people, and all other adversities whatsoever, for reverence and love of God? Believe me, brothers, [and] the saying of the Apostle when he says: Patience is very necessary for you, so that, doing the will of God, you may receive [the promise].

121
Que sint vere humilitatis indicia. mones superant. Affluentia ciborum sermones comitatis inutiles: vino replectus vester imundas concitat suggestiones carnis et libidinis. Si vis esse castus: abstemius esto. Turpissimus est monacho ventri servire et gule: quod pro dei amore cunctis suis mundi voluptatibus renunciavit. Quod decimus quod monachus in observantia regulari facit utile et strenuus: est ut sit diligentissimus circa divinitatis obsequium: Enimvero quod verus dei est servus (quod esse monachus omnes debent) semper in opere creatoris lui feriud: et ut diligat: et quod ubi veraciter novit esse plenitudo se illi deuotione parat in ministerio obsequiosum. Scripturis est enim: Maledictus homo qui facit opus dei negligentemente. Accedetis igitur ad futurum sumi et inconstitabilis dei frateres carissimi: dulciter: sapienter: ferue ter et hilariter psallite: et qua potestis de notione ac puritate mentis creatoris et salvatoris vetro sedulo collaudate. Absit, pucul a cordiis psallentium omnis pigritia: non admittat vila inter laudandus somnolentia quin cui deus sit plens in medio plallentii Decet olim feruozè adesse devotionis animae mori. Quia tenebrae divini obsequiis sunt multa: omnia pura olim feruozè charitatis plenissima: quibus simplice cogitationes loquuntur: et oia debite fiunt. Per contra die completorius et moris decantato monachus ad secretu celiuque veniret: examinet conscientiam suam quid se nego cius occupauit. Hoc fratru colactuuo est burkfeldine reformationis optima atque laudabilis: ut se nulli post completorius superstratu sui plumar reponere: nisi prius conscientiam suam super cõnissis in die culpis vel negligentice diligenterstudie examinare. Qui si offendisse vos habito examine p die in aliq dependeritis: quid faciendu sit docti loqae coluetudine scitis. Occulta moris in crastinu et cotritione humile confessione delata sunt: manifesta vero ad capituli culpauit quod servat quotidiane referenda. Quod mos reformati est ordinis: hec laetitio reformationis: ut culpas delinquentium fratru nunc pinniant crescere: si moris olim ceperint cas curenti amputare. Quondie purgat? est anima: quidie positus scitatis renquandu: qu sicur in eo de statu fi postum: sine mutatio: sifere sic necariu: e nob mete ad pinnu charitas feruozè prino exercicio crebru excitare. Que sint vere humilitatis indicia: Hermo tertius. Amo se vestru amantissimi: prius sui estimatio decipiat: nemo cor suum stulta et iani plumpione seducat. Nò omnes qui videre cupiunt cora deo suum humiles: nec qui tacet ad iniurias semper paciaetes. Verum enim virtutis radices colisit in abscondito cordis: et in sola exterioris demonstratione exhibitionis. Eterni quod si in vobis qui humiles reputari potius esse veraciter apperit: et superbus signa multa: humilitas vero aut nulla aut certe paucissima ostendit. Si patiatur vehemeter nimium errantibus sic ut iure debemus: qui noni virutis habere cupiunt: sed virtute cotentunt. Quò rogò de cipitis misericordia: non vosipso turpiter se ducento perimitis: qui contempta veritatem mendacii amaris. Ut aut sciatis quò superbe vivitis: indicia vero signa vere humilitatis pordimè dicem: quò quaedà in corde duntaxat manet abscondita: quaedà vero etiam erupitia: cunctis intuentibus fiat oportet manifesta. Si hò monachus vero pefecte humilitatis speculuz: in quo singulis diebus respiciens examinet semet ipsum. Primum igitur vere humilitatis indicium in dicu: unusquisque in semetipso pot agnoscer quò se pot cunctis hominibus inferiori et viro: non sermone fucato: sed humili cordis iudicio reputare. Hoc signum punde humilitatis est maximu: vermonachus ad meliori conversatione semper pficiens: inutili se dei servu credat et indignu. Lordis est vera humilitas non sermonis: mensis est studiù non solius corporalis demonstrationis. Monachus ille veraciter est humilis: qui deu sup omnia diligit: qui se ab omni transgressione magistrati dei et reguli puru in omnibus semper custodit: qui magna pietatis et justitie facit opart de se apudse vera estimatione sentit humilis. Secundum vere ac profunde humilitatis indicium ille consequitur: qui bene currès in timore domini ac perseverans suas negleuatiis omnitemporo coraz deo et hominibus confiteretur. Quanto enim plus in bonis operibus profecerit: tanto magis peccata sua et negleuatiis ante meris oculos ponit. Contritionem pro suis deliciis in

What are the signs of true humility.

[unclear] overcome. An abundance of foods [brings with it?] useless courteous talk; your belly, filled with wine, stirs up unclean promptings of the flesh and of lust. If you wish to be chaste, be abstemious. It is most shameful for a monk to serve the belly and gluttony, since for love of God he has renounced all his pleasures of the world.

The tenth thing which a monk in regular observance does as useful and strenuous is that he be most diligent concerning the service of God. For indeed he who is a true servant of God, as all monks ought to be, is always fervent in the work of his Creator, both that he may love, and because, where he truly knows fullness to be, he prepares himself to be dutiful to Him in ministry with devotion. For it is in the Scriptures: Cursed is the man who does the work of God negligently. Therefore, dearest brothers, you will approach the future [unclear] of the supreme and unchangeable God; sweetly, wisely, fervently, and cheerfully sing psalms, and with all the devotion and purity of mind that you can, diligently praise your Creator and Savior. Far, far from the hearts of those singing psalms be all sloth; let no drowsiness be admitted in life among those praising [Him], since God is present in the midst of those singing psalms. It is fitting for souls of devotion to be present with fervor. Because there are many [unclear] in the divine services, all pure, [unclear], and most full of charity, in which simple thoughts speak and all things are done duly.

On the other hand, when Compline has been sung by day and in due manner, let the monk come to the secret place and to his cell; let him examine his conscience as to what business has occupied him. This is the excellent and praiseworthy practice of the brothers of the Bursfeld reform: that after Compline no one should lay himself down upon the coverlet of his bed unless he has first diligently and earnestly examined his conscience concerning faults or negligences committed during the day. If, after this examination, you find that you have offended in anything during the day, you know from learned custom what must be done. Hidden things are to be carried over to the morrow with contrition and humble confession; manifest things, however, are to be reported daily at chapter for blame, as is observed. For this is the practice of the reformed order, this the gladness of the reform: that they do not now allow the faults of offending brothers to grow, if once they have begun to cut them away with care. How is the soul purified day by day? [unclear] as in that state [unclear] without change; thus it is almost necessary, and charity must first be stirred up often by fervent exercise toward [unclear].

What are the signs of true humility: third sermon.

Most beloved, let no one deceive himself by his own estimation; let no one lead his heart astray by foolish and empty presumption. Not all who wish to appear humble before God are humble, nor are those who keep silence under injuries always patient. For the roots of true virtue are hidden in the secret of the heart, and not in the display of outward show alone. For often one who wishes rather to be considered humble than truly to be so appears among you, and shows many signs of pride, but either no signs of humility or certainly very few. If he suffers vehemently and excessively from those who err, as by right we ought [unclear], who desire to have not virtue but the appearance of virtue. Why, I ask, do you deceive yourselves, [unclear] mercy, and shamefully destroy yourselves by misleading yourselves, you who, despising truth, love falsehood?

So that you may know how proudly you live, we shall say plainly the signs and true marks of true humility, because some of them remain hidden in the heart alone, while others must also break forth and become manifest to all who behold them. Let this be for the true monk a mirror of perfect humility, in which, looking each day, he may examine himself. Therefore the first sign of true humility, I say, is one that each person can recognize in himself: that he is able to regard himself as lower and more vile than all people, not with painted speech, but by the humble judgment of the heart. This is the greatest sign of profound humility: that the true monk, always advancing toward a better manner of life, believes himself a useless and unworthy servant of God. True humility belongs to the heart, not to speech; it is the pursuit of the mind, not of bodily display alone. That monk is truly humble who loves God above all things; who always keeps himself pure in all things from every transgression of the command of God and of the rule; who does great works of piety and justice and, by a true estimation of himself within himself, feels humble.

The second sign of true and profound humility is attained by the man who, running well in the fear of the Lord and persevering, would confess his negligences at all times before God and human beings. For the more he has advanced in good works, the more he sets his sins and negligences before the eyes of his mind. Contrition for his delights in

Germo.III. Fo.LXIII. corde gerit continuaʒ: et semꝑ cōpunetus anīo. orās et gemēs ad dn̄o cuʒ lachrymis petit veniā et miseratione. Nec solum ꝓ fuis: ẜ etiaʒ pro totius mundi orat pctīs Maximū cōtra mētis elationē remediuʒ pprioꝝ est memoria delictoꝝ. ¶ Tertiuʒ buiuitatꝭ iudiciuʒ om̄ia que facit opera bona penes se in secreto cōseruare deside rat: et suū pfectū propter humilitatis stu¬ diū occultat. Nō ei vane gloriat̉ qͥ humi lis est: nec laude q̄rit ab hominibꝰ: qͥ gl̓iaʒ sperat eterne felicitatꝭ. Quicūqꝫ se vestrū humilē esse et verū monachum existimat: hoc signū ꝓfūde submissionis et abiectio nis ꝓpter deū nō cōtēnat: ¶ Quartū ve¬ re humilitatis indiciiū ī abyssū cōtēptus suīpsiꝰ volūtarie descēdens. om̄es cōfra tres suos etiā aꝑte peccātes coram deo se meliores existitat: sua mala bonoꝝ obli¬ tus sapienter cōsidetat: aliorū vero inała filētio trāsciens. que fecerint bona oportu¬ ne manifestat. Hec est vere humilitas cō¬ ditio: vt semꝑ alioꝝ opa bona intret̉ et pre dicet: sua vilipendat propter euitationem sup̓bie prudenter et occultet. ¶ Quintū pͥe humilitatis signū cōsecutus. in sua sim¬ plicitate qͥetus est et de alioꝝ defectibꝰ nō loquit̉: nisi vel ratiōe no̓ pōt efficere leniter et mansuete studeat admonere. In¬ crepationes etiā interdū sapiēter dissimu¬ lat: et magis oportunū tēpus exspectat et obseruat. ¶ Sextū humilitatis signū ostē dit̉: qn̄ monachꝰ ad arguēdū et reprehen de̓cuʒ alioꝝ pctā humilitatꝭ amore tardꝰ et nō facilis inuenit̉. Qui etenī veraciter ē humilis semꝑ ppriā infirmitatē cōsiderat et qͣcta cōmiserit ipse cōtra dei iusticiā ma la tacitus in occulto pensat. Hinc aliorū facta rep̄hendere valde metuit: qm̄ se pec catorē et ꝓpterea iudicare alios indignū recognoscit. Monachorū p̄latos atqꝫ re¬ ctores ab hac norma humilitatis ꝓ tāto excipimus: pro quāto eos fore obligatos ad correctionē subditioꝝ sciunt. ¶ Septi¬ mū vere humilitatis signū correptiones et emēdationes pro culpis et negligētijs fuis libenter suscipit: et nullo cōtra repr̄e¬ bendentē se dolore amarescit. Quotiens vero humilis ab aliquo corripitur: cuʒ ꝓ pheta in spū letatur dicēs. Corripiat me iustꝰ in misericordia et īcrepabit me: oleū aūt pctōris nō impinguet caput meum. De sup̓bis vero dicit scriptura. Oderuns corriipientē in porta. Qui vere humilis est corriipientē se diligit: adulantē vero fugit. ¶ Octauū vere humilitatis indiciciū mani¬ feste ostendit̉: qn̄ correptus culpā nō de¬ fēdit nōnegat. nō palliat. nō excusat sed simplici verecūdia cōfitetur. Monachꝰ vere humilis dū corrīpit̉ nō murmurat: se mēsurā equitatꝭ excessisse nō reclamat: sꝫ mox cadens in terrā corā iudice māsue¬ tissime clamat. Peccaui: culpā fateor: ve¬ niā precoremendā polliceor. ¶ Nonum monastice humilitatis indicicū: habenteʒ facit eloquio muteʒ. dulce. modestūqꝫ et in voçe nō clamosum. Monachū quē in lo¬ quēdo clamosū et p̄cipitē videris: non hu¬ milē ẜ sup̓bū et temerariū iudicabis. Hu¬ milis aūt indeste et quasi sub silentio lo¬ quitur: et semꝑ audire paratior quā loqui corā alijs inuenitur. Turpe est monacho vocē nimiū exaltare duʒ loquit̉: quippe qͥ mūdo crucifixus amare silentiū iubetur. ¶ Decimū ꝑfecte humilitatis indiciciū ille possidet qui om̄ia quecūqꝫ audierit de ꝓ¬ ximo interpretari ad meliorē parteʒ soler. Dicit em̄ saluator noster in sancto euāge¬ lio. Nolite iudicare et non iudicabimini. Et iterū. Qua mēsura mensi fueritis: re¬ meiet̉ vobis. Scitūs quoqꝫ apostolꝰ di¬ cit. Nolite ante tēpꝰ iudicare quo ad vs¬ qꝫ veniat dn̄s: qͦ et illuminabit abscondita tn̄brarū. et manifestabit ꝯsilia cordiū. Tu¬ quis es qͥ iudicas alienū seruū? Tuo do¬ mino stat aut cadit nō aūt tibi. ¶ Undeci¬ mū sancte humilitatis indiciciū: nulluʒ ho¬ minē propter quosecūqꝫ excessus in corde suo despicit: ẜ om̄es sibi sactitatis merito preponit. Omnes etiā delinquētes publi¬ ce meliores sibi fore existimat: et ppterea neminē eōdemnat. Quid ip̄e fecerit mali semꝑ in corde secū cogitat: alioꝝ vero bo¬ na prepōderare suis humiliter pēsat. Un̄ neminē spernit. nem inē vilipendit. nemī¬ ne cōtēnit: qͥ saluos fieri om̄es in domino cōcupiscit. Duodecinū ꝑfectū vere humi¬ litatis signū laudari ab hominibus non appetit: ẜ quotiens cōmendatur ab ali¬ quo. cū dolore mentis ingemiscēs erube¬ scit. Cū vero laudes aliorū recitari in con¬ u

Sermon III. Folio LXIII.

...he bears continual [unclear] in his heart; and, always contrite in spirit, praying and groaning to the Lord with tears, he asks pardon and mercy. Nor does he pray only for his own sins, but also for the sins of the whole world. The greatest remedy against elation of mind is the remembrance of one’s own faults.

The third test of humility is that he desires to keep in secret with himself all the good works that he does, and conceals his own progress out of zeal for humility. For he who is humble does not boast vainly, nor does he seek praise from men, since he hopes for the glory of eternal happiness. Whoever among you considers himself humble and a true monk should not, for God’s sake, despise this sign of profound submission and abasement.

The fourth mark of true humility is this: descending voluntarily into the abyss of contempt for himself, he regards all his brethren, even those openly sinning, as better than himself before God. Forgetful of his own good deeds, he wisely considers his own evils; but passing over the evils of others in silence, he makes known at the proper time the good things they have done. This is the condition of true humility: always to [unclear] and proclaim the good works of others, but prudently to disparage and conceal one’s own for the avoidance of pride.

Having attained the fifth sign of pious humility, he is quiet in his simplicity and does not speak of others’ defects, unless, when reason cannot do otherwise, he strives to admonish gently and meekly. At times he also wisely dissimulates rebukes, and waits for and observes a more opportune time.

The sixth sign of humility is shown when a monk, out of love of humility, is found slow and not ready to accuse and reprehend the sins of others. For one who is truly humble always considers his own weakness, and silently ponders in secret how many evils he himself has committed against God’s justice. Hence he is greatly afraid to reprehend the deeds of others, because he recognizes himself as a sinner and therefore unworthy to judge others. We except the prelates and rectors of monks from this rule of humility to the extent that they know themselves to be obliged to the correction of subjects.

The seventh sign of true humility is that he gladly receives corrections and amendments for his faults and negligences, and is not embittered by any pain against the one who reprehends him. Whenever the humble man is corrected by someone, he rejoices in spirit with the prophet, saying: Let the just man correct me in mercy and rebuke me; but let not the oil of the sinner fatten my head. Of the proud, however, Scripture says: They have hated the one who rebukes in the gate. He who is truly humble loves the one who corrects him, but flees the flatterer.

The eighth mark of true humility is plainly shown when, after being corrected, he does not defend, deny, cloak, or excuse his fault, but confesses it with simple shamefastness. A truly humble monk, when he is corrected, does not murmur; he does not protest that he has exceeded the measure of equity, but immediately, falling to the ground before the judge, cries out most meekly: I have sinned; I confess my fault; I ask pardon; I promise amendment.

The ninth mark of monastic humility makes those who possess it mute in speech: sweet, modest, and not clamorous in voice. A monk whom you see clamorous and headlong in speaking you will judge not humble, but proud and rash. The humble man, however, speaks modestly and as if under silence, and is always found readier to hear than to speak before others. It is shameful for a monk to raise his voice too much while he speaks, since, crucified to the world, he is commanded to love silence.

The tenth mark of perfect humility is possessed by the one who is accustomed to interpret everything whatsoever he hears about his neighbor in the better part. For our Savior says in the holy Gospel: Do not judge, and you will not be judged. And again: With whatever measure you have measured, it shall be measured back to you. The apostle also says: Do not judge before the time, until the Lord comes, who will also illuminate the hidden things of darkness and manifest the counsels of hearts. Who are you, who judge another’s servant? To his own lord he stands or falls, not to you.

The eleventh mark of holy humility is that he despises no man in his heart on account of any excesses whatsoever, but sets all before himself by merit of sanctity. He also considers all who publicly offend to be better than himself, and therefore condemns no one. He always considers in his heart with himself what evil he himself has done; but he humbly weighs the good deeds of others as outweighing his own. Therefore he spurns no one, disparages no one, contemns no one, since he desires all to be saved in the Lord.

The twelfth perfect sign of true humility is that he does not desire to be praised by men, but whenever he is commended by someone, he blushes, groaning with sorrow of mind. But when the praises of others are recited in the con...

One sint vere humilitatis indicia. iesum reposuit: omnē huiꝰ vite gl̓iam cōtẽnit. ¶ Tertiū vero supra decimum vere humilitatis indiciū est laudes et fauores nō solũ in veritate mentis contẽnere: sed eos etiā a qͥbus laudari se cōspicit prudē ter declinare. Qui vere humiles sūt laudores suos fugiūt: et quotiens laudant̉ nihil respōdentes obmutescūt. Grauis ē humili magne reputationis estimatio: et tāto plus in semetip̄o cōfundit̉: quāto ab homimibꝰ ampliꝰ p̄dicat̉. Uera na̓qꝫ hu¬ militas vituperata proficit: lauda ta peri culū incurrit. ¶ Quartū post decimū per fectū humilitatis monasticę signū. in cor reptiōibꝰ et detractionibꝰ si quas patitur spūale cōcipit gaudū: et magnum diui ni amoris incrementū. Iniuriatus cōpūgi¬ tur: et ꝑampliꝰ ad mūdi cōtēptum prouocatur. Quotiēs iniuriose ab aliquo reprehendiť: si humilis est: se iuste correptū arbitratur. Nō em̄ suā innocentiā inobiectiōe cōsiderat: sꝫ qͥa deū grauiter in alijs offēderit humili ter et cōpunctus pensat. ¶ Quintū vero post decimū perfecte humili tatis indiciū nūquam se corripiēti recal curat: sed in omni tranqͥllitate animi silen ciū seruat. Uicia reprehensori suo etiā no rissima in faciem nec verbis verba consue uit reprehendere: sꝫ velut mutꝰ ad om̄ia tacere. ¶ Sextū supra decimū .pfūde hu militatꝭ signū cūcta mūdi sola cia despicit et nullas mortaliuꝫ amicitias reqͥrit. Si qͥs venit ad me. et nō odit patrē suū et matreꝫ et vxorem et filios. et fr̄es et sorores: adhuc anīaꝫ suā. non pōt meus esse discipulus. ¶ Septimū vero post decimũ humilitatꝭ signũ. in plura se nō diuidit: hominũ subuentiōes et bn̄ficia magnopere nō requirit: led in sua mediocritate vl̓ etiā extremitate humili ter cōsistit. Animuero qui vere humili tes est mun darioꝛ nō delectat̉ colloquijs qm̄ sepe im pediūt proposituꝫ puritatꝭ. What are the signs of true humility.

has placed [it] in Jesus: he despises all the glory of this life. The thirteenth sign of true humility is not only to despise praises and favors in the truth of the mind, but also prudently to avoid those by whom he sees that he is praised. Those who are truly humble flee their praisers, and whenever they are praised, making no reply, they fall silent. The esteem of a great reputation is burdensome to the humble man, and the more he is proclaimed by men, the more he is confounded within himself. For true humility advances when it is reviled; when praised, it incurs danger.

The fourteenth perfect sign of monastic humility: in rebukes and disparagements, if he suffers any, he conceives spiritual joy, and a great increase of divine love. When wronged he is pierced with compunction, and is all the more strongly stirred to contempt of the world. Whenever he is reproved insultingly by someone, if he is humble, he judges himself justly corrected. For he does not consider his own innocence in the charge, but humbly and compunctiously weighs that he has gravely offended God in other things.

The fifteenth sign of perfect humility: he never kicks back against one who corrects him, but preserves silence in all tranquility of soul. He is not accustomed to rebuke to his face, nor word for word, even the faults very well known in his reprover, but, as if mute, to keep silence about everything.

The sixteenth sign of profound humility: he despises all the consolations of the world and seeks no friendships of mortals. For true humility, which is taken up for love of Christ, delights nowhere except in Christ alone. But he cannot abide in the love of Christ unless he has learned to deny both his own will and the world with all its disordered pleasures. Thus the Lord says in the holy Gospel: If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father and mother and wife and children and brothers and sisters, and even his own soul, he cannot be my disciple.

The seventeenth sign of humility: he does not divide himself among many things; he does not greatly seek the assistance and benefits of men, but remains humbly in his own moderation or even extremity. For benefits received from men he is not accustomed to applaud much, but to show himself grateful in few and simple words. The little gifts of the weak loosen minds, and often render the unwary useless and superfluous in speech. But the mind that is truly humble does not delight in the conversations of worldly men, because they often impede the purpose of purity. The love of Christ does not love publicity.

The eighteenth sign of humility: from the heart he has compassion for all who suffer for the love of Christ, and he most patiently tolerates the defects and weaknesses of others, and prays for the amendment of sinners. For true humility shows to the weak who sin the inward feelings of piety and compassion; but false and simulated humility, because it is truly pride, swells against the frail with hard and undiscerning severity, and becomes the cause of danger to many when, in correcting, it exceeds the norm of the charity of God. But he who is truly humble always fears to exceed the due measure of correction, and therefore is inclined more to mercy than to excessive severity.

The nineteenth sign of true humility: the mind perseveres free from all envy, and favors all men and prays for them. By divine judgment, [unclear] of God favors all, and rejoices together in the perfections of others. He judges no one unworthy of God's benefits; he thinks all better than himself. He regards all as his foremost ones, because he loves all as himself.

The twentieth sign of perfect humility: with bitterness of heart he recalls to memory the multitude of his sins, and therefore considers himself unworthy of every benefit and grace of God. Hence, seeking the depth of humility, he imitates the publican of the Gospel, who, having the memory of his offenses, did not wish even to lift his eyes to heaven. For the monk who is truly humble for the love of Christ always bears in his heart the holy sadness of compunction and repentance for the evils that he has done.

The twenty-first sign of cenobitic humility: he trusts the judgment of others more than his own, and for Christ's sake totally subjects his own will to another's command. When we attend to the signs of monastic humility, we perceive today few observers of it, though we see many monks professing it. O times, O morals, in which we all promise humility, and very few of us truly take care to keep inviolate what has been promised.

Sermon VI. Fol. LXV.

He longs to put on [unclear]: he gladly uses cheaper garments, and takes very great delight in those things which others despise. Fine garments, beautifully arranged, do not befit a monk, but the very cheapest, with which the body may be protected only from the injury of harsh weather. For all fastidiousness is forbidden to cloistered men, since by reason of their profession made before God they are bound to contempt of the world. Humility flees lofty things; it seeks the things that are humble.

The twenty-third sign of the humility of the monastery shows a monk servile toward the brethren and voluntarily devoted to acts of service, and ready for everything whatsoever he may be ordered to do. For true humility obeys even inferiors with a most ready will, and is never indignant against the one who commands. As much as he can, he desires to serve all for love of Christ, since he faithfully loves God with his whole heart. For whatever service he has bestowed upon the brethren, he firmly believes that it has all been shown to Christ.

The twenty-fourth sign of humility a monk then attains in truth, when, for love of God, he delights to take care of the meaner offices in the monastery, which the rest despise. We have read that many have ascended this degree of true humility, and we do not doubt that they are of great merit before God. For the Lord says in the holy Gospel: Everyone who humbles himself shall be exalted; for God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble. The humble monk imitates Christ; the proud one, the devil.

The twenty-fifth sign of monastic humility is, in an assembly of any people whatsoever, always to seek the lower place for sitting, and to prefer oneself neither to an equal nor to an inferior. It is not for monks proudly to contend over preeminence of place, nor does it befit a soldier of Christ to wish to surpass others in honor. For the true monk who loves humility, content with every lowest position, desires to excel no one.

The twenty-sixth indication of humility most especially suits him who, though he is learned and educated, because of the lowly humbling of himself, hides all learning and knowledge. For the monk who is truly humble is always found readier to listen than to speak. For the divine priest Jerome says: A monk has the office not of teaching but of lamenting, that he may either mourn himself or the world, and await the Lord's coming in fear. The arrogance of monks is hateful both to God and to men, and is always liable to sin.

The twenty-seventh sign of humility is perfectly attained by him who, for love of regular discipline, delights more in being silent than in speaking. The humble lover of Christ loves silence, and, lest he offend in speech, is accustomed to say very little. Humility is rarely found among the talkative; and he who is swift to speak casts down his own soul. A talkative and garrulous monk is not without pride, and he who is foolish multiplies words. Whoever desires in spiritual combat to overcome his adversary through humility must not refuse to restrain his tongue from much speaking and from every idle word. It is written in the book of Proverbs that in much speaking sin will not be lacking.

Whoever has attained the twenty-eighth sign of perfect humility will avoid laughter and all [unclear] gestures of those guffawing. Weeping, not laughter, most befits a monk, since he is dead to all the frivolities of the world. For the wise man says: The fool raises his voice in laughter, but a wise man will scarcely laugh silently.

The twenty-ninth indication of perfect humility takes its beginning from the fear of the Lord; for whose honor, as much as he can, it flees and detests every sin. For a monk who does not fear to sin has not truly been humble. But the monk who follows Christ according to his powers in true humility is accustomed to flee every sin, and, as much as he can, to exercise himself in the pursuit of virtues. Humility confesses its sin; and as often as it has offended even in the smallest matters, it does not rest until it has amended all things through true penitence. He who is truly humble is also always found zealous for preserving purity of conscience. For the nourishment of humility is charity, which does not permit the one who has it to be idle.

The thirtieth sign of true humility shows a monk confirmed in the purpose of holiness, and makes him subject to all the brethren, even the younger. Whatever the shepherd commands, he obeys simply; he never debates the precepts of the elder; he does not ask the reason why he commands so. If impossible things are commanded, he is ready in spirit; for whatever is hard and arduous, he is prepared without contradiction. He is directed by the counsel of his shepherd; he believes him, trusts him, obeys him; he willingly is governed by his command. You have now heard, my dearest brothers, the thirty indications of true humility. O good God, where are the works? Which of us will boast that he has true humility, so that in these signs he suffers no defect? [unclear] shame are they

Ho nachi nostri sanctitatē querūt sine virtutā merito: meritū habere volūt sine laboris exercitio: propterea sctūs hodie nō reperit̉ in monasterio. Feruoꝛ scetē compūctionis in multis nimiū est aut rarus aut teptdꝰ: qm̄ vbi carni et sanguini viuit̉: feruor interne charitatis nō habet̉. Nō satīs est tibi o monache qui ꝺe obseruantia gloriaris. nihil habere propriū. feminam nō tangere. sub obedietia pastoris in monasterio refedere. nō māducare carnes: et inceteris que sūt exteriora disciplinę reuātie regularis: ad cuius acquisitiouē cetera omnia sūt principaliter iustituta. Un̄ sine charitate dei nihil tibi prosunt omnia: qm̄ ipsa et vnica est et sola que discernit inferoꝑa bona et mala. O monache monache quicūqꝫ sine feruore charitatꝭ tepide conuersaris in monasterio: putasne quoꝺ exterior apparatꝰ discipline saluū te face re possit? Charitas est que habentē sanctificat: charitas reliquas deo vͥtutes et omniam bona opa comendat. Habeto chari¬tatem: et erunt grata ꝺeo cuncta que facis opera pietatis. De ardua via que du cit ad vitā. ¶ Sermo .iiij. A Udiuistis fratres charifsimi dn̄m nostruʒ iesum christū hodierna lectiōe in sctō euāgelio dicenteʒ Quaʒ angusta est porta et arta via que ducit advita: et pauci sūt qui inueniūt eā. Nonne ipse christus est via: qui dixerat. ego sumvia veritas et vita? At quomodo nunc dicit eā artaʒ euā gelio: cũ ip̄e sit qui dixerat: tollite iugū meuʒ suꝑ vos et discite qͥa mitis sum et humilis corde? Iugū em̄meū suaue est: et onꝰ meū leue. Quid aliḋ est iugum christi: quā arta via et angustatad regnū dei? Quomodo ergo et angusta? Audiat charitas vestra. Iugūdn̄i iesu suaue ē bonis: durū et importabile reprobis. Via christi ad vitā lata est et iocūda exercitatis incharitate humiliꝝ: angusta vero et amara suꝑbis. Nihil estam tam durū nihil tam terribile. nihil taʒarduū: qd̓ amāti deū n̄ sit facile et iocūdū. Rufus nihil est tā leue. nihil tā facile: nihil tā paruū: qd̓ male volūtati n̄ sit graue et onerosum. Idcirco dixit dn̄s. Discite a me qͥa mitis fuʒ et humilis corde. Si vul¬tis portare iugū meū suꝑ vos primo mā/suetudinem et humilitatem cordis mei discite: quoniam nisi mites et humiles fue¬ritis: sarcinam meam quasi graue pondꝰet importabileonus portare minime sufficietis. Dumilis sum via superbos nō capio: angusta sum porta tumidos non admitto. Nisi omnia que mũdana sūt animospreueritis: nisi carnis voluptatibus vimnecessariaʒ diligētia: quasi onussū pec/catis animal ꝑ me ad regnuʒ intrare nonpotestis. Via sum humilis et mitis humilesqꝫ recipio: ianua suʒ arta pauꝑes spiritu et corde mũdos intromitto. Ad vitani eternā fratres ꝑ viam veritatis angustātendimus: oportet vt nobis om̄ia que atam arduū iter sunt necessaria in tempore ꝓcurum? Sunt aūt viatoribus quatuor in primis necessaria: sine quibus ꝑiculosū est iter: et ad scopon raro peruenitur. ¶ Primū quod viatoribꝰ dicimus esse neccessariū: cognitionem esse credimus via/ruā. Nam qui sine cognitione viarum p̄/uia procul ambulare nititur: periculosisquādoqꝫ erroribus implicatur. Aut ergo viam prius discat prudens viatoꝛ aut peritus sibi assumat comitē itineris: ne velmanus latronū incidat: vel a recto itineris tramite recedat. Ad patriam igitur celestis regni cupiētes redire per viā nimisangustam et paucis cognitam: ipsum necesse est itineris habeamus duceʒ et comitem: ihesum christum qui se viam nominauit et veritatem. Extra christuʒ non estvera scientiarꝛ qui christum sui comitemitineris habere negligit. inuanum et sinefructu currit. Discamus ergo viam vitecharissimi fratres sine cuius scientia nemo pertingit ad patriarchad vitam nemoperueniet eternam. Aredamus firmiterdominum nostrum iesum christum vnicum mediatoꝝ dei et hominem. Veruʒdeum et hominem: extra cuius fidem nemofaluabitur: quantumlibet innocenterconuersari videatur. Ipse quippe in sancto euāgelio dicit. Qui credit in vnigenium filium dei: habet vitam eternam in

On the arduous way that leads to life.

our times, in which the charity of many has grown cold; the integrity of holy religion has perished; the devotion of almost all has breathed its last. Our monks seek holiness without the merit of virtues; they wish to have merit without the exercise of labor; for that reason a saint is not found today in the monastery. The fervor of holy compunction in very many is either rare or lukewarm, because where one lives for flesh and blood, the fervor of inward charity is not possessed. It is not enough for you, O monk who glory in observance, to have nothing of your own, not to touch a woman, to reside in the monastery under obedience to the shepherd, not to eat meat, and in the other things that are external matters of regular discipline, for the acquisition of which all other things have chiefly been instituted. Therefore without the charity of God all things profit you nothing, because it alone and uniquely is what distinguishes between good and evil works. O monk, monk, whoever you are who live lukewarmly in the monastery without the fervor of charity, do you think that the outward apparatus of discipline can make you safe? Charity is what sanctifies the one who has it; charity commends the other virtues and all good works to God. Have charity, and all the works of piety that you do will be pleasing to God.

On the arduous way that leads to life.

Sermon IV.

You have heard, most dear brothers, our Lord Jesus Christ saying in today’s reading in the holy Gospel: “How narrow is the gate and strait the way that leads to life, and few are those who find it.” Is not Christ himself the way, who had said, “I am the way, the truth, and the life”? But how does he now call it strait in the Gospel, when he himself is the one who had said: “Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart. For my yoke is sweet, and my burden light”? What else is the yoke of Christ but the strait and narrow way to the kingdom of God? How then is it also narrow? Let your charity hear. The yoke of the Lord Jesus is sweet to the good, hard and unbearable to the reprobate. The way of Christ to life is broad and pleasant to those trained in humble charity, but narrow and bitter to the proud. Nothing is so hard, nothing so terrible, nothing so arduous, that it is not easy and pleasant to one who loves God. Again, nothing is so light, nothing so easy, nothing so small, that it is not heavy and burdensome to an evil will. Therefore the Lord said: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart.” If you wish to carry my yoke upon you, first learn the meekness and humility of my heart, because unless you are meek and humble, you will by no means be able to carry my burden, as though it were a heavy weight and an unbearable load. I am a humble way; I do not contain the proud. I am a narrow gate; I do not admit the swollen with pride. Unless you despise in spirit all things that are worldly, unless [unclear] the pleasures of the flesh with necessary diligence, as [unclear] burdened with sins, you cannot enter the kingdom through me. I am a humble and meek way, and I receive the humble; I am a strait door, and I admit the poor in spirit and the clean of heart.

Brothers, we are hastening to eternal life by the narrow way of truth; it is necessary that we procure in time all things that are necessary for so arduous a journey. There are, moreover, four things especially necessary for travelers; without them the journey is dangerous, and the goal is rarely reached.

The first thing that we say is necessary for travelers we believe to be knowledge of the roads. For one who strives to walk far through trackless places without knowledge of the roads is sometimes entangled in dangerous errors. Therefore let the prudent traveler either first learn the road, or take to himself a skilled companion for the journey, lest he either fall into the hands of robbers or depart from the straight path of the journey. Therefore, since we desire to return to the fatherland of the heavenly kingdom by a very narrow way known to few, it is necessary that we have as guide and companion of the journey Jesus Christ himself, who named himself the way and the truth. Outside Christ there is no true knowledge; he who neglects to have Christ as the companion of his journey runs in vain and without fruit. Therefore let us learn the way of life, most dear brothers, without knowledge of which no one reaches the fatherland, no one will come to eternal life. Let us firmly believe our Lord Jesus Christ, the one mediator of God and human beings, true God and human being, outside faith in whom no one will be saved, however innocently he may seem to live. For he himself says in the holy Gospel: “He who believes in the only-begotten Son of God has eternal life in
